I went to camp for a few years in middle school in North Carolina which was all-girls. We had to wear uniforms and were not allowed to have food in the cabin or make phone calls home. We did have electricity in the cabin, and I ended up with a group of fairly high-maintenance girls as cabin-mates. Four or five of the 8-10 of us in the cabin insisted on washing, blow-drying and straightening their hair every day. Though I, too, straightened my hair fairly often at home (though certainly not every day), all of this personal maintenance seemed completely superfluous to me. It's summer! It's camp! There aren't even boys around to impress! You're going to jump in the lake and ruin your hair this afternoon! All of the hairdryers would frequently cause a fuse to blow in the cabin, and our counselor actually had to make a rule saying that no more than two electronic hair appliances could be plugged in at the same time. I loved camp, but it made me resolve never to go to an all-girls school again or, if at all possible, live with a group of only girls in college, when it came to that. When I was a little kid (about 5 or 6), my mom used to take me and my sister to a park that had a big duck pond. One time we went there and saw a bunch of little boys that had caught a large, white duck and were trying to force it into the water. My mom ran over and took the duck from them. It didn't seem to be able to fly or swim. She decided to bring it home with us, so he stood on the back seat in between my sister and I, quacking occasionally and looking very strange and confused. When we got home, we let him go in the back yard and filled our kiddy pool in case he would try to swim. We named him Mr. Bill. He became the king of our back yard. I was a little afraid of him because I was very short and he was pretty tall: we almost met eye to eye. I had the idea that I would collect all of the feathers he dropped and make a pillow out of them. So, very quietly, I would sneak out the side door and grab a few feathers, but he would always hear me and come charging around the side of the house, quacking, run up to me and nibble on my kneecaps. After a week or so at our house, Mr. Bill still refused to go in the water. Deciding the let him go, my family took him to a different, more secluded park where there were fewer children and released him.

During the summer of 2007, I had surgery preformed on my upper jaw in order to correct a severe underbite brought about by my bilateral cleft lip and palate. The surgery took place at Shriners Children's Hospital in Portland, Oregon (approximately 3.5 hours from my hometown of Yakima, WA). I have had over 20 surgeries with regard to my cleft lip and palate, but this by far was the most intense. The surgery consisted of breaking my upper jaw and bringing it forward several inches. During the surgery, two screws were put in the back of my upper jaw and twice a day after my surgery, I had to manually turn these screws, in order to make sure that my upper jaw did not proceed to move back to where it was prior the surgery. I spent eight days in the hospital post-surgery and a few days over a month in the Portland area (with family) in order to have constant check ups. This month consisted of sleeping in bed and a pure liquid diet, as well as tons of pain! During this month, I lost around 20 pounds. I consider this a self-defining memory as I had lots of free time for reflection during my recovery. Most of this time was spent thinking about my cleft lip and palate. I experienced a wide array of emotions when pondering upon this issue, which I had obviously already done throughout various points in my life. I experienced emotions of anger (for being born with such condition), depression (from being in bed for so long) but eventually settled upon the great opportunity I had to develop perseverance, just in terms of making it through both physical and emotional pain.

Every day brought new sights and new challenges. We would get up early before the sun every morning, the porters were already awake and starting breakfast. We would wash our faces and hands in warm water basins outside of our tents and then drink coca tea with our delicious breakfasts. My family got really close with Vlad. We all would tell stories and laugh, or walk in silence, depending on our mood. Vlad took good care of us, and shared his country's beauty. On our final day, we crested a hill and finally rested our eyes upon Machu Picchu. As great as it was to see it, the entire journey leading up to that view seemed more special than the destination. And it was easy to be a little angry at arriving at our destination because that means that our special time on the Inca Trail was coming to an end. After touring the ruins, we slept well in a hotel with real beds and real showers. The next day, we said goodbye to Vlad and all boarded a train that took us back to Cusco. It was a long ride back. One school morning, I woke up and walked downstairs to eat breakfast. I noticed that my dad's truck was still in the garage, which was odd because he normally leaves for work before I am awake. I asked my mom, "Is Dad taking today off or something?" To which she replied, "Your father spend the night in jail." Surprisingly, I remained calm and simply asked why. She informed me, with a sigh, that my father had received a DUII the previous night, and had spent the night in jail. Dumbstruck, I simply mumbled, "Oh." And continued finished my granola. I blocked the issues from my thoughts that day and did not return to the subject until later that night. I distinctly remember not speaking to my father at all... and vice versa. I remember shooting a series of direct questions at him, like "How high was your blood alcohol level?" and "Why were you driving home at two in the morning?" I remained completely emotionless at his answers. However, I screamed at my mom. I yelled questions, tears pouring down my face. I specifically remember screaming loudly because I wanted my dad to hear my frustrations, as he was down in the basement at the time. I was too scared to yell at him upfront.

The day I came out to someone. I had just turned 18; the Christmas before I had been given a laptop for college. Without telling me, my Dad took my laptop so could install some new programs. While doing so, he found some porn that I had forgotten to erase/delete. He waited to confront me until the two of us were alone outside; he was doing yard work, I was reading. He said that he had found the porn, and was very disappointed, that it was not okay…and that he was going to call my older sister to tell her to stop sending me porn and trying to "convert" me. (My older sister had come out as bisexual two years before and had already been in a relationship; my Dad was convinced she was trying to make me and my younger sister gay by taking us to Pride events.) I had panicked as soon as the topic had come up, but I hadn't said anything yet, so I tried to regain composure and said something noncommittal along the lines of "No, I promise I'll never look at porn from --- again" (she had absolutely never sent me porn, or done anything of the kind). He was seemingly satisfied, and went back to work. I was still in a panic; I had accepted I was gay, but had imagined never telling anyone, especially not my parents. I ran upstairs to grab my cell phone. We live on an old farm; to look busy, I grabbed a random hoe from the shed and headed to the back of our property. There I hid behind an apple tree that had been completely taken over by blackberries, hiding me completely from view. I made a frantic call to my older sister, starting along the lines of, "So you were right: I am gay, but I really need your help right now." I explained the situation to her, and begged her to accept the blame. She was good about it and agreed to help, although I'm sure she had a talking-down about it later. However, the next time she came back from college we snuck off together and had a long talk.

I guess I'm an extremely thoughtful person. I always try to make sure that I'm not putting people out of their way to do things for me. I hate the idea of people spending more money on me or devoting more time to me than that which they feel comfortable giving, and I'm always nervous that people are giving me things out of a feeling of duty. One memory regarding this that, for some reason, I have recalled so many times comes from when I was very young -- perhaps around five. I was with my mom's subordinate, Coleen. My mom has always taken the initiative to really get to know her coworkers and subordinates; they would often come over for dinner or go out to coffee with her. They would also occasionally do something with me. This time, Coleen decided to take me for ice cream. We went over to the TCBY that used to be in Eastgate, and she told me to order whatever I wanted. I remember that my favorite thing at TCBY was a parfait of vanilla ice cream, chocolate sauce, peanut butter sauce, peanuts, reeses, and chocolate chips. I also remember that this decadent display of dessert cost somewhere around $5, rather expensive for ice cream. Regardless, I was five, I had just been told to order whatever I wanted, and I was going to have a parfait. So I ordered. I told the lady who was wearing the traditional TCBY blue apron that I wanted a parfait. Coleen automatically looked up at the menu board, and, seeing that what I had just ordered probably cost double what she was intending to pay, turned to me and said, "Why don't you get the kids cone? When recalling a self-defining memory of myself I think back to my sister and her essay on her personal hero. It was expected that she would write about my mom or dad who are the usual suspects to children but instead she wrote about me, her older sister by more than seven years. I feel that her image of me is reinforced by my parents and not necessarily by me and my actions alone. This happened a few years ago when she tried to test into a well known private school but to this day I still feel pride in myself for being someone's number one role model.

This memory is of me when I was a freshman in high school. I was already playing for the Junior Varsity team and experiencing great success. I was content with my teammates and how the team was doing so much so that the thought of me moving up to the Varsity team that season hadn't even crossed my mind. We had a game against another strong JV team from Grant High School that night and the game was close the whole way. sometime during the third quarter I went on a tear, getting steals and hitting three pointers. We ended up winning the game and I had scored over 30 points. As I ran down the stairs to our locker room with our teammates, we walked into the varsity locker room and the coach asked if I wanted to suit up for the varsity team that night. I was stunned and before I knew it, one of the varsity players threw me their jersey and I was back on the court for the varsity game. It was one of the biggest thrills of my life.

When I was 15, my home had been determined as unsafe due to a possible landslide and so my family was more or less forced to move. We didn't have much time, a couple months maybe, to not only find another home, but move and take any material from our home that we wanted to keep. The week before I started high school was when we finally finished moving into the ""new"" home. My old home was built by my father 25 years before and everyone in my family, at one point or another, had helped work on it. Leaving it was like losing a dear friend. It was everything I had known until that point and I loved everything about it; the layout, the hidden ""gems"" of the house, the surrounding property, my ducks and chickens, the tree-house, etc. My memory is of the last time I left that house, or what was left of it. The home we'd bought was only five minutes away, so the drive was short, but I remember it was late at night and just me and my mom in the car. The feeling of loss, of death, of almost homelessness was overwhelming. Most, in my situation, probably would have cried. I wanted to. I wanted my grief and sadness to be physically expressed. But I couldn't. Nor could I speak. My mom asked if I was sad but I couldn't form the words to answer her. I still wish I could have cried about losing my home.

Throughout my childhood my sister and I never got along. In fact, we fought constantly. My parents became hopeless, as they had tried everything in their power to get us to stop fighting, let alone actually enjoy each other's company. Things didn't change much as we grew up. Because she was 5 years older, she left for college when I was entering the 8th grade. It was the night before she was leaving for college, and I hadn't thought much about it all summer, I was more focused on taking over her room and all the stuff she was leaving behind. But that night for some reason it hit me that my sister was moving across the country and I wouldn't see her for a long time. I started balling uncontrollably, which made her do the same. We just laid in her bed the entire night crying and sharing stories and then laughing about everything we've been through. Since that night, we have been best friends.

I remember, back in middle school, when I was twelve and in the seventh grade. I went to a little tiny school, where there were twelve people in the seventh grade and maybe twenty in the sixth grade. I think an important piece to understanding this story is that I was the popular kid in middle school. There weren’t a lot of us, and I was the smart one, the blonde one, the one who could be friends with anyone. Even among the eighth graders, I was the popular kid. Everyone liked me, everyone knew me, everyone respected me. I had golden middle school years—they weren’t awkward or weird or uncomfortable. I always got along with my parents, never struggled in school, was loved by my teachers. I wasn’t a loud kid. I was quiet. I played by the rules. But somehow I was the kid that everyone wanted to be. I always sort of knew that but dismissed it because the idea made me feel uncomfortable—I was just being me, the way I’ve always been. Being in the spotlight was unnerving so I pretended like the spotlight wasn’t there and went about my life like I always had. There was a kid named Jonathan Mosher in the sixth grade. He was a little kid, and I think he must have had some sort of disorder that made him a little slow with academics, pretty socially awkward, and just plain different. He continually crossed my radar because I always saw him alone and I would feel a pang of sadness that I was walking in the middle of all my friends and he was walking by himself. There was another kid named Scott (I don’t remember his last name…) in the sixth grade and he was the cool kid. One time I walking with all my friends to lunch, and I saw Jonathan ahead of us, alone as always. He had his lunchbox. He was minding his own business, walking with his head down, so incredibly alone. And out of nowhere, Scott appeared and grabbed Jonathan’s lunchbox and pushed him to the ground and actually began to kick him. Jonathan didn’t make a sound. And everyone I was with started to laugh. I couldn’t believe it. And so, being me, I pushed through my friends, grabbed Scott by the arm which caught him totally off guard, and said something to the effect of don’t let me ever see you touch him again. I remember this intense silence that seemed to go on forever and the scene was frozen with Jonathan on his side in a ball on the ground and me holding Scott’s arm and his other arm up as if he was going to slap me and all of my friends behind me. He let his arm down and I let go of his other arm and he walked off. And all of my friends followed him. I watched them all walk by me, no one looked at me. No one said anything. They all left. I picked up Joanthan’s lunch box and helped him up. He never looked me in the eye. But he mumbled thank-you and continued down the hallway with his head down and his lunchbox held in both of his arms against his chest like a shield, alone. I went to the bathroom and threw up. The whole memory is so painfully clear in my mind. It’s like it just happened. Even now, writing this, I feel sick to my stomach. It was the first time I realized just how cruel people can be to those who show any signs of weakness, who are just a little bit different. It was shocking. It was sickening. It made me sad in a way I can’t describe. And now, eight years later, it makes me almost more sick to think that Scott was just eleven or twelve years old. No kid should be able to exhibit such hate and cruelty and they especially shouldn’t be able to manifest it in physical violence. It’s horrifying. What horrifies me even more is that Jonathan never made a sound. How often did that happen to him? He seemed so defeated. It was like he went away to another place when Scott started to kick him. He didn’t fight back, he didn’t cry, he didn’t yell. Nothing. God it makes me sick and actually brings tears to my eyes, to think about him, lying on the ground, so little and so alone and so hurt. Later that day Scott walked up to me and apologized. I told him he should apolo

One of my most poignant memories is one summer night riding in my dad's car with him. We drove to a local ice cream shop to get ice cream, and then just drove around really pretty aimlessly for a while. We were just talking about life and what we thought heaven would be like, and I remember closing my eyes while listening to him talk, and feeling the warm wind in my hair. We were listening to some of his favorite songs on his i-Pod, and even thought it may seem like a really insignificant moment, that is the moment I come back to when I think of complete happiness.

When I was younger I went to a sleep-away camp every summer. Every year I was placed in a cabin with the same group of girls, because they wanted to keep friends together. When I was in eighth grade, about a month before I was to go to my fifth and final year of camp, I received a message on Myspace from nearly all the girls in the cabin. The message told me that they all hated me and pretty much every aspect of who I was (my appearance, my voice, my talents) sucked. They also told me that the boy from camp that I had a crush on hated me. When I asked him about this, he denied it, but then blocked me once our conversation was over, confirming that what the girls had told me was true. I still think of this frequently and have stressful dreams about the camp girls once every couple of months. I believe this is the primary cause for my severe self-esteem issues and insecurity in social situations.

Three years ago I received some devastating news that impacted me greatly. I am a highly competitive soccer player and at that time was playing for three different teams. It was early June of 2008 and I had just completed my club soccer and Olympic Development Program seasons. In my last few games I had noticed an intense pain in my left shin, however there were games to be played and playing through pain was nothing new to me. So after the season was finally over, I went and saw my doctor to address this nagging pain that I had thought was simply bad shin splints. Following my routine x-ray's the doctor sat me down, what happened next shook me and would shape the next 6 months of my life. That nagging pain that I had played through turned out to be a grade III stress fracture. I was told no running, no soccer, no nothing for the next 4 months at minimum. I was beyond devastated, soccer was my life and I just had that ripped away from me for the immediate future. Not to mention my whole summer was thrown off. That moment in the doctor's office when he broke the news I doubt I will ever forget. I went in expecting to be told rest and ice for the next couple days and I'd be fine, and left with instructions to not run for at least 4 months.

I have been unfortunate enough to have known a lot of people who have died at a young age. This includes friends who have committed suicide, a family friend who died of a drug overdose, and some children who lived at the home where my mom worked as a nurse (an adoptive home for the care of multi-handicapped children). The first death of a close friend happened when I was only six years old, and he was seven. He had fetal alcohol syndrome, which caused heart disease, delayed development and facial deformities. In addition, he was fed through a gastric feeding tube because he couldn't eat. We were very close friends from when I was four years old to his death. I went to work with my mom often, and outside of school, he was the closest friend I had that I was able to see all the time. We would play inside and outside together, watch movies, and have as much fun as two kids at that age could have, despite his disabilities. Of course, at the time I was unaware of all of his health problems and what they meant. He had to have cardiac surgery at the age of seven, and tragically passed away on the table. My mom explaining to me that he had died was one of the earliest vivid memories that I had. I of course didn't understand at first, and I remember crying when I realized it meant I would never see him again. I remember hugging his adoptive mother (my mom's boss) at the funeral and being so surprised to see so many sad adults. I believe this experience was one of my first exposures to reality when it comes to death, or at the time, what it was like to have someone who was always there not be there anymore. It definitely helped me understand the concept of death, appreciate life, and, sad to say, it prepared me to deal with other deaths that happened in the future. Luckily, besides grandparents, I have had no immediate family members pass away, but by the time I was a teenager I had known more people who have died than any kid should have.
Waking up to find my mother sitting at the edge of my bed early in the morning to tell me that my grandmother had just died from a battle with cancer.

When I was in the Czech Republic visiting my cousin who was teaching English there, I remember we would go out to bars and things at night, and though I had a lot of fun I often felt very uncomfortable, because I was only 16 at the time. A particular night was the second night that i was there and we went to this bar with her students for one of their birthdays and the entire time they were talking in Czech so I didn't know what they were saying, but I know that there was smoke everywhere, and finally at the end of the night my cousin told me that they had been smoking pot, because it is legal there, but I remember realizing that I had not been exposed to many things before in my life.

I can remember my first visit to the Boston Children's Hospital when I was much younger. I had been diagnosed with sensorineural hearing loss at the age of two, but this is the first appointment that I can vividly recall with regards to this diagnosis. My mom and I spent the entire day at the hospital as I was taken from room to room for various speech, hearing, and cognitive tests, and I remember growing more and more frustrated with each one. I was uncomfortable and surrounded by various medical students and doctors whom I'd never met until now, and the distinct impression that I got from this testing was that there was something wrong with me. The last phase of the testing, which involved one of the doctors interviewing me and my mother, resulted in my breaking down in tears, exhausted and irritated. To this day, even as an adult, nearly every single one of my audiologist appointments ends in tears and frustration, especially if there has been even the slightest of changes in my hearing. I can trace the discomfort I have with any audiologist or hearing related appointments to that one day spent at Boston Children's Hospital more than 15 years ago.

Last year as part of the Connecticut College Men's Lacrosse team we had our best season ever in college history. We finished as the number one team in the NESCAC during the regular season and went on to make the NCAA tournament. This is a self-defining memory for me because I was able to be apart of something that was bigger then myself. I had worked for 16 years of my life playing lacrosse for majority of the year and last years performance made all of that feel worth it for me. However, we lost in the first round of the NCAA's and it just goes to show how hard it is to reach an elite level at something and you must never quit and even if you work incredibly hard it still may not work out the way you dreamed it or wanted it. Last year was incredibly rewarding but a learning experience in the same.

The night of senior prom in high school, we had an afterprom that went until 5am the next day. Me and my friends decided we wanted to play sunrise frisbee, so we did that as soon as the afterprom ended and then went and got bagels at a local shop. After that, basically everyone decided to go to sleep except me and my friend Katie, who decided to go to the beach. Now, I hadn't known Katie very well for very long, and I had a bit of a crush on her, so this was a pretty cool setup for me. We spent 8 hours on the local beach just sitting and talking, and trying to keep from falling asleep. Just cause, no real reason. I'd been having a really hard time with some other stuff in my life at that point, and it was just one of the most relaxing, happy days I can remember. Obviously anytime you get to just hang out with your crush thats awesome (and cheesy, but whatever, everyone can relate), but combined with the whole prom night feel and everything it was just a very unique experience that helped me decompress.

A few years ago, I played an online multiplayer game (MMORPG) called Maplestory. I have many, many fond memories from the game, which I did play extensively for about two years, but the fondest ones are those that involved the escapist properties of video games. For instance, I distinctly remember one day in middle school when I feigned sickness to get out of going to school and waited in bed for my parents to leave for work. As soon as I heard the car pull out of the driveway, I scampered over to the computer and hurriedly started up the game. I remember finding a music video of someone playing the game to Holiday by Linkin Park and one other song I didn't like nearly as much, but I still played the video over and over because listening to Holiday in the background while climbing up and down a castle and bashing monsters with magic spells was just too amazing a feeling. I felt free, no parents, no school, just me and my in-game avatar kicking ass to some rock music. Of course, when my parents got home, I was forced to log off, but I still remember that as one of my fondest gaming experiences, if not experiences in general.

When I was 16 I was involved in a serious bicycle accident and since then I have had retrograde amnesia for all explicit memories that were formed before the event. One of the most defining the memories I have of my self, was two months later when I was sitting in my room and first able to really comprehend the frustration I felt towards the duplicity of what my life had become. I was feeling very angry that people I supposedly knew thought it was appropriate to push the values, ideas, or interests I supposedly held onto me, and didn't realize that I was a new person. I realized that the people around me genuinely thought the best course of action was to help me recover to my former self, and that this would always be in conflict with my desire to become my own new person. This realization helped me to respond in more positive way to the people influencing my life instead merely becoming angry or frustrated.

I played soccer through most of my youth. I was a goalie, and my dad was my coach during the regular season. When I was around 9 I think, I started getting really good. I hadn't played goalie before, but the position really clicked with me - I had good hand-eye coordination, and would charge out of the goal and tackle the ball, or take it out from girls' feet. The all star coach talked to me during one tournament, and really gave me the impression that he was very impressed with me and planned to offer me a spot on the all star team (the year before I was only an alternate). I was so excited. But then my letter came, and I was only an alternate again. I found out that he offered the goalie position to a girl who wasn't as good as me - she was his girlfriend's daughter. I was livid. I joined a tournament team of the "alternates", and a couple months later we ended up playing in a tournament against the all star team from our district. It was the ultimate showdown, and we were the rejects. I decided to get my revenge. I played my HEART out - all of the best scorers were on their team, and I was jumping and diving and blocking shots left and right. They spent almost the whole game on the offense, but I blocked EVERYTHING. I could see the parents and coaches twittering - they knew I deserved a spot on that team. The game ended 0-0, entirely because of me. I was so proud. My dad was really proud of me too - he knew, like I knew, that we had sent a clear message. The coach (of a team of 9 and 10 year olds!) had played favorites and didn't give me the place I deserved. I remember my uncle doing a play-by-play at his house after the game.

When I was twelve we had a family gathering at my house for Christmas. I remember I had opened my presents earlier that day and had received a monopoly board game. At some point at least 7 members of my family were playing and I was the banker. The game was dragging on and I was losing. I attempted to make a shifty exchange and grab a couple extra hundreds in the process. My aunt noticed and called me out on it. To this day, it still comes up that I cheated on that game.

this is actually the first memory i have. i was about two and a half, i was in the car with my dad, i asked him to turn on the radio, he did, i said no the other radio, so he changed the station, we did this several times until he finally asked what radio did i want, we'd tried a lot of them couldn't this one be okay, i said no, i wanted the radio that played satisfaction (as in "i can't get no satisfaction" by the rolling stones, my favourite song at the time) and he laughed at me and tried to explain that every song in the world didn't have it's own radio station. i remember being a little upset but not saying anything.

After I was raped I went home. I don't think I've ever felt so confused. I was in a really bad place. I didn't really understand what had happened or who's fault it was. Then my friend Lily told me that Tyler had said that I "took of his belt with one hand." That was a lie, and I knew it was a lie, and it was something I could hang onto when I was feeling really confused. But that lie helped me to lay claim to the fact that something very very wrong had happened. I went back to that house and I asked to talk to Tyler outside. He didn't want to talk to me. He refused until his friend said "talk to the woman!" I told him what he had said to Lily and how it wasn't true. He said "We fooled around. What's the big deal?" And I, in one sane glorious moment of knowing the truth, said: "I didn't want to, and you knew it. That's the big deal."

I was sitting in the classroom used for speech and debate. The speech coach, Gorne, had told us to come to meet the debate coach. He didn't work at the highscool - he is a lawyer in Seattle. I remember my first impressions of him. He was super direct but kind of odd. And I remmber really, really wanting to impress him. I made sure I asked the best questions and I was so determined to do as well as Felicia and Tulley, the two current debaters on the team.

It took me a long time to realize why I was so unhappy. But once I did, I refused to admit that there could be a solution. It was a internal battle, and I didn't know what to do, it stuck me into a state of confusion, and a stale-mate, for over 2 years. I was 18, and on my way to meet my parents in hawaii. I had just gotten an iPhone and decided to download a season of a show I had never seen to pass the time on the flight. I chose one called South of Nowhere, and made myself comfortable after takeoff, ready to enjoy this new show. I knew it was about teenagers and love, and figured I would really enjoy it, but I also had an idea in the back of my mind, that it might mean more to me than that, and that I might know more about the show that I was letting on, even to myself. After just the first episode, I knew, it was a coming out story. Since I had already bought the whole season I might as well watch it right? it didn't mean that I was gay too, right? on that trip I watched 3 seasons of South of Nowhere, read message board posts and explored the idea that had always been sitting just out of conscious reach in my mind. Me and a friend had just "broken up," and I thought about her constantly, I was devastated, more so than any relationship with a boy had ever made me. I admitted to myself on that trip, that I had feelings for her, feelings for a girl.

When I was in 3rd grade, when my family and I lived in ironwood, MI, my dad had a porn stash. My dad was a single parent raising his 3 children. I knew where he kept his porn and I read them quite frequently. However, one day my sister and I burned his porn stash outside. We left him a note on his pillow saying that we had burned his porn magazines. He later talked to me about the note incredulously, "Lauren, are you talking about your YM's?or other teen magazines? Those aren't porn."

The first time I tried pot was when I was fifteen. Most of my friends had done it and I felt the it was probably something I should at least try before I died. I was over at my friend Luke's house when I tried it. Luke had been my closest friend since I moved to Seaside when I was four and he was also the friend who had had the most experience with drugs and alcohol. We were standing on his balcony overlooking the ocean, when he started making a pipe out of an apple. He took out his sack and loaded the bowl as I had seen him do before and he started smoking. He didn't offer it to me because I had turned him down each time before, but was pretty stoked when I asked him if I could try it. I didnt' get high that time because we didn't smoke enough, but I didn't mind smoking as much as I thought I would and decided that next time I did it I was going to get as high as I could, whatever that means.

I am in class, reading under my desk. My teacher comes up and takes my book away. She asks me to pay attention and a simple question about the material we are studying. I answer it correctly. My heart beats in my chest and I flush with pride. When she walks up to the front of the room, I take another book out of my backpack.

Every summer since I was five years old, three of my friends and I would spend a few nights at a cabin in the mountains with one of my friend's grandmother. I have countless memories from these times, but one of my favorites is this. We're all lying in our bunk beds in the bedroom and the room is almost completely dark, except for the flashlight that the grandmother, Shirley, is holding. She's reading aloud to us from a novel - I don't remember its title, but it was about a young man living near the ocean. The girls are dozing off, comforted by the sound of her voice. When she stops reading, everything is completely silent except for the faint sound of wind in the pines around the cabin. One of the girls sleepily asks Shirley to sing a song, and so she begins singing an old Appalachian folk song in her husky voice, until we're all asleep.

I was in the best shape of my life. Running faster than i had ever run before. i was number one on the cross-country team for junior varsity. it was the day before the manchester invitational and i was going to lead my girls across the finish line. we were doing one of the easier, slow-paced two miles runs the day before the race. we weren't a quarter of the way done when i saw a friend of mine on the same street walking home from school. i immediately started waving my hands and jumping up and down (dancing almost) to get his attention. what i didn't see in from of me was a massive pothole. my foot went right into it in the wrong angle and i sprained it. the worst sprain i had ever had before than and still to this day. i never got back to my place in the roster after that and never ran as fast again.

After a rough night in high school, one of my best friends and I went for a walk. We talked about everything that had been going on, our annoyance and disappointment at the results of senior awards night, our desire to do well. At one point, I told him, tearing up a little, about how much he meant to me. He then told me that when he came out, I was the only person that really made him feel accepted. I was shocked, because I didn't remember doing anything in particular to help him, but it was nevertheless one of the most powerful things anyone had ever told me. The last thing I remember was that we both cried.

I went to UW my freshman year of college. I loved so many things about that year that it is always difficult to explain to someone why I transferred to Whitman. But I can trace back my decision to one memory. I was in the Quad sitting on a bench. I don't remember what I was doing, perhaps writing or reading. I start to daydream and people watch as students and adults walk by. Then I see it. I see something that just screams college. A barefoot girl rolls by on a skateboard. It's not something I see a lot of at UW. But I love it, and I realize that I need to be somewhere where that is the norm. I need to leave this campus and go to a campus where things are a little funkier. A college where I can be free to go to class barefoot on a skateboard. Why not? My life is now in my hands. I can change directions if I want to.

When I left for college, I didn't expect to be homesick. I had been itching to leave my hometown since I was born, and having spent a year on exchange in high school, I didn't think there would be any sort of separation issues with my parents. When I hugged them good-bye at the end of freshman orientation, however, I noticed that my dad was not speaking normally, and eventually he started crying and had trouble letting go. Never having seen my dad cry, I was really surprised and a little scared. Upon returning to my room I felt something I hadn't felt before, and to this day I have trouble identifying exactly what those feelings were.

The day I told my family I was gay. I had come back from freshman year and was working in the evenings for the summer. My Dad had been acting strangely lately, but I couldn't attribute it to anything in particular. I was watching a Barbara Streisand film (Yentl, a gift from a gay best friend at school), and he came in at one point and started watching it with me. That wouldn't have been so strange - he was a Streisand fan himself, and I really became interested in her when he received her Christmas album as a present - but he was obviously "making an effort". I hadn't intended to watch the whole thing, since I was supposed to go to work soon, so after a bit I turned the film off and went to go change. My Dad decided this was a good point to come vacuum my bedroom; I was mildly annoyed, and asked him to come back when I was done changing. He left in a huff (I definitely knew something was up at this point), probably thinking he had to come back so I had time to hide incriminating evidence à la laptop episode. Very soon he returned, and in a terse voice announced that he had "known for some time that I was trying to join the gay community". I was stunned - I still had thought I would never tell my parents, even imagining deathbed scenes where I didn't tell them. I told him he had picked a strange time to talk about it (I was still only half-dressed and without a shirt), but I had been out at college and to friends long enough to want this to be a positive moment, so I went up to him and hugged him, but he didn't hug me back. I still had to go to work, so I dashed off to make it in time. I didn't give up right away. I couldn't reconcile my sexual desires with my religious convictions. I told him, "I can't sleep with you until I can feel like what I'm doing isn't a big 'fuck you' to God." I'm not fully sure how the change happened. But it did. When my great-aunt died when I was 12 years old, my entire family traveled to Schoul, Switzerland to mourn her death. Schoul is a very important place for us--we still have relatives there, and those of us who moved to the U.S. still have a strong connec

It was section preliminaries during my senior year of varsity swimming in high school, and I was swimming against Natalia Gonzalez from our biggest rival school, Blake. It was the 200 free relay, and I was so sick of swimming distance races that by the end of senior year, it had become my favorite race because it was such a sort period of intensity. I was full of adrenaline as I dove into the water. My first thought was of fear that my toes had left the block too soon and we'd be disqualified, but that thought occupied my mind for only a millisecond before I realized I was full of energy and keeping up with Natalia. Natalia was fast. I couldn't feel the pain or strain in my muscles, just adrenaline as I gave the race everything I had. When I reached the wall, I was relieved the outcome of the race no longer depended on me as my teammate dove over me and raced down the lane. I looked at the time board and my heart leapt when I saw the time. I'd gotten down to a 25-second range 50 free, and for a second I thought I was looking at the wrong lane's time, and then I worried the touchpad had malfunctioned and mis-timed me. Only when I checked with my coaches did I let it sink in that it was my actual time.

I was at a basketball camp at Western Washington University over the summer between fifth and sixth grade. i was there with my team and I was staying in a dorm with the coach's daughter. I had a lot of fun during the day, but at night I couldn't fall asleep. I got so homesick that I called my mom up in the middle of the night and made her drive an hour and a half to pick me up. Although she tried to convince me to stay, all I wanted to do was go home. I remember feeling so embarrassed about leaving the first night. However, I had always had a hard time sleeping over at people's houses. I always got very homesick when I thought I was the last one to fall asleep. I remember I used to beg myself to fall asleep.

When I was in the 6th grade we had an assignment to make a book of poems that we had written. I included in mine the lyrics to the theme song of a show I loved because I loved it and felt it represented me so well, damned if it was cheating. My teacher either recognized or knew it was too good to come from a 6th grader, and this self-defining memory is when she pulled me aside and asked me questions trying to have me fess up. I wouldn't, and I got more and more entrenched and creative in my defense until she finally had to point blank tell me she knew I didn't write this. And the rest of that experience was just drowned in shame. Over the next hour I think I was made to call and tell my mom, and talked about what should happen next, and finally wound up in my science class, but that's all a blur of shame. The moments of terror leading up to the confrontation remain very, very clear. I remember the awkward positions of my hands and legs, the way my teacher leaned forward, the steel of her eyes, and I can almost feel the blood rushing out of my face. It's an experience that's made it pretty much impossible for me to cheat on anything sense- if I ever did, it'd just trigger those same moments of humiliation.

Another memory I have is the day I graduated high school. It was a sunny morning and we had the ceremony outside. I graduated fourth in my class so was seated in the front row. About 800 kids graduated that day. I remember walking out and down the senior steps to our seats and I almost began to cry. We were seated and the ceremony began. I had to introduce one of the guest speakers and my legs were shaking beneath me as I spoke in front of thousands of people. I was seated next to my best friend and we cheered people on as they went up onto the stage to get our diplomas. When I finally receive mine my chemistry teacher was at the bottom of the stage, taking pictures of everyone. My family came over to my house afterward to celebrate and a couple of my close friends stopped by. We all went out to dinner later that night to celebrate.

A memory I remember very vividly was when I first started reading Harry Potter. This memory is very important to me because Harry Potter was a huge part of my childhood and I sort of grew up with the characters and books. Also, reading Harry Potter was the first time I really enjoyed reading and now it is a big part of who I am. I remember my sister had really wanted to read the first book to me when I was like 8 and I remember that I didn't want to hear it because I thought it sounded dumb. I went in my room and started playing with my action figures but my sister wouldn't give up on making me read it so she started reading it really loudly from the other room so I had to hear it. I remember that after a while I got so engrossed in it that I left my action figures and agreed to read it with her. After that I fell in love with the series and read each book as it came out.

In high school, I had just transferred for my sophomore year, and I decided not to take Honors Chemistry, the only Honors course offered for sophomores, because I had struggled with science courses in the past. All of the ""smart"" students in my grade were taking Honors Chemistry. This same year, we took the PSAT's, and I got the 2nd highest score in our grade. One day at lunch, a group of sophomores (including myself) were sitting around, discussing who the smartest kids in the grade were. I was sitting quietly in the corner, and one of my friends mentions that I am one of the smartest kids, because I had really high PSAT scores. Almost immediately, an acquaintance (who wasn't in any of my academic classes) chimes in, and declares, ""NO, she is NOT that smart!"", presuming that because I wasn't in the difficult science class, I must not have a brain. I stormed out, and went to the library and cried, but I knew how much I was capable, more than this girl ever would. Later on, this same girl TANKED the SAT's, and got wait-listed at a college that I got accepted to with flying colors. Recalling this memory, I feel vindicated, and people should not be so quick to judge.

When I was in the 5th grade, one of my classmates was passing out these Dunkin' Donuts breath mints to people in line about to go to Art class. Our teacher was on the other side of the classroom and concerned about what he was distributing. She asked a couple of people at the front of the line. No one answered. She got really angry when she finally asked me and I told her, oh, so timidly: ""He was passing out mints."" She praised my honesty and said I set an example for the class. I didn't feel like I deserved any praise at all. I simply did what was asked of me and what was right. I didn't think any of it was a big deal, but strangely, it was.

When I was in pre-school around age 4 or 5, my mom's car caught on fire while we were in it. My mother, my sister, my older brother and I were driving to bring my brother to a doctor's appointment in town. I had talked my sister into bringing some of our favorite toys (stuffed dog, plastic trucks of mine, etc) on the ride because doing errands with mom was always boring. While we were driving, the car apparently experienced electrical problems and the rear windshield wiper started swiping back and fourth at its fastest speed on its own, and my mom couldn't stop it. Then, she rolled down her window and it wouldn't roll back up. We had arrived at my brother's appointment and, not yet parked but just driving in the parking lot, and my smoke started rising from the dashboard. My mom turned off the car and called someone about what to do. They said not to move the car, by my mom needed to get out of the way and pull into a parking space. When she turned on the car, flames came out of the dashboard very fast. We were in an old dodge caravan, and I was in a booster seat on the side that didn't have a sliding door (only one on the right side of the car). My mom was able to pull us out pretty quickly, but I remember running from the car and seeing the biggest fire I had ever seen (it burned very quickly). I had trouble dealing with situations as a kid so I was freaking out, but some girl in the doctors office sat my sister and I down and read us a story while my mom dealt with everything with the car. My sister was more traumatized over the loss of all the toys we had, and blamed me for making her bring them. What got me the most was seeing the skeleton of the car after, and how it was able to just disintegrate like that. I was very afraid of fire for a long time after that, always worrying about the smoke detectors in our house, making sure I could open the window to my room, etc. I believe this event made me overly cautious as a kid, and I will never forget that.

In my sophomore year of highschool I was in an emotionally abusive relationship. My boyfriend would take his anger or discontent out on me, telling me that the problems in his life were my fault. At the time I believed him and felt guilty for what he was feeling. This continued on and off for several years until I was finally able to stand up for myself and end things officially. This was the best thing that could have happened because the relationship was making me depressed and taking a toll on other aspects of my life. Being in this situation has made me wary of relationships and unable to connect to one person for a long period of time.
When my sister was first born, I recall the first time I carried her on my own and looked in her eyes. The instant we made eye contact she gave me a little smirk.

This sounds silly but I remember it having a big affect on me at the time. In 4th grade my male friend told me never to wear leggings again as pants. I think it may have sparked an unhealthy relationship with food because I thought he was calling me fat. I think back to that memory sometimes when I see girls wearing leggings, and I think about how simple remarks can have a big affect on self-esteem.

I remember the first day I came to Whitman. My mom and I started unpacking things in my Jewett bedroom, and I guess my younger brother must have been there too. I just met my RA, and there were a few other people around. I was about to meet my roommate who I was intimidated by because I saw her myspace profile (I think it was before I had facebook...) and it said she was working for an important government agency and looked very important. I was wondering who she was and if we'd get along before school, but when she saw me and my mom standing in the dorm room, unpacking, she got very excited, ran at me, and hugged me. Later that evening, I told my mom that she could leave, and my roommmate and I jumped around because we were so excited that we were finally at college, and (more) independent. I think we might have even jumped on our new beds. I might have helped her make her bed, and then we both went out to dinner with my new RA. I didn't realize this would happen, but she paid for our dinners. We ate at the Mill Creek Brew pub and I thought my food was really good. I can't really remember who else was there, but it might have been other residents or maybe other residency staff.

I got caught shoplifting. I had done it a lot before that, but there was a special tag that I didn't notice, so the beeper went off when I went through the sensors. I remember the day that my first boyfriend broke up with me. I had been upset ahead of time because I did not think that I did well at a choir audition and was homesick. Because I was already upset, I had driven my car to Wildwood Park and sat in my car and cried. My boyfriend then called me on the phone and said that he didn't think he wanted to enter college in a relationship. I remember that I was looking at the side mirror in my car as he said this. I almost couldn't believe it. I felt completely nauseas. I just started to cry harder and harder into my phone. I told him that I would call him back and then I called my mom. Thanksgiving break of sophomore year of college, I came out to my best friend from high school. I am not one who shares his innermost feelings and thoughts with others. It is definitely a big step, especially something this important to me. It also was the gateway that has allowed me to become comfortable with myself as a bisexual man and that allowed me to share that part of myself with others. It is hard to be yourself when people don't know who exactly you are. My parents were out for the evening, and it was just me and Brittany sitting upstairs in my kitchen. I popped a bottle of Martinelli's Sparking Cider (because we were under the legal drinking age of course) and asked her what her New Years resolution was. I then told her what mine was: "to be true to myself," and then I told her about my sexuality. She of course laughed, hugged me, told me how happy she was, and that she had always know.

I attended a private Christian school for my sophomore and junior years of high school. During the second to last week of school every year, the school would have an assembly recognizing the top students in each class provided at the school (it was a small school). During this ceremony, I received recognition for each class that I was in (I was also introduced into the National Honor Society). It was great to feel such accomplishment and be recognized for such academic achievement.

As a child, and even preteen, I was really attached to my mom. I would cry all the time when she went to work and had a hard time spending the night at anyone's house because I didn't want to be away from her. My mom has always had a huge self-confidence issue, and it's affected the way she sees herself as a parent. I recall being very upset one time about something and her sitting on my bed next to me while I was crying, trying to comfort me. Then she began to cry too and asked me if I thought she was a bad parent and told me that sometimes when she feels like she's failed she goes into the bathroom and sits in the bathtub and cries. There was a point when I talked to my mom and trusted her with everything and wanted to go to her with my problems, but I don't anymore. When I hear girls say "My mom is my best friend," I'm jealous. I stopped telling my mom about my struggles and concerns because I decided that she might think that I was struggling not because I was a kid and that happens, but because she had failed as a parent, and I never wanted to be the reason she felt that way.

My first day at Whitman I was so anxious and excited to meet new people but I've always been a shy child so I was not that talkative. My grandparents drove all the way down here with my sister, who lives in Seattle with her father. There was a lot of people throughout the dorms; it was exciting because I rarely went anywhere without my family. It made me very anxious because I was scared to become an adult. The hours on my clock made me apprehensive as each tick reminded me of them leaving and then I'd be all alone. I remember going to a five-week summer program that intended to teach me about "College Life" but with it becoming reality caused it to be overwhelming. An adult at 17.

Last summer I lived with my sister in Boston. For the most part it was great. But we were pretty much forced (by some strange sister God) to do everything together. We shared a bed, we spent the weekends together. We had dinners together. We went grocery shopping together. I had very little time to myself outside of my job. The few times included the one day a week off that my sister had to work, and my commute to and from work. During those times to myself, I enjoyed reading or exploring new places. I liked to be spontaneous and not plan where I was going. My sister got in the habit of meeting me after work so that we could ride the T together back to our apartment. I was sort of ok with this because I knew she enjoyed it. But the time after work was the time I really needed to myself. It was the time to unwind and not think of anything. It was also a time that I could do whatever I wanted without having to discuss plans with my sister. One time, after a particularly challenging day at work, my sister called me and told me that she was going to meet me. We got our wires crossed a little and I didn't know exactly where I was meeting her. I was getting more and more pissed off because I just wanted to do my own thing. By the time I met up with her, I told her that I didn't want her to meet me every single evening. She took it the wrong way and was upset. And I probably said some more negative things as we were taking the escalator down to the T. She began to ignore me and just walked away onto another train. We ended up taking different trains home, I think. I think we forgave each other that night, but I just remember pretty well me being finally fed up with having her always always there.

For my English class, we were required to prepare a "spirituality speech," which described our spiritual beliefs (not necessarily religious). Being shy, I was extremely nervous for my report, and I had prepared a long sheet of notes for myself. I was too afraid to volunteer to go first, so I was one of the last few people to give their speech. My heart was practically beating out of my chest, I was so nervous. But I just went for it. I was probably more myself in those two minutes than I had been in that classroom the entire school year. I just talked. I described how listening to other people is an integral part of my beliefs (specifically, the ability to learn from others). Later, several people, who I did not know very well, came up to me personally and told me how impressed they were with my speech. A few of my close friends mentioned how they had heard other people talking about it in passing.

Valentine's day. I was very young (probably around second grade) and had gotten unusually excited about the coming holiday. I decided to make myself a mailbox for cards, which I hung above my bed (not exactly realizing the obstacle this might create). Valentine's day morning, at an hour early enough for it to be Christmas, I jumped out of bed and eagerly checked my mailbox. I didn't find anything except a small scrap of scratch paper with a pen squiggle (the kind you make to check a pen is working) on it. Hurt and angry by the absence of any cards and the mocking presence of a piece of scratch paper, without thinking I tore the paper to bits. It was only then that I saw and realized that there had been writing on the other side, at which I burst into tears. I must have been trying to piece the pieces back together when my Dad came in. He tried to comfort me, but was seemingly taken aback by how distraught I was (and that I had reacted the way I had). He tried to calm me and tell me it was from him and Mom, that it said how much they loved me. I always thought it emblematic I tore such a card to shreds.
