The same year as I was born, my family got a Husky puppy. Her name was Sasha and she was one of the first animals that I really loved. Being the same age as her was lots of fun except that when I was 13, she was elderly and showing it physically. She was diagnosed with hip-dysplasia and eventually it got so bad that in order for her to move, we had to put a towel under her belly and lift her while she walked with her front legs. It progressed to the point that she didn't want to move at all so we kept her in the kitchen and fed her chicken noodle soup since it was easier to consume than hard dog food. My mom had more than hinted at the fact that eventually we'd have to put her down, but I was persistent and confident that she'd get better. Of course she didn't and it came time to take her to the vet. We had her in the back of our car and since we were planning to take her back home and bury her under a special tree, the vet did the euthanasia right there in the parking lot. When he shaved some of her fur off at the injection site, I kept the fur and put it in a small heart-shaped box. I remember watching Sasha as she died. The life just seemed to disappear from her body. I'd started to cry and before long I had mascara lines down my cheeks from the tears. I didn't even bother to wipe them clean as we drove back home. I still have the little bit of fur in the heart-shaped box.

When I was a sophmore in high school I punched a girl during a basketball game. I never thought I was capable of hitting someone until this moment. Our team had been beating the other team by 20 points the whole game. The girl guarding me had been fouling me and hitting me when the refs weren't looking the whole game. I was dribbling down the court and when I passed the ball this girl shoved me in the back, so i turned around and punched the girl right in the gut. Well, I got a technical foul and my coach bennched me the rest of the game. I remember looking up at the crowd at my parents. My mom was cheering and clearly did not realize what happened, but my dad just looked at me and gave me a comforting smile. I knew I shouldn't have hit the girl, but my dad may me feel better. After the game I apologized to my coach, team, and the other player. SInce that day, I have never gotten into another physical fight during the game but I continue to be a hot headed player.

I was in middle school and having trouble at home. I really loved my school guidance counselor, even she clearly did not like me. I set up an appointment with her one afternoon in the summer that I had looked forward to for weeks. We talked in her office, and then she had me leave. I was so let down (I don't know what I'd expected) that I got to the end of the street and sat down on the curb and cried. I felt like I had nothing else to look forward to. She drove by and told me to go home or she was going to call the police.

The day I received notification about the colleges I got accepted to is another self-defining memory. My top schools were 1. Middlebury , 2. Tufts and 3. Connecticut College. I had my heart set on Middlebury, I had nailed the interview and I had wanted to go there more than anything. I had worked hard all throughout high school and I was hoping that it would pay off when the college applying and acceptance process came around. I nailed the interview and thought that I had a good chance of getting accepted. It was March 28, my mom's birthday. She was taking care of my sick grandmother in Minnesota. I woke up and immediately checked Middlebury's website to see if I had been accepted. It hadn't been loaded on the website yet so my dad and I decided to drive to Hampton Beach and take the dogs for a long walk there. When I came back I checked the website again. I was extremely nervous. I finally opened up the letter of notification. I had been wait-listed. I didn't want to make a big deal out of it and be emotional but I started to cry and I was devastated deep down. My dad tried to console me but I felt cheated and despaired and I was too upset to listen to reason. My mom called and I told her crying that I didn't get in. I apologized profusely because it was her birthday and I didn't want to cry and make her upset on her birthday. My grandmother then and there knew I was going to be accepted to Connecticut College and would decide to go there. How she knew, I still have no clue. I hung up with my mom and took a nap and later than day one of my friends took me out to dinner to get my mind off things and just to cheer me up. Over the next few days I got more college notifications, most of which were good news. When I got the acceptance letter from Conn, I knew I wanted to go there.

I liked this guy in my 5th grade class and apparently he liked me too. I wasn't sure though, because I had heard that through other friends. After class on a Friday one day (we had just gotten some sort of candy, I'm not sure why - lollipops), we were both walking down the hallway, in the same direction. He approached me and we were walking together. We may have had a conversation before this, I don't remember, but he asked ""Do you like me?"" (maybe he said 'like-like', as opposed to just 'like,' I'm not sure). I said, ""You go first, do YOU like me?"" We came to the conclusion that we would both answer simultaneously, because that was most equitable. At the same time, we said ""No."" That was the end of that. This situation is representative in my life of basically all my relationships with guys. I refuse to express my feelings and always, always air on the side of caution, to the point where I may be blatantly lying. I remember continuing walking down the hallway, down the staircase, outside to the buses. I was thinking about the fact that this was perhaps a big deal. I couldn't believe what had just happened; it didn't seem real. My encounters like that with guys never seem real. I can't believe they are happening to me.

I was at a volleyball clinic at a local school when I saw posters for audition for a production of Peter Pan. I had never gotten a callback for any audition before and I had nothing prepared, but I figured it would be fun to sign up and come back on the day of the auditions having prepared a song and a dance. Little did I know, those auditions were happening that day, and I soon as I was done with my volleyball practice, they called me in. I was petrified and and still sweating in my knee pads and volleyball spandex but I sang and danced for them anyway. To my surprise I did get a call back and eventually won the part of Tiger Lily. The reason this memory is important to me is because it reminds me that I am capable and I don't have to spend forever obsessively preparing for everything that I do. It reminds me that it's good to take chances and put myself out there even if it means that I might make a fool of myself. I have never been overflowing with self-confidence, so this impromptu audition showed me that I shouldn't not do something for fear of being rejected because I never know what might happen.

When I was in third grade my class was waiting outside in the hallway. A small group of boys started making fun of me, so I began kicking at them, not intending to actually hit them. One of them got to close, and I accidentally kicked him hard in the foot. He began to cry, and he told the teacher. One of the other boys told me that I was going to get sent to the principal's office. I was terrified because I had never gotten in trouble before. My teacher took me aside and told me that what I did was wrong, and if I ever did it again she would talk to my parents. She didn't punish me, however.

I work in the kitchen at my old hight school in the summers. I prepare food to about 230 campers who are all high school age. I generally do not know any of the campers. I often ended up working on my birthday. Well on my birthday i was working and was putting a fresh batch of tomato sauce in the line. I caught the spoon that was in the sauce in the pan next to the sauce and ended up burning my arm with hot tomato sauce! So I went back into the kitchen and got a bag of ice and put it on my arm. A few minutes later I was called into the dining room. As I walked in I saw the rest of the kitchen staff standing around a huge cake. My boss than got up on a chair and made an announcement to the entire camp about how most of them didn't know me but that I was polite positive and productive worker and that I was one of the best workers he had ever had. Then the entire camp sang happy birthday to me while I held ice to my burnt arm and my entire face turned the color of the tomato sauce that had burned it!

Two years ago in the Massachusetts State Cup club soccer state championship, my team made an improbable run to the final. We ended up winning the state championship and shocking the soccer community. I remember the utter elation of that moment because of all the hard work and sacrifice we put in as a team and how we overcame a lot of challenges to become the best team in the state. It was the first state championship I won and that memory of lifting the trophy with my team will always stay with me.

When I was a junior in high school, my parents were in New York and I was home with my sister and a woman who watches our dogs when our parents were away (because my mom didn't trust us with the dogs at the time). One of our dogs who was 5 years old was prone to seizures. He apparently started seizing at around 2am while I was asleep. I had woken up at some point to the sound of something moving around downstairs, but I tossed and turned for about 45 minutes trying to fall back asleep before I checked out what was going on. Our dog had been having seizure after seizure the whole time. The woman who watches our dogs was doing nothing, she didn't call a vet, didn't call my parents, didn't wake us up. She just sat there freaking out, smoking cigarettes because she didn't know how to handle the situation. I called my parents and was on the phone with my mom for an hour while our dog continued to seize, snap out of the seizure but still act strange, and then seize again. Half the house was covered in vomit, urine and feces from him losing control of his bodily functions during the seizures. I was in a very serious mood at the time because I didn't know how to handle the situation. By the time I called my mom, he had been seizing for so long that there was no reason to even call the vet, because even if they revived him, he would have to be put to sleep. We knew he was going to die at that point. I didn't even know how long he had been seizing before I woke up, the lady never told me. But he had to be brain-dead by then. Eventually he stopped seizing and laid there breathing very lightly. I was finally allowed to touch him (mom wouldn't let me before in case his instincts made him attack) to check his pulse, which was faint and within minutes he died. Once I was out of his sight, I immediately broke down crying and cried for hours. Even though I had been around human death, this was the first death in my home, the first I had seen, and I was incredibly close with this dog. It took me a while to get over it, and it may have been the saddest event in my life thus far. In addition to sadness, I've always had mixed feelings toward the woman who was supposed to watch our dogs. I wouldn't say I blame her, but I know if she had dealt with the situation better, things might have turned out differently. She is still a part of my parent's life, and I will always feel some anger and blame towards her, while still feeling bad that she had to go through what I went through. However, she sees it as a bonding moment between us, and I definitely do not. She was an adult, but I still feel like I went through the night alone (besides my mom on the phone) because she provided no comfort or help for me.

My cousin got married when I was in Eighth grade and at the wedding I ended up being paired with three different groomsmen. I was only 14 at the time, and the third youngest person at the entire wedding, and the youngest person in the wedding party but at least 10 years. I remember I had to walk down the aisle with my cousin Jeff, walk back up the aisle with some other guy, and then dance the dance for the wedding party with the groom's brother, and at the time it was a bit awkward for me, because he was 18, and at the time I thought it was such a huge deal that we were dancing together, because he was cute, but now looking back I realize just how much of a difference there is between 14 and 18.

The middle school jazz band in my town was pretty good for that age level, and at the end of every year we used to pick a song to play for our director without her help. Thats a pretty challenging thing for kids that level to do; it wasn't really easy music. Anyway, my 8th grade year we did a terrible job of organizing that, and on the day of our last concert we were basically like shit, we don't have anything. I took charge of the group and told everyone that they had to meet a half hour early to go over something. Basically everyone in the band's favorite piece was a funk song called Watermelon Man, and we had tried to pla it a few times in rehearsal but never got it down. Well, this one day we were all feeling it, and we managed to get it down well enough that we thought it was worth a try on stage. It came out pretty good, and it really impressed our director. I guess that stands out because it was one of the first times that me and my peers were really old enough to do something that felt significant and adult, and it was just an amazing time.

For some reason, I remember my first day of pre-school so vividly. There have been so many other days since then but that one day stands out very clearly in my mind. We arrived at my pre-school and as soon as we got in the door, I spotted a bookshelf, immediately ran over, pulled Rainbow Fish off the shelf, and began to look through it. Of course I didn't know how to read yet, and perhaps the book only caught my eye because it was so shiny and colorful, but I was loving every minute of it. I also remember telling my mom that she could leave and that I would be okay. She was probably shocked, since most kids probably scream and cry when they have to leave their mother's side, but there I was, barely 5 years old, telling her to go away and come back later. This memory is important to me for several reasons. I believe this is when I first truly fell in love with books and my fate with them was sealed. Ever since then I'd had a desire of becoming an author (this is partly because of the Harry Potter series) and even though it's not my main goal in life right now, it's something I'd love to accomplish in the future. This memory, I believe, was also one very big step in my process of going from childhood to independence from my parent. Of course, at 5 years old no one can be on their own, but I must have been pretty mentally prepared if I could have just sent my mother off like that because my brother cried every single day of pre-school and so she had to stay there with him almost everyday, and my grandmother stayed the days my mother couldn't. I look upon this memory a bit smugly, seeing as how I've grown up to be a pretty independent young adult while my younger brother who even now as a Junior in high school is still so attached to my mother. I love my mother but I can definitely function on my own without her, which is how I can go to college in Connecticut and leave her back in California without feeling too horrible.
Last year I studied abroad in New Zealand, and went skydiving for my 21st birthday!

I remember hearing my big brothers talk about girls. I don't remember exactly what they said but it was to the effect that getting girls is like playing a game; the girls don't matter as much as the sex does. From then on I questioned the motive behind every boy interacting with me. I don't trust well. I think most guys don't care about me for me. I think guys just want to have a sexual encounter with me. I turned it around so that I act toward guys how my brothers said they acted toward women. I don't get emotionally involved or attached or expect much real support from a guy.

After dinner one day my mom and i were cleaning up the dishes. I was washing and she was drying them and putting them away. As i was washing one particularly large pan, my mom snuck up behind me and she had a sprouted onion in her hand(I do not like onions). She stuck the sprouts near my face, and i screamed in surprise. That assault led to me being chased around our house with my mom following with the onion, both of us screaming and laughing, our dog barking and us being very silly. I was laying on the couch with a pillow over my head, my mom over me with the onion when one of my mom's friends knocked on the door. We were so loud that we could not hear him knocking earlier, and so he had see us. Before we got a chance to open the door, we both doubled over with laughter and laughed and laughed.

We were prowling the Beijing streets on the lookout for knock-off designer sunglasses. As we nonchalantly browsed through the open-air shops, a man approached us. "Sunglasses?" he asked, eagerly. "Yes, sunglasses!" Alex responded. In a single-file line, as if we were an elementary school class, we trotted behind him... and kept trotting... and kept trotting... Eventually, we had been following this guy for a suspiciously long time. We had left the crowded, urban area and had reached an area full of narrow alleyways and close-together, overshadowing houses. Still, encouraged by our numbers, we plodded on. We reached a clay house that seemed to blend into the gray, smoggy sky. Catching each others' eyes, we hesitantly walked inside. On the inside of the house, there was no door handle. Instead, there were about six locks that a woman inside quickly snapped closed. Our uneasiness increased. We looked behind us and saw about 5 big thugs, hovering and following us with nothing but their eyes. Disconcerted, we followed the woman into a tiny room filled with glass cases displaying sunglasses. Since all 6 of us were straight out of a 5th year Spanish class, we started speaking in Spanish to discuss both the creepiness of the situation and the yuan we were willing to spend on the sunglasses, certain that this was our best chance of discussing the scenario undisturbed. The woman grew gradually more and more irate. She interrupted us-- IN SPANISH--and started the bartering. Soon, we had stepped backwards so many times that we'd hit the wall. We demanded that we be let out. When she unenthusiastically opened the door, we all burst into relieved laughter. The man followed us all the back to the market, shouting deals at us. We did our best to ignore him.
I was laying in my sister's room on the floor and I decided to run for ASB president.

It was Halloween and a group of my friends went out to an all campus Greek party. We had had a little to drink before. I was currently sort of dating this guy, but it wasn't official because I wasn't ready to commit and was interested in other guys. At the party, I started dancing with this guy but soon spotted another guy who I was a little interested in. I started dancing with him and the guy I had come with got angry and left. Maybe because of the alcohol or because it is just my personality, the other guy eventually started kissing. One of friends of the guy I was seeing saw and told the guy I was seeing. He came storming back to the dance and started cursing me out, extremely angry that I had kissed the other guy. I adamantly denied it but he stormed off as I followed him. My friend, Abby came running after us and told him that deep down he knows that I didn't do it because I wasn't that kind of girl and I could tell she believed it. He ended up believing it to and forgave me. I then knew that they had the wrong idea about me because I would do it and I had done it and yet they both believed that I wouldn't have done such a thing.

I'll try to keep it to a memory this time. Let's see. When I was 9 or ten years old, my little sister had a seizure in the middle of the night. At the time my older sister and I shared a bedroom on one side of the hall and my parents on the other side. My little sister technically shared a room with us, but she pretty much always ended up in with my mom and dad. That night, she had been staying up late watching TV with my dad (I think 'late' then meant ten'o'clock or something). My dad woke us up in the middle of the night and told us that Emma was in the hospital, that the ambulance had taken her there, my mom was with her (my mom worked at the hospital she had been taken to) and he told us that she'd had a seizure, but was alright. I don't remember all of this clearly, but I vividly remember my sister and I hugging my dad as he sat on our mattress on the floor. It didn't register to me completely the gravity of what had happened, but I remember that it shook us all. Thinking back on it now, I realize how scary that was, and whenever I think of it I always want to call my little sister to check to make sure she's alright.

When I was a child, I remember moving from California to Seattle. I wasn't that upset at first, but over the summer I vividly remember packing a lunch box and planning to head South and get back home. I even started walking one day, but forgot a water bottle so I had to turn back. It's funny how I still remember that lunchbox.

Last summer I really started running. I was following a plan for cross country and slowly increasing my long runs. I remember my first really long long run that I did along Green River in Kent. I went slow. At the end of about 9 miles, I was exhausted but completely content with life, my body, the day, the weather, and pretty much everything else was just wonderful.

I recall walking into Inglemoor Senior High School for the first time. Each year, the upper-class at the Junior High School took a field trip to the High School to hear the ASB president and the counselors speak about what to expect in high school. The memory is not as clear as other memories but I remember being fascinated about some of the opportunities that the were being presented at the assembly. I wanted to one day be a part of the student government body and to participate in the International Baccalaureate program. I do not remember my surroundings but I vividly remember the information that was being presented to me.
My mother called me before and told me that there was a camera in box in her apartment. She told me that there was a camera in her fire alarm. My mother is schizophrenic.

My older brother and I used to fight a lot. It was never really anything too serious, usually we would wrestle and punch each other in the stomachs or back, but we were never really out to hurt one another. Then there was this one time, I don't remember why we were fighting, but my brother punched me in the face. I remember being shocked and just running away crying. After that, whenever we fought, I was usually out to hurt him, but we don't fight anymore.

My dad smoked heavily and deeply for 40 years before he finally quit, but by that point, it was too late. In the winter of my senior year of high school, he got pneumonia and my mom put him in the hospital right away since he had been struggling with his breathing for a few years and she knew it could get bad really quickly. I stopped by to visit him right before a big annual event with our rival school, but ended up going to the event and having a great time. He wasn't too sick, but part of me wondered if I shouldn't stay with him. That hospital stay marked the beginning of my dad's use of oxygen tanks. He's now on oxygen 24-7, which makes him feel a little better, but he still can't do much and gets winded really easily. I've seen it put a lot of strain on my parents' relationship, and I wonder if he's like this now what he'll be like in a few more years when I want him to walk me down the aisle, or in 10 more years when I have kids that want to play with their grandpa. Sometimes I wonder if he'll even be alive.

It's the summer before I leave home for college, and my family takes a roadtrip around my homestate, Colorado. We spend the majority of the trip with my mom's cousin and her husband in Durango, in the southwest part of the state. The cousin's husband is an avid jeeper, and he takes two of us at a time on jeep rides through the surrounding mountains. I ask him to take us to high elevations, and so he drives my mom and I up to a high ridge (12,000 feet elevation) several hours from the nearest town. We're in the middle of nowhere, with the steep dirt jeep road the only sign of civilization. To one side is a mountain stained a brilliant red by iron ore, to the other side is a dangerous-looking black jagged cliff. Below us is a lush green valley with a quiet stream and wildflowers, and all around are high peaks as far as the eye can see. I think it might be the most beautiful place on earth. I try to imprint it in my memory so that any time I'm homesick for Colorado when I'm at college, I can remember this scene.

My best friend and I would always walk back from school with each other. We'd talk and talk about nothing in particular. This certain day, there had been a birthday party in our class and we had all eaten cupcakes. MaryEllen had saved the ladybug ring from her cupcake and she showed it to me. I laughed at the cross eyes on it and she began laughing too. We decided to name it Bob. After the name came, both of us started throwing out lines for a song to sing. It went like this. "Bob is a big ladybug. He is the king of all the lady bugs. He likes to eat and eat and eat." Only a few repetitions reduced us to tears of laughter and we laughed for ten minutes straight (the time it took for us to finish our walk back home). The next day, we repeated the same song and added hand motions. For the rest of the week we laughed the whole two miles it took for us to walk back home just because of the song and the cupcake figurine.

When I was up doing service work in Alaska, one of the locals took me out in his fishing boat to catch salmon. I had been there a week or two already, and I felt like I didn't really have a sense of what the people were all about. I knew that it was the Tlingit Native American Tribe, I knew some of their customs and I had met a lot of really nice people, but I still felt like I hadn't connected. So, he took me out on his boat at sunrise, and I as we rode the sun started to rise over the Chilkat river up over the mountains. And it was these beautiful pastel colors. As we were riding, he told us all about the tradition of catching fish on the river and how important it was to him and his people. And I was overwhelmed by the beauty of the land and how much it meant to the man who was giving me this tour of his world. I felt like my eyes were opened to the importance of not only appreciating nature, tradition, the spirit of the world and so on, but also how important it was to listen to other people and try to connect with what their background has been and how it effects their unique perspective.

One time my dad and my sister were in a car accident while I was a freshman at college. I got the news over the phone, and I started crying because I was scared. I knew they were ok, but I just felt like I shouldn't be at college. I should be with them right then. My best friend was with me and talked with me and comforted me. It was weird because earlier that evening, I hadn't worn my special bracelets that represented that my family was safe. And walking back to my dorm from a chem lab, I couldn't get a hold of anybody's cell phone. I thought that was really strange because usually I could get a hold of somebody at that time of night. I had that feeling that something wasn't quite right. When I heard about the accident, my stomach dropped and I didn't know what to do. Luckily they were ok.

I have always loved learning. Even in elementary school, when I had no close friends, I would sit by myself on the playground and happily and enthusiastically read my way through each and every recess. My teachers recognized that I frequently got bored and despite the fact that my school lacked the money for any sort of talented/gifted program, they were happy to give me more challenging work as necessary. With the arrival of middle school in fifth grade, however, everything changed. My teacher didn't care about teaching, and when she handed out our first spelling list, I felt my jaw hit the floor - even the hardest words could be easily spelled with the most basic phonetic principles. I asked if there was a way to possibly test out of the list and make up a harder one on my own, but she refused, and I went home crushed, knowing that it was going to be (at the very least) a very, very long year.

It was on a summer evening, before dinner. The sunlight filtered through the trees and the air was comfortable - warm with a breeze. And I needed to get out. My brain was trapped, my body was tense, and the only thing I wanted to do was leave my house... and swing on a playset. The reasons behind my stress are not clear to me now; I think my parents and my brother were arguing. So I left. I grabbed my car keys and I drove to the "Little Store," a small market by my house owned by a cute Japanese family. I always find that store amusing because there is a complete lack of customer service. The wife, when a customer is purchasing something, stays completely silent. No "hello" or "have a nice day" or even "your total is "$3.15." Anyway, I bought a pack of peppermint gum and then I went to a park nearby. I had brought my book with me; I went to a swing and tried to reach the highest possible spot, pumping my legs back and forth, thinking. After awhile I let the swing die down, and I sat reading and chewing gum in the park for at least an hour. It relaxed me. Eventually, however, I became hungry, so I went home for dinner. Alas, my stress level then went right back up.

When I was in the eight grade I remember that I was thinking about playing volleyball with one of my friends. I told this to my grandpa and he laughed. I was a little on the heavier side as an adolescent and not too sporty at that. I already had an interest in volleyball but I was busy doing other things. But when I did suggest this to my grandpa, he laughed. He didn't think that it suited me very well but nonetheless said that I should try. By my senior year I was the district leader in assists per game. This makes me feel very proud because of the drive that I had and sacrifices I made to be good at what I came to love.

I remember when I was about 12 and I started my period for the first time, I woke up and I thought I had crapped my pants. Once I figured out what happened I was too embarrassed to tell my mom and I never really did. I always remember how wierd it was that I never told her and why I thought it was a big deal.

I used to cut when I was younger. I remember the last time I ever cut; that night was an absolute nightmare. I accidentally cut way too deep on the inside of my left wrist. I remember so clearly seeing my skin completely split open, and blood rush out incredibly quickly. I was so scared. I immediately tried to staunch the bleeding and for a second the thought went through my head that maybe I can hide this. Quickly, though, I knew that I was in way over my head. The blood was soaking through everything. I was losing a lot. I called my mom and had her come home. I remember not wanting to show her, and when I finally did, she said ""oh my gosh, we have to go to the hospital."" We drove to the ER and the bleeding went through every bandage they tried. I was having panic attack after panic attack I was so scared. Finally, they stitched my up and after hours of questioning let me go home. I still have a huge, ugly scar. Whenever I think about that, I get a cold sweat. It scared the crap out of me. I have not cut at all since.

The day I got my Nintendo Wii game system is a memory I remember very well. I'd been waiting for the Wii to come out for months and months and I was soooo excited to get one. I remember going to Target at four in the morning with my mom to get one on the day it came out but unfortunately there was already a gigantic line. We ended up putting in a pre-order for the next shipment at FYE. I remember being really sad that Christmas because the shipment still hadn't come in and all I wanted was a Wii. But then, a few days after Christmas, I came back from my job at a comic book store and decided to call FYE just to make sure that it hadn't come in yet. It was a longshot because they were supposed to call me when it came in and they hadn't but I figured I'd try. When I called they said ""Oh, yeah we just had a shipment come in 10 minutes ago,"" and I spazzed out. I was so excited. My mom immediately took me to pick it up and playing it for the first time was so awesome. I think that day really kind of the epitome of my childhood.

The first time I was uncontrollably angry at someone that was not in my immediate family. I was angry at something that I couldn't control nor become angry at, or at least openly, and a friend of mine said something that set me off almost immediately after the original stressor. I was so angry and out of control that she hid from me as I yelled at her, even though I knew it wasn't her that I was angry with.

In September of my 8th grade year, my grandfather passed away after a long bout with cancer. My Grandpa Hank was the first person close to me who died. I was watching the Patriots game vs the Oakland Raiders, it was the inaugural game of the NFL season and I was very excited. I remember the phone ringing and my Dad's reaction to the news that his father had just passed. It was not a surprising death but incredibly devastating at the same time. I will never forget the death of my grandfather.

I went to my teacher's house to pick up my friend to go to lunch. He was staying there because he was house sitting for her. When I walked in he was still in bed, which was a sleeping bag on a blow up mattress on the floor. I came in and sat on the sofa next to where he was slowly waking up. We talked about our failing relationships despondently and eventually the conversation evolved into what would happen if the two of us hooked up. I told him I was against it considering the fact that I was not even close to getting over my boyfriend and that we would probably would regret it. I said these things but I did not mean them. The truth was I loved my boyfriend and my friend but I knew the consequences for getting involved with my friend would be bad. After I finally got him our of bed we left in his prius for lunch.

I remember going on a trip to Arizona with 5 other Whitman students, to volunteer with an organization called No More Deaths. One of the most memorable moments of the trip was one of the hikes I went on to put out water. Our group was being led by a geologist, and she told us stories about how the layers of rocks had made the pattern that they were in right now. We were walking through something called an arroyo, which is basically a canyon on a smaller scale (but it looked pretty big to me). The rock formations on either side of us were a deep, dusty red-brown and were pretty jagged. In parts of the bottom of the canyon were streams. We saw a jug put out by volunteers a week ago, and noticed it to one side of the arroyo wall. Our volunteer guide also noticed a footprint left by whoever was drinking that water. Then a border patrol helicopter swooped down over us three times, and I was a bit startled, but our guide was right -- there were too many of us who were blonde and our backpacks were too nice for them to come down over us too closely. We were told earlier that the reason the helicopters do this is to scatter people so they become separated from their group. Later, when we learned that the most dangerous thing in the desert was to become lost from your group, because people would get lost, just walk in circles, and eventually be very much in danger of dying from heat-exhausion or dehydration, I put two and two together.

We have moved a lot in my childhood. I grew up in Wisconsin for my elementary school years. I remember my parents telling me when we were moving to Oregon and being devastated. My mom and dad sat me down and told me that they told me they knew it would be hard for me but that it would be good for me in the long run. I was so upset, I locked myself in my room and did not talk to my parents for days.
I was eating and I decided to throw up on purpose.

I had been with my boyfriend for almost two years, but had never told him that I cheated when we first started dating. We were studying abroad together, and I realized that I really loved him and could see myself spending the rest of my life with him. With that in mind, I couldn't hold in my secret any longer. He deserved to know, and I wanted to come clean. I would rather him know and leave me, rather than to keep such a thing hiding from him. I cared so much about him, that I wanted things completely honest before moving forward. I felt as though he had never hidden anything from me, and he deserved the same respect that he gave me. I told him, and he was shocked and extremely hurt. We worked through it, and I'm proud of myself for laying it all out. I feel like sometimes I don't deserve such a great guy who would never do such a thing to me. I can't believe that we're still together, and as much as I want to, I know we can never celebrate an "anniversary" together of when we first started dating. That's all my fault, and it really is a small price to pay for what I did to him.

It was parent's weekend here at Whitman and both my parents had come up as well as a lot of my friends' parents. One of my good friends, Brett, didn't have his parents there so he tagged along with my parents and me for most of the night. The first time I drank. I was at a festival at the seattle center with my best friend lindsey. I tasted whisky for the first time thinking that I was so cool to be drinking out of a water bottle in public with older guys. I ended up getting really drunk/sick. The morning after my high school graduation was a very telling time. We had our senior the night before, and then were having a breakfast provided by the parents when we came back. My whole class was in our school cafeteria, tired after the long sleepless night. A lot of girls were holding each other in groups, saying how sad they were to graduate. They kept saying how they were going to miss everyone. I looked around at my group of friends, smiled, and told my mom I was good to go. I would see all the people I loved all the time. And I have.

When I was in elementary school, our teacher had us write a poem. We were supposed to describe an object by simply filling in the blanks for a series of phrases: "It feels like _____/It smells like _____/It tastes like _____" and so on. This was my first poem. That night, I woke up in the dark, walked into the kitchen to find a pen and a pad of paper and wrote a poem I called "My Life is a Song," a short, highly metaphorical and image-filled poem. I felt like it just burst out of me--I didn't know where it came from. My mom found it the next morning and was amazed. She and my teachers encouraged me to write from then on.

I decided to take a yoga class on a whim- well I guess with my mother's encouragement and the first class was just me and my soon-to-be mentor Cathy. We were in a very small room and I had never done yoga before-I was nervous. We started doing yoga and talking about yoga and I became less and less nervous. Eventually, she demonstrated head-stand, which looked so graceful and strong. I was so inspired. I made it a mission to master that pose and then it happened! I was so excited and so thankful that I had found something that I was naturally good at and still had the patience and time to keep improving. Cathy has been such a friend to me and I still recall how empowered I felt when I first mastered head-stand.

I was never raised with any sort of religion. I would say that I was raised with a sort of spirituality and I think that it was heavily influenced by a lot of stereotypically Native American values. What I mean by that is a sense of valuing life and the natural world. When I was really young my family was out camping. My dad had just given my brother and I a bow with arrows. It wasn't anything major, just a little composite bow that could shoot arrows maybe 20 feet max. Cam and I were running around shooting stumps and the like, but we were getting into that sort of "hunting" mode and were trying to creep up on birds and squirrels. Well we managed to sneak up on a squirrel getting within feet of it and my brother shot it with an arrow. The arrow went through the animal and pinned it to the ground. The thing thrashed around for a while while my brother and I were yelling and crying not knowing what to do. My dad came over to where we were and the squirrel died. We buried it and I forget exactly what my dad said but it was something to the effect of "life is valuable and you should never take it lightly." I have a lot of trouble killing anything including spiders and believe that if anyone kills an animal they should do everything in their power to use that animal in every way possible and give thanks for it. I strongly dislike the idea of sport hunting.

When I got into Whitman, I was stoked. I called one of my best friends to celebrate, and was just so excited. We were talking about it, and just merrily discussing my future plans and she says, "okay, you can go to whitman, but, don't turn into a lesbian. I have known three people that went to Whitman, and all three have ended up coming out, so don't do it!" It was a complete joke, but it struck close to home. I asked her if she would still love me if I did, and she said of course, but not to become a statistic. I knew she was just playing around, and I had never confided in her about my inner turmoil. But despite that, part of me got really excited. I thought that, wow, I could try a new identity, I could just tell everyone that I liked girls from the get-go, because nobody there would know me..

I was in Nicaragua with several good friends of mine (or at least they were now good friends, after we'd been traveling together for a week), and we were following around a group of American doctors as they made rounds through the nearby villages. We'd spent the morning touring the hospital in the district center, a smelly, dirty, understaffed place, and now we were seeing children with untreated infections, borken bones set wrong, sick older men and women whose grown children didn't know how to care for them. We also saw children with new casts and bandages, doing much better with the expertise and supplies of the American doctors. We carried toothbrushes and notebooks in our backpacks to pass out at any local schools we came across. Even though none of the young people spoke much Spanish, the way life continued in spite of extreme poverty and hardship made a strong impact on all of us. I also began to wonder about the best ways we could hope to help these people.

And I kissed him on the cheek. Even though Avis was looking. I'd forgotten about that. At my first track meet, in sixth grade, I was going to run a mile and do hurdles. I had joined the team because I wasn't athletic but wanted to get into better shape. I was feeling pretty good about myself as I crouched on the starting line of the hurdles. I came in dead last. A bit discouraged, I got up to do the mile later. I came in dead last, but with a personal best, which only made it worse. I got really pissed off, especially at my mom because she tried to comfort me. I apologized the next day, and she forgave me, saying that it was very mature of me to apologize and she knew I would do better next time. I was walking on sunshine when she said that. I did do better the next time, though I eventually stopped doing hurdles because at a practice I failed to clear one and made one hell of a mess of my left knee, and took up shotput instead, and I was rather good at it for being a scrawny preteen, not quite 100lb but 5'4" when all the other girl throwers were taller and much beefier. That's off topic from the memory, but I just wanted to share it. So yeah, to sum it up, I got royally pissed off, and apologized later, and when I was praised for apologizing I felt really, really good about myself.

In seven grade I started to like another guy, and that was the worst thing ever. He was the cousin of one of my friends. He was on top of everything, a musician, he was more than perfect for me. We were always few in each promotion, We were 50 in total for my entire grade, and we were split in three. He was in one of the other two grades, but everybody knew. I would go to my house and look at the mirror and understand why I could not find the self-control to stop eating while all her girlfriends were thin. I would eat even more, with more anxiety than before. As soon as I stopped eating I felt bad, but I never stopped. I would not get nera him because I feared the others who were his friends would give me a bad look or just tell me to go away, that I was ridiculous and that I did not have the right to talk to him. My friend's fifth grade birthday party was a disaster. It was early May on a Saturday and everything started out fine. She asked all of the girls coming to bring a cd of our favorite music. They voted to play mine first and when it came on, they just laughed at me and the cd. I was a little hurt but played along. A girl I wasn't fond of, Marissa made the worst comments and was allowed to choose her cd. Marissa opted for Brittany Spears to play and so we listened to her until dinner. Fallon brought out permanent markers so we could all write and draw in these little notebooks. Instead of writing or drawing in the notebook, I sneakily wrote "I love Eric Pierce" on Marissa's leg when she stood up. She didn't notice until later and Caitlin, one of the girls who saw me ratted me out. I laughed it off and everyone joined in thinking it was hilarious and wanting a tattoo of their own. The markers ended up on everyone but me. Then the other girls were upset that marker had gotten on their clothes. I loved one of my high school English teachers. He was a great man. After seniors left school (we got out a couple weeks earlier than everyone else) I went back to my high school to thank him for everything. Walking down the hall to go see him, I started crying (I cry easily) because of how much he meant to me. When I got to his class room, he said, "Oh! Oh dear! Why are you crying?" Probably thinking something horrible had happened to me. I then told him it was just because I wanted to come tell him thank you. After we got to talking, he said to me, "You have a deep mind." It's the greatest compliment I have ever received and I can't imagine getting a better one.

When joined the youth commission I never thought it would have such a profound affect on me, but upon arriving at the party to celebrate our community being one of the top 100 communities for youth in the U.S.A, I realized that I loved serving as a spokesperson for worthy causes and meeting with other people who wanted to better communities. Standing in front of the people proposing new ideas and talking with our senator just felt so right. I remember making friends with people over cheese and exchanging many ideas. I know it doesn't sound like much, but the feeling from that is just so strong.

Helping coordinate m brother's 4th birthday party. I communicated with the parents of the other kids through e-mail, made him a dinosaur cake, got all the decorations and invited my friends to help me decorate and set up on the day of the event.

When I was very young, my parents fought often. One night, I was hiding in the bathroom and my father yelled abnormally loudly and I heard a loud thud or bang, then a crash. After he stormed out of the house, I came to see what happened. He'd punched a whole in the wall and thrown his plate of dinner on the floor. My mother was sitting in the middle of the room crying, and I went and hugged her. She didn't let me go for a long time.

In English class, we were working on our final term papers, written on the nature of Comedy or Tragedy in literature. Each student had met with the teacher to discuss our thesis, and my meeting left me more confused than ready to write. So I decided to just write my introduction and then e-mail it her to receive some feedback. Her reply was cordial; she told me I had a good start and offered me some suggestions for improvement. The next day in class, she handed out a worksheet about "what not to do in your introduction." She began to read an "example" paragraph from the worksheet, and to my mortification, it was the exact introduction I had e-mailed her the night before! I was sitting right next to her! I kept my gaze down and just hoped nobody would notice the red tint to my face. Needless to say, I completely rewrote my introduction... and she became my least favorite teacher of the year.

I have seven close friends from high school. We've been friends since elementary school. I love them all dearly. They have been an amazing source of support, love, and fun for years. We scattered all across the state for college. The first Christmas back, we decided to get together and reconnect. We had a sleepover at Tia's house (she almost always hosted the sleepovers). We did our traditional Secret Santa exchange (that we've been doing since we were 12). The criteria this time were: one gift that's edible, one gift that's "fabulous" that cost less than 5 dollars, and cute underwear. It was great. I gave Chantel a pink and blue thong with penguins on it, a gingerbread house, and a sparkly pair of earrings. Elaine gave me a silver and black pair of underwear with "You're on my list" written across the bum, some candied almonds, and two pairs of knee-length socks in beautiful colors. Samantha baked her white chocolate raspberry bars, Ashley made fudge, and Stephanie made sugar cookies. We ate a lot of treats and played "blue pillow of truth." When you're holding the blue pillow of truth, everyone gets to ask you one question, and you answer truthfully. Simple enough. It was a great way to see what had happened and how we had changed after the first few months of college. A lot of the talk was focused on drinking and sex, but it was all positive and nonjudgmental. It was hot in Tia's room, since we were all piled on Tia's bed and wearing winter sweaters, but it was wonderful. I love those girls, and always will. As we fell asleep that night, I thought about how easy it was to pick up where we had left off. A few details had to be sorted out, but there was no loss of intimacy or friendship between us. We'll be lifelong friends. How lucky I am.

Growing up in Hawaii, trips to the beach were weekly and all day long. I distinctly remember one day when I was with my grandma, small enough for her to carry, in the ocean just hanging out. As she was holding me I looked down to see our shadow moving by the currents of the water. For some reason I thought this was an xray and started to scream and get excited. I was so scared for my grandma and for myself because I thought she didn't see it as she tried to calm me down. When I finally figured it out, I just laughed as if nothing had happened but was still weary of the water. I think of this memory because my grandma always described me as a "wimpy" child and I laugh as I try to defend myself although I know that I am still "wimpy."

Erik and I were walking home from across Isaacs. I was wearing a pink and white striped tank top and jeans underneath my trench coat, and we crossed the bridge between Douglas and Prentiss, directly in front of the dining hall. Erik stopped, turned to me, and said, "Hayley. Can I kiss you?" It was near the end of winter of my freshman year of college. I didn't know Erik extremely well, but we'd started talking over winter break. I said "Sure" because that's the answer that usually comes out when I'm unprepared for the question but am inclined to say "Yes". His arms held mine and I was warm and totally consumed with the internal jolt that comes with the thrill of a first kiss. I smiled all the way back to the dorm, unsure of whether this would amount to anything and whether I wanted it to. We separated in the entryway and I went to my room, but he texted me and we met again in the stairway between his section and B-section on my floor. We kept kissing as a girl from my section slid past us back to her room. Finally, but too soon, we said good night and went back to our rooms.

As a freshman in high school I asked a girl out in the middle of a do-homework class period. I sat next to her and very quietly and feebly asked. I knew it was hopeless to ask, and I made it all the more pathetic in the balls-less way that I did it. I know what she said- that she would have to think about it- but I don't remember her saying it. When I recall this memory, I see myself from a 3rd person point of view and I don't as much feel the fearful anticipation that I felt in that moment, but a disappointment and embarrassment over how pathetic I was in that moment. My focus turns toward the other people in the room, who I'm sure must have overheard this exchange but of whom I have no actual memory, and I imagine what they must have been thinking. A sort of pity over the embarrassing situation. And I haven't asked anyone else since then. I'll put myself out there and flirt, but always to prompt someone else to ask me out, never able to make the move myself.

When I was younger, my family would always go to the river. My dad knew how to wakeboard and decided that I could try when I was ready. I was about 6 when I first tried the wakeboard. Our friends had a a boom which is a pole that comes off the side of the boat. It is used for people learning how to wakeboard that are not strong enough to get pulled behind the boat. I was really excited to finally get to wakeboard because all the older kids could do it but none of the younger kids knew how. I wanted to be the first one to try. I grabbed on to the pole and popped my board halfway out of the water and the boat started to move. I was able to stand up right on the first try. It seemed almost too east. When my arms got tired of holding on, I let go. When the boat came around, I asked my dad if I could wakeboard for real. The first two times, I wasn't able to pop up but on the third try I was out of the water. I had no control over my body and it felt like the board was controlling me. Everyone was cheering and screaming at me. I was so happy, all I could was smile and hang on for dear life.

When I started the 7th grade I transfered to VBFS from another school. I got put in the regular math class that all the other 7th graders were in, by default. The first day of class we took a test to determine our knowledge of math. I guess I did very well, because I was put in a class with the 8th graders. I remained a year ahead of everyone else in math until senior year. Since then I've also done very well at almost every class I've been in. I've even turned grades around mid-semester, to a ridiculous degree. At one point I had a 30% in an online AP chemistry class mid-semester during the first semester of the year, but ended up getting a 92 in the class and a 5 on the AP exam. I feel like I've done well in school without even having to try very hard. I feel like I've just sort of fallen into being able to do work well. And in the school I went to before 7th grade, I never had any indication I was any smarter than average, I didn't think I was any better at school work. I still don't think I'm smarter than average, I just feel like I am a fairly good problem solver. But, back to the original memory, I think that that time showed me that I wasn't going to be going down the same path that the rest of my classmates were, it showed me that if I wanted, I really could do big things with my life. And since then, I've had pretty high aspirations for myself.

When I was really little my brother got a toy for Christmas that i really wanted. It was robot type thing that had wires connected to a remote that made it move. I remember being really jealous and for some reason I thought the logical thing to do was cut the wires with a pair of scissors... I remember my brother was devastated and my parents were very upset with me, rightfully so.

My mom came and picked me up from school one day. When I opened the door to the front seat there were tissues everywhere. I asked her why and she told me she had been crying. I didn't want to ask her why, even though I knew she would have loved to talk to me about it. I didn't want to ask her why because I knew it would be another awful story about my dad that I did not want to hear. I looked out the window instead and silently cried because I could not stop the tears from rolling down my face. I wouldn't turn my face towards her because I didn't want her to see and try to prompt me to talk about it
Spending a whole Saturday afternoon waiting for my dad to come spend time with me.

When the Nintendo Wii was first announced, I was ecstatic. I remember vividly driving with my dad and brother to BestBuy at 12:30 in the morning to wait in line to get it. We were the first ones in line, but before long, the line was massive. A couple of guys right behind us in line brought a table and a laptop and started watching a movie. I remember taking shifts--sleeping in the car while my brother held the place in line and vice versa. When the doors finally opened at 11 AM, we were tired yet completely and stupidly excited. Walking out of there with the wii box in my arms was an unforgettable feeling.
When I got my first ticket, I cried. I wasn't even speeding, and I got a ticket. I was SO MAD. Expired plates is such a stupid reason to get a ticket. I was really bitter.

In ninth grade we had a job shadow day. My friend and I job shadowed our other friend's mom who was a personal trainer. As part of the day we went through a workout in her gym. Part of which, included a body fat analysis. My friend was always very involved in soccer and was always very fit. I had recently put on some weight. When the scale read my weigh at 137, I was mortified and embarrassed.

The day that I received my acceptance letter to Whitman college was one of relief and happiness. I received the letter a day after my fellow high school classmates who applied to Whitman got their acceptance letters. I recall thinking that I was going to be rejected from the school and not expecting to find a large envelope in the mail from Whitman. I don't even think I read the entire acceptance letter before calling my parents about the good news.

I remember my second day at Whitman. I was so incredibly nervous. I was meeting a million different people and there were absolutely no familiar faces. The first day had been even worse, and I was just incredibly overwhelmed, but I decided that today, I was going to put myself out there, I was going to make a friend. I was walking around, and I met this girl, and we got to talking, and she invited me back to her room in anderson. I lived in Prentiss, so I was super excited to get out of my dorm. We talked for a while, and I met some of her section mates, I had to go back for section dinner, but I left feeling very proud. I had made my first friend.

When I started junior high, I literally had no friends, but by the end of 7th grade I had made some good ones who stuck with me all through high school. They were all honor students and Christians like me, which was nice, but didn't help our social standing at all. I went through high school and made some friends through theatre, and also earned people's respect, but definitely wasn't cool by any stretch of the imagination. I remember the day when people started looking at me differently though. I went to my senior prom with the guy who I was dating at the time. He was tall and handsome and I got a lot of compliments about him whispered in my ear. I also got a lot of stares from all the girls who had never seen me with a guy before (I didn't date through most high school and never saw anyone at my school). All the girls who had never seemed to need to pay attention to me before were smiling at me and telling me I looked beautiful. I was so happy. I didn't feel very real, but it didn't matter. It was the end of our senior year and I think everyone was ready to leave a lot of that silly stuff behind them. It also gave me just a little more confidence, and the realization that everyone is a person with flaws, but with a heart too...even the popular girls.

Sophomore year of college, I went with the rugby team on our annual trip to Vancouver BC. We were driving on I 5 and it was dark and raining. The girl who was driving our car was looking at her GPS device and didn't realize that the car in front of us had braked. When she realized it, she braked but the brakes didn't respond quick enough because of the water on the road. She veered into the next lane to avoid hitting the car in front of us, but the car kept turning and we began to spin 360s in the middle of the highway. I remember closing my eyes shut tight and covering them with my hands, waiting to feel the crash, believing we were about to die. The crash didn't come though and we spun off the side of the road; it was a miracle we didn't hit anyone because the road was pretty busy. I was mainly surprised to be alive afterward.

We were n recess time in fifth grade, and one of my friends were in a playful mood. She came to me and took my shoes off. She ran away with them. Recess was over and she had disappeared. I went back to my class and I saw two guys playing volleyball with my shoes. I wanted to cry. Then I remember that I saw my sister and she saw me crying. She took my shoes away from them, and gave them back to me. I went to cry to the bathroom. I told my mom and the next day she showed up in the class ans asked the teacher to talk to the class. She went in, and my heart just turned around and started beating backward. I felt my blood going the other way around. She said what had to say, she is still a very hard-personality and confident woman, and she got out. Then I remember the teacher saying something about my mom being right, and one of the kids that grabbed my shoes was trying to speak out and defend himself. I was observing everything. It was very shameful.

I remember going to the 5th Harry Potter book release party at Border's Bookstore in South Tacoma. My friends and I got all dressed up in our best Harry Potter gear and set out for the party around 8 pm to wait for the books to be released at midnight. Dana dressed as a dementor, Maddie dressed like Professor Trelawney, and I dressed like Angelina Johnson. Maddie's brother dressed like Harry Potter and all the kids wanted to take pictures with him. We played a trivia game and I met a little boy who loved Harry Potter and we talked for a while and I entertained him to give his Mom a break. I remember this because it made me alter my mantra of "i hate kids unless they look like me" to "i hate kids unless they look like me or they like harry potter." We were in line from 11 pm - 12:30 am but then I got my book! My mom and brother picked me up, my brother had just got home from some trip. As soon as I got in the car, I handed the book to my brother. Mine was coming on Amazon the next day. Even though I gave him my book I waited so long for, it was much more about the experience with friends and fellow fans than about the actual book.

When I was a little girl, I was extremely shy that I barely spoke. I cried a lot. I always wore a jacket with a hood because my mom cut my hair because I never took care of it when I was small. Since I had a lot of boy cousins, I always played outside and never with dolls. Especially since my brothers would cut the heads off them and throw them back and forth in the front yard. I was quiet because I was always picked on, even by my friends. One day this little boy and I got into a fight, I remember him trying to kick me and I grabbed his foot and threw him down. He cried and I felt guilty but happy. Guilty for making him cry, but happy because I was able to defend myself at school.

My mom and my brother and I were checking on the new house we were moving into to pretty much finalize my parents divorce. And, I couldn't have been more than 11 years old, but we were getting the house tested for Radon and we had to run in and out of the house really quickly in order not to spoil the test. I went upstairs to set up my room, and as I was unpacking, as an 11 year old might, I started to daydream and my mind started to wander. And I decided to open my window for some air. Anyway, when it was time to leave about 10 minutes later, I called to my mom and told her I couldn't get the window to close. She was livid. She and my brother both berated me about how dumb I must be to open the window. And I remember vividly them asking me how I could be so stupid and how many times did we have to tell you... on and on. And at the time, what I felt like I learned from the experience was that I needed to pay attention and that I was really dumb. But now, when I look back on it, I feel a little bad for my little 11 year old self. I made a mistake.

When I was doing my homework in fourth grade, I asked my dad what the difference between a country and a continent was. His description didn't make sense to me, and I told him so. He tried detailing his previous description, but I told him I still didn't
