Going to summer camp in my open toed pocahontas shoes and being told i couldn't wear them by a councelor

When I realized that my mom was abusing her prescription medication in high school and understood that my quality of life was low at home as a result, I confronted her about it. I do not let injustices go without being heard, such as the lashing out she

I decided to run-walk around the Lake of the Isles. I started running, and it felt easy so I kept running instead of walking after a certain amount of time, as I'd planned. I kept going and passed Cyprien and his family, feeling proud because Cyprien ran on the cross-country team and I was running past him, even though he was walking. I was wearing a tank top I'd gotten on my 13th birthday with really skinny straps. During the final stretch of the 3-mile lake, I started feeling nauseous, but I made it the whole way around. I'd never run so far without stopping. I started to walk through the neighborhood to cool down and called my mom because she used to run marathons and I wanted to tell her about my accomplishment and make her proud. Then I called my dad because he used to run around the lakes with me in a sport-carriage when I was little and would also appreciate running a distance.

My friend Claire also had a creek in her backyard, although it wasn't near as large as mine. We did walk up it occasionally. One time we were especially adventurous and went farther than we had before. We came to a point where the creek went over a small waterfall, maybe 7-8 ft tall. We were discussing if it'd be possible to climb and I decided I'd just go for it and try to get up it. I did manage to get on top, but had forgotten to think about how to get down. Claire wasn't sure what to do, but I insisted that since I'd gotten up it, she could, and we might as well keep going a little further. We walked a little ways more and decided to turn around. We got back to the waterfall but couldn't get down it. So we look for an alternative way down. It seemed that the waterfall had brought us up a pretty steep hill that we couldn't just run down. And there were a lot of stinging nettles. Despite our efforts we just couldn't get down to get back home. We eventually started to get scared that we'd be stuck there and no one would come find us. We starting yelling for help and saying some silly things, for example I said I loved my older brothers and regretted ever trying to hit them and promised to be nice from then on. Claire said some similar things, although not about siblings since she is an only child. After an incredibly long-seeming short time, we heard Linda, Claire's mom calling for us. We were so relieved. Of course escape wasn't easy. With Linda's encouragement we ended up running through a very dense area of stinging nettles, which would have been fine but we were both in sandals and shorts. Toothpaste to the rescue.

I kept a diary of everything that went on in my life, and every emotion that I experienced as a kid. I would hide it in my drawer, which looking back wasn't the greatest hiding place. One day I got home and all the pages were ripped out and were scattered throughout the room. My sister had gone through my diary and her and her friends were sitting in the other room laughing about it. Once again, I cried my eyes out. I never kept a diary again.

I remember at my aunt's wedding when I was about 13 years old we were watching the couple have their first dance, and my grandfather was across the room for me. I was kind of trying to blend in when my grandfather (GP) walked across the dance floor and pulled me out. At first I was completely mortified; I wanted out of there. But as soon as I was able to let go of the embarrassment of people looking at me, I was really happy. I remember exactly how it felt; he was holding me close and twirling me around. I felt very loved.

It was a Saturday morning. My mom was making us do our weekly readings from this spiritual book of hers. The whole family participated, we each had to read a few pages. I had been told I had to participate if I wanted to get my new camera. It was her attempt at having me follow her beliefs. This had been going on for several weeks. While reading, I kept imagining bloody images of slapping my mother and father. Finally, I stood up and said, ""I am not going to do this anymore."" I went to shower.

One year, when I was trying to organize my birthday party, I could not decide what to do. I could not decide between having a swim party, a rock climbing party, and a Ropes course (like zipline course) party. One of my best friends and I were on the phone debating, and I was getting really frustrated. She wanted me do have a type of party that I wasn't sure I wanted. I did not know how to please everyone. My mom could hear me on the phone. When I got off the phone, my mom came up to me and told me that I shouldn't let Emily tell me what to do and that it was MY party, not Emily's party. I got even more upset. That was the day I realized that my friendship with Emily was very controlling. I am sure my mom realized it earlier, but that is the first time she told me. I began to realize that my personality allows people to control and that I tend to please others. I realized I have to go with my heart.

My sixth memory is of my sister leaving the house for college. It was really difficult for me because growing up my sister had been my best friend. She was the greatest and kindest person ever. We were really close and spent tons of time together. I remember being really sad and knowing that things would never be the same now that we weren't living in the same house. I also remember going into her barren empty room and just being overwhelmed by sadness. That was a tough year for me.

I don't like to bring this up often, but for the sake of a self-defining memory... In my past, my parents used to be intolerably strict on us 5 kids. Whenever I took criticism badly and cried, my mother would take out duct tape and tape my mouth shut. I have a distinct memory of myself crying uncontrollably and her slapping me and taping my mouth. I went to my room and my sister and I were together. My sister told me to take the tape off, but I refused. After some time, I convinced myself I truly deserved it even though I'm not sure if I actually did. This memory helps explain my attitude towards any form of criticism. Even if indirectly affected, I feel self-loathing and guilt.

When I sang to help people. A group of people and I went to sing for fatally ill patients at a hospital. It was a wonderful feeling to know that we helped people feel better through music. All the people watching were truly moved, and all of us singing were really proud that we could help make them feel better in any way possible.

At my eighth grade graduation, there was an awards ceremony where each department handed out an award, usually to graduating eighth graders, for academic excellence and improvement within their respective subject areas. All year I had been working extremely hard in my history class, driven by a passion for the subject, but the award had also definitely been in the back of my mind. Hearing my teacher call my name for that award was such a rewarding moment. I remember walking across the stage in a daze, shaking my teacher's hand and feeling so proud. I had worked hard, doing something I loved, and I had been rewarded for my success. My interest in history had sparked in middle school and it has continued to be one of my passions, and this memory reminds me that when I put in the effort, especially when it's doing something that I am enthusiastic about, with or without an award, the experience is rewarding enough.

As a kid I used to go on hikes with my Papa (my mom's dad) all the time. He is the adult I was closest to growing up, and definitely one of my biggest role models in life. I slept over my grandparents house all the time just to spend time with them. Anyway, on one hike we went a particularly long way (for us, I was young and he was old), about 5 miles, and it was just a very interesting hike. We found a lean-to someone had set up in the woods, and I spent some time playing and exploring that. Then we saw a pretty big owl just hanging out in a tree. And finally, we saw a deer from pretty close by, something that usually was just a quick glimpse at a distance in this area. To anyone who actually hikes it was pretty much nothing, but to a kid it was a total adventure, and one of the best memories I have with Papa.

My first all nighter of doing work at Conn made me realize how much work I actually had ahead of me. It was about five o' clock in the morning and I was reviewing the paper I was working on. I sat back in my chair, looked around and noticed how there was absolutely nobody around me as well as the complete silence.

My first day of middle school was a big step, I was no longer in elementary school and I remember immediately ""clinging"" to one of my friends from elementary who I had known since Kindergarten (and am still good friends with) and we made it through that first day and the three years of middle school together. Of course I made a lot more friends since then but that first day was so intimidating, with kids who were pretty much ready to go to high school going to the same school as us. I never felt this in elementary where there's an even wider gap between 5th graders and first graders but for some reason middle school was just really eye-opening and it was a time when most social skills developed and you either were really friendly and outgoing or you were a quiet wallflower, and I think I took the more outgoing role, even though I'm really a shy person.

When I was 7 it was just before Christmas and I was in London with my family when I found out my cousin on my dad's side had passed away from sudden infant death syndrome in her sleep. I remember not really understanding what had happened because nobody close to me had ever died.

My mom finally delivered an envelope to me, a large envelope stuffed with the script. Amy Colvin and I had slaved over this script, a parody of the Parent Trap that involved groups of French revolutionaries and Indians. We were unconcerned and oblivious to political correctness - we had seized an opportunity to apply our vast knowledge of history to theatre. My teacher allowed us to perform the play. We rented the auditorium, held practices and auditions on the playground, and I crafted an elaborate scene. I was born to perform, I thought.

The first time I drank alcohol was at my friend's 16th birthday party. It took place at a hotel. I think it was cheap vodka, but I can't remember completely. I wish I hadn't drank that night. I ended up kissing a boy that was my friend's ex-boyfriend. It was horrible.

Last year I was sitting at my dining room table, doing homework for one of my high school classes late at night.I was sitting there, when suddenly I realized that I was so sick of high school. I remember thinking that the people were immature and that I was just doing busy-work, and not actually learning. I decide at that time, at that table, to do things that I want to from then on.

Right after my parents dropped me off and drove away at the beginning of freshman year I was sitting on my new bed and grabbed my wallet to find something. A note dropped out that my father had slipped in without me knowing that was written on a scrap of paper that had been in the backseat of my car. He knew I was scared about my first year at school and the note read "You will find your way. You always have, you always will." It was the most important thing that anyone had ever said to me- and I didn't cry after they dropped me off until I read it.

Freshman year of high school I gave probably the worst speech ever. Okay it probably wasn't the worst, probably not even my worst, but from my viewpoint it was awful. I hadn't been great at speeches before this, but I had never been so awful before. I felt like freshman year of high school just sort of stole my mojo. Like in elementary school life had been okay, I didn't really get all that self-reflective about it but i was a relatively carefree kid so why not. Middle school had been like my golden years. I went to this amazing middle school for really bright kids. It was kind of hippie-ish and had a drama department that was the bee's knees, let me tell you. I'd had a ton of friends and had done non stop amazing things for 3 years, I'd really started to become a little person all my own, top of my game and then here comes freshman year to knock me down. Anyway it blew (freshman year) and reduced me to this puddle of social awkward, and this speech just underlined that for me. I was in this great english class with a teacher I totally had a crush on (Mr. Golden) and what's more he'd been really impressed by how well read I was and thought I was really intelligent. We each had to give a speech on a book of our choosing and I did Mrs. Dalloway by Virginia Woolf. I was talking about the themes of the book or something and I remember leading up to my speech I'd been totally chill about it, only a little nervous (things as per usual), and then while the kid who went before me talked I had a total freak out. I got sweaty and my heart pounded, I really hurt. While i was talking my heart and my breathing and my words too wen a mile a minute, I remember focusing on the face of this really stuck up girl I didn't like and I was pretty sure I saw pity on her face, I stuttered and wavered the entire time. It was like a completely different person speaking. I was a wreck, freshman year definitely stole my mojo.

When I met my boyfriend I wasn't interested in him at all. I remember that after we'd known each other almost a year I started thinking that he really had a lot of integrity. But I wasn't attracted to him. I'd been single for about a year and a half and I wanted a boyfriend. I wanted to try doing that thing where you flirt with a guy by looking at him from under your glasses. I decided to try it with -----, a no-risk person, I figured, since there was no attraction there. I looked up at him from beneath my glasses and wham! We both started cracking up. I think we were both shocked and knew right away that something was changing and just couldn't stop laughing. We've been dating almost two years now.

On my first weekend as a college freshman I went out to a party that I was invited to by my orientation leader. I ended up spending the night at his house, we hooked up but didn't have sex. The next morning he drove me back to my dorm.

I can recall the first day that I was in Paris during my semester abroad perfectly. I arrived in Paris late the night before. I flew from Seattle to London and then to Paris. I traveled with a friend from Whitman which made the trip a lot less stressful. I stayed with a family friend that night because I arrived in Paris a night before we could move into our homestays. The morning was a little stressful because there was a misunderstanding with my homestay. Apparently, the program forgot to inform me that they had changed my homestay family. Luckily, our family friend helped me figure out the situation. He then dropped in at my homestay in the early afternoon. I spent most of the afternoon unpacking. I then went for a walk around our neighborhood with my housemate ( who was another American student), had dinner, and then went to bed.

Midway through high school, I distanced myself from my group of friends because I didn't really feel comfortable around them. But my school had such defined cliques that it wasn't easy to find a new group. I spent about a semester alone, finding obscure places to eat lunch and wandering around with a false appearance of purpose during breaks, pretending I was busy and had places to go, when I really had no such agenda. By the end of the year, I had made some faint friendships with a few girls, some of whom I liked a lot and some of whom I wasn't sure about, but it became somewhat acceptable to sit with them at lunch, and I was incredibly grateful for the inclusion. When they invited me to join the six of them at one of the girl's grandparents' house for a 3-day retreat by the pool, I was thrilled. This was my initiation into their group, a sign that I was actually welcome. I found out later, while talking to a few of them at a party where they were moderately intoxicated that they had all discussed whether I was worthy of the invitation beforehand. It reminded me of the scene in the movie Mean Girls where the three popular girls discuss behind their hands whether Lindsay Lohan should be able to sit with them. The good thing was that, in revealing this catty secret, they also revealed that they were glad I had made the cut.

While in Honduras, I discovered my great love of Hip Hop and Reggaeton music. I had already been a huge fan of writing, and upon discovering the urban genres of music, I began to write raps to instrumentals I downloaded off the internet. I wasn't too serious about rapping, but would often preform to and with my friends. One night, a kid came to my house and told me that I enjoyed rapping. He told me that he too rapped and was interested to know if I wanted to start a group with him. During this time, I only rapped in English and he, being from Honduras, only rapped in Spanish. We took turns rapping for each other and while not completely understanding everything that the other said, we were both impressed. That night we went to a home studio owned and ran by one of the kid's friends and recorded our first song "Damas", a soft romantic Reggaeton song. It was great spending the night in a room filled with people who enjoyed this music as much as I do.

I remember my friend's mother's funeral when I was in fifth grade. I remember it was a beautiful day and there were tons of butterflies everywhere. I remember the casket was white and I remember it looked whiter in the bright sunlight; I saw my friend as she watched the casket being lowered into the grave and she appeared remarkably stoic, but I felt like I should cry for her. Afterwards she watched the butterflies fly over the gravestones and I remember thinking that they were like the souls of the dead. My friend's dad also released some doves after the funeral service.

I used to go to a little town with my family where I was born in my country. I liked the son of an old cousin and I knew he liked me too, he is just one year older than I. We had little but intense interaction, he was different, self centered, he thought he was too cute to be with others, but he would always behave differently with me. One time, I felt he wanted to tell me something, he would go after me if I moved, and he would try to call my attention, but it was really naive. I loved to go and see him because I loved attention form others, specially him, who was beautiful and smart. I loved the confidence I gained around him. One time, we were in that naive but intese game where he did not let me go through a door, he had put his arm impeding me to go ahead, he looked at me and said something, he was very close to me, and I did not feel nervous at all! At all! I just did not like to give him the chance to take advantage of me and moved his arm and got away. I felt like in a soup opera. It was great! haha I loved this kind of drama.. not the drama I had at school. That was the last time we saw each other.

I was in second grade and I missed the bus. My mother said we (my sister and I) could walk to school or we could pay her a dollar to get a ride. We walked the 5 miles (uphill, in our new shoes) to school. I was 2 or 3 hours late. That afternoon my feet were so blistered I refused to try out for the swim team. So I tried out a year later. I learned you always pay for mistakes. Also, I didn't miss the bus again that year.

I remember running around in the sunshine outside when I heard people singing a song. Curious, I walked over to the slats in the fence to find out where the song was coming from. "Clean up, clean up, everybody do your chores" was sung repeatedly by older children. Peering through the wood, I could barely make out the forms of other children racing around a giant sand box, picking up their toys. I tried to hop on several of the slats to peer over the fence but I wasn't tall enough. This was my first real awareness of other people in my neighborhood. I'd been to preschool and I'd played with other children, but I didn't fathom that I could find children so close to me. I called out to the other children and the came over to their side of the fence to peer back. They asked me my name and why I wasn't with them. I could only tell them my name. When they left, I was upset that I hadn't been able to communicate better. I asked my mom about the other children but her answers didn't satisfy me. The next few days I'd peer through holes in the fence, hoping to catch a glimpse of my fellows.

Prom 2004 was on my 16th Birthday. I had a fabulous black dress reminiscent of Audrey Hepburn's in Breakfast at Tiffany's. I got my makeup, hair, and nails all done up. My makeup I got done at MAC and it was a little dramatic but it was for a dance and it was also MAC so it could only be expected. I remember my dad telling me I didn't look good (he didn't like my make up). And then crying. My mom told me not to ruin my make up and that I looked beautiful. I never felt more beautiful than I did that night regardless of what my dad had said and made me feel. I joke that I hit my peak that night.

My senior year of high school my mom was diagnosed with colon cancer. When she had her colonoscopy I was the one there to pick her up, and the doctor took me into a little room to explain the situation, because though he had told her she was still loopy from the drugs and might not remember. Sure enough, as we were getting into the car she started asking what happened, and essentially I had to be the one to tell her that she had cancer. Her reaction was kind of disbelieve but a bit offsetting and not at the full magnitude that it should be because of the drugs, and I just remember having no idea what to say.

I remember my senior violin recital. I played the entire Mendelssohn concerto, a movement of unaccompanied Bach, a Grieg Sonata, a Ravel Sonata, Beethoven Spring Sonata, and Sicilienne (I know there are a lot of "Sicilienne"s, but I only know one and I can't remember the composer except that she is a woman and that's why I chose to play her piece). Some of my relatives came, and a lot of other students who take lessons from my teacher. My parents were there, and my boyfriend was there with his family. I had never played for his family before and I remember being excited to impress them because they are easily impressed and I had worked really hard to prepare this recital since age four. Anyway, I wore a white dress and black flats. I had a haircut that morning, and I was so excited. Although I invited several of my friends, only one came (Andrea Lindsay) and she brought me a rose as well. I didn't even care that none of my other friends came because I was lost in the music, happy to be playing for who was there, and I was feeling really happy and accomplished.

I was once offered the lead in a community play in which I was by far the oldest person cast. At the end of the first rehearsal, I felt very awkward and out-of-place, and decided to tell the director that I didn't want to participate anymore. She was understandably quite hurt and asked me to reconsider. Seeing how hurt she was made me fully realize that my decision to commit to a project involves others just as much as it involves me and today I take commitments extremely seriously, only agreeing to do something when I am positive that I will be able to follow through.

I took Tae Kwon Do lessons when I was young. I started when I was 8 years old; the membership was a Christmas gift from my mother. I loved it. My teacher, Mr. Garwood, was definitely a father figure to me, and I wanted so much to be good at martial arts and to make him proud. I don't think he ever really knew how important he was to me while I was growing up (I took lessons from him for about 5 or 6 years). My second test was for my yellow belt. And the most difficult part of it by far was the break. I had to break a pine board with a jumping front kick (amongst other criteria) to be awarded the promotion to yellow belt. I'd only practiced breaking a few times. I failed. I think that was probably the first test I'd ever failed. I was devastated. I cried and cried. I felt so ashamed. I told my mother I wanted to quit. She, being the supportive and gentle parent that she was, left the choice up to me. She said she'd support me no matter what I decided. That was no help. I went to my next lesson. Everyone else looked so spiffy in their brand new belts. I looked at the floor a lot. The lesson ended early, and Mr. Garwood asked me to stay after. He got out the breaking boards and set one up for me. He told me to break it. I didn't want to, I told him I couldn't. He told me that if I did, I could earn my yellow belt. We stayed there for probably thirty minutes, me just doing the same jumping front kick into that board over and over and over again. I wanted to stop. Mr. Garwood wouldn't let me, he told me to keep going, he told me to yell, he told me to focus, to aim, to be strong, to be confident. The board FINALLY broke. It crashed onto the floor in two wonderful pieces. Success! Mr. Garwood went to his desk and pulled out my beautiful new yellow belt. I stood in the middle of the dojo and he tied it around me. I bowed to him and shook his hand. It was the proudest moment of my young life.

My dad had been on one of his angry tirades. A photography vest he had bought for my mom to embroider for him had not turned out as he had wanted due to some sort of faulty error in the machine. He was telling her to give him the vest so he could rip it up. The vest had cost $150, more than my family could really afford to spend on a photography vest for my father. Additionally, it wouldn't be that hard for my mom (or me, for that matter) to use a seam ripper to take out the faulty embroidery and then hook it up to the machine once again for a correct job. Nonetheless, he wanted to rip it. He had done this before, so there was no precedent saying he wouldn't do it. While he was in the kitchen, I quietly sneaked into the living room where my mom's embroidery machine and my dad's new vest sat. I took the vest downstairs to my room, hiding it under my mattress where I knew my dad would never look. He walked back into the living room to grab his vest and tear it to shreds, only to find that his vest was not there. Knowing which of his two daughters would be one to rebel, he called on me. "Where the hell is my vest? I need to rip it!" He said. I told him that I wasn't going to let him throw our family's money and my mom's hard work down the drain. This made him angrier, of course. He told me that I shouldn't interfere with things in which I wasn't financially invested, but I told him that he used the family's money to buy it, making me financially invested. Aside from that, I was morally invested since his tirade was largely against my mom, whom he blamed for the machine's failure. I told him that he had always taught me to fight for what I believed in, and I believed in this, in standing up to him in this instance. He finally calmed down, my mom had me give her the vest, she used the seam ripper and then re-embroidered it without machine error. I don't know if he ever forgave me for no

In eighth grade I was still stuck in a stage of my life similar to that of an elementary school boy. My social interactions with others had been restricted by years of almost no social interaction going to a school where all I did was study and play sport.

The best concert I've ever been to was at Bumbershoot, Seattle's main annual music festival. The memory stands out for me because the concert was so intimate. I was literally feet away from Zero 7, one of my favorite bands, and it was truly magical to e

The first day of high school was nerve-wracking for me. I not only was starting at a new school, but I was starting it in a new town, in a new country, and knew absolutely no one. I had moved from Europe to the USA only two months before, and was complete

I was sitting on the floor of the meeting room at the Breck Ice Arena during our end of season banquet. It was winter of my junior year and I was wearing brown corduroy pants, a white tank top, and a black long-sleeved shirt. Coach Maya was announcing awards. Finally, she began talking about the requirements for being captain. There were four of us upcoming seniors and two captain spots. Sammi was the fastest on the team, beautiful, and popular. Alli was attractive, fast, and popular as well, but not nearly dedicated enough to be captain. Shelby was whiny, decently fast, and pretty, but her personality was very unattractive. I thought I was too shy to have been elected captain, but I had a small amount of hope tucked away because my sister had been campaigning for me. Coach Maya smiled as she announced Sammi and I as captains. I got up from my spot on the floor to accept my gift bag. I was so surprised and so proud. I looked at my coach, and then at my parents. Shelby's mother looked very unhappy. Gaby Keller's mom was smiling as much as my mom.

When I was a kid the first time I became lost was when I was at the beach near my house in Massachusetts. Some how, I was separated from my mother and I found myself surrounded by the sand dunes. To a toddler, these hills of sand seemed massive and I quickly became panicked. Because this was my first time getting really lost, this memory is very vivid. However, when i finally found my mother she had not even realized that I was missing so I felt a little embarrassed at the time

One of my closest friends from high school, after half a year of college, had gotten pregnant and decided to keep the baby. I got a call from one of our close mutual friends to tell me that Anne was pregnant, had decided to keep it, and she was marrying the father who just so happened to be her TA for one of her classes. I was shocked. I was sitting in my room at my desk doing homework. My roommate was there, at her desk, doing her homework. I hung up the phone and I remember sitting there, looking around, thinking about giving all of this up to get married and have a baby I hadn't planned on having. I couldn't imagine it. At home it's a common nonoccurence for girls to get married and have babies very early. It happens because it's planned and because they accidentally get pregnant and where I come from you don't get pregnant and not get married. It made me glad that I was away from that, that I had the opportunity to be here in college, focusing on school and myself and my future and that people up here respect that and no one expects me to get married in the next few years. And I felt even more glad that I have never been in a position where I had to make the kinds of choices that Anne did.

My dad used to be incredibly violent and short tempered when we were younger. One time, I screamed and was an incredibly petulant baby sister. My older sister and I have had an inconsistent relationship. She made me angry and my father said that the next time she made me scream would be the ""last time."" She made me scream and cry and he took my sister and pulled her to the front door. He threw her down our stone steps without any shoes or coat. Her face was so red from crying. I felt so terribly awful. I had no idea. I still feel so guilty. I don't even understand why I was so ridiculous and obnoxious.

I met a guy in the first week of school and had a huge crush on him. I became friend with him and finally hooked up with him. The next night he would not pay attention to me. So the next morning I cried in the shower for over an hour!

Some of my friends in high school had a band called The Valar that was really good. They entered into the BRU (a new england radio station) Rock Hunt senior year, and they qualified for the semi-final battle of the bands show. no high school group had qualified in like 10 years, so this was a pretty big deal. I was a part of the whole group of jam musicians in our school, so me and a few of my friends were doubly invested in them doing well; we played with them all the time. At the actual event they played great, and I went absolutely nuts dancing and screaming and generally doing everything I could to create more energy. They ended up losing to a band of adults who came from all over South America and played latin music, and they just barely lost. The whole thing was just the pinnacle of our whole musician group's experience in high school.

In december one year, we were out of school for winter break, and we had our house all decorated for christmas. We had the tree up and decorated, and we were baking cookies and playing games. My whole family was there as well as one of my oldest sister's best friends. When we were all getting up to go into the kitchen or somewhere, the tree, which was not too stable, toppled over. It was so surprising, but so funny at the same time. Even though many of our ornaments broke and the tree fell over were could not stop laughing, and we just kept having a good time.

My best friend and I were in Southern California visiting another good friend of ours who had moved my freshman year of high school. We were talking too loud to the fill the silence of the desert. We were walking in the middle of the road, certain no cars would come by. The asphalt looked dark and smooth, as if it was made of sheet metal. The hills to our right were glowing orange in the hot sky. We were discussing gay rights in one of those conversations that sound like debates but actually everyone is agreeing with each other. "...After all," I finished, "I'm bisexual", voicing it aloud for the first time. My friends looked at me. "You are?" they asked. "Yeah," I answered, and we continued walking.

Junior year of high school I got a crush on a boy named Daniel. He was in my circle of friends, but not a close friend. He was in choir with me. The week before a choir trip to Yosemite, we got closer and closer, hanging out often. I overheard someone asking him if he had a crush on anyone while we were in a big group, and he got embarrassed and didn't answer. I thought that meant that he liked me. Right before we left for the trip, though, he asked another girl in our group, Katie, (who wasn't in choir) out. I was devastated. On the trip, though, we hung out all the time, along with our other friend Danielle. We would talk about philosophy and life and religion, and everyone else found that kind of weird. People would accuse us of flirting, but I couldn't help it, I liked him so much. People would bring up Katie and kind of ostracize us, saying he really should think more about her and her feelings (even though they had been dating for about a day, literally). The two weeks after we got back, we hung out all the time. I'd go to his house after school, we'd laugh and talk and he'd tickle me, etc. Everyone was suspicious that something was happening between us, and they all blamed me. I was so hurt that I wound up only hanging out with Daniel and Danielle. Two weeks after the trip was our homecoming dance. Katie and Daniel went together, and he hardly spoke to me there. I was hurt, and he later told me via text message that he was sorry, he was just trying to pay attention to her. The two minutes we did talk at the dance caused quite a controversy. Daniel invited people over to his place after, but only I and one other kid could go. We hung out til about 5 in the morning, and when we finally left, Daniel asked if he could talk to me alone. We went into his garage, and he told me that he liked me and asked if I liked him. i remember having a pet butterfly that i kept because it had a malformed wing and couldn't fly. it lived a lot longer than butterflies are supposed to, and so i was really surprised when it died. i buried it in a jewlery box in my backyard in front of a tree when we moved i felt sad that i was leaving it behind.

I remember my first night in Honduras. I was to stay there for three months and had almost immediately become extremely homesick. I just remember lying in a twin size bed in a somewhat dingy hotel in sheets that were damp because it was so humid. I was looking out the window and listening to Frank Sinatra. All I could think over and over was, "What in the world have I done?"

I have lived a pretty sheltered life, growing up in suburbia and being protected by my parents. My freshman year of high school, we took a trip to the Yucatan peninsula. This was the first time I had been outside of the well developed world, and it scared me. The first night I had a panic attack because I was worried about getting diseases, being attacked, robbed, killed. I was freaking out. I think it was important for me to go through that experience (and my parents finally got me calmed down with bad bar nachos). After that I was more relaxed in Mexico, but it was a very eye-opening experience to see real poverty along the roads we drove as we headed south out of the tourist area and into the heart of Mexico. It was after that Spring that I decided I wanted to do medical volunteer work in South America.

When I was eight I drew a sketch of a dog that belonged to a family we were friends with. I drew it downstairs while my family was watching T.V. It was just a quick sketch" hoping to fool them so they would be impressed when I could say that it was really mine.

When I was small my brother and I dug a fort near the road by our house. (We lived in a rural area, no trees, by a high way so you could see the freeway from the house.) We spent all day digging that fort. We spent about as much time waiting for mom to get back from work. We stared at the road that was two-miles away, staring at our entrance for the glint of her car. It was so shiny from a distance. The color of it seemed to magnify the heat of the sun, or the heat of the sun seemed to magnify the color. We would sometimes wait so long that we would have to rely on the shape of the headlights to tell if it was our mom, or how fast the car was moving or how it was moving. We grew to recognize so much about that car. The car still runs, but the fort we built became a moist, low to the ground hole for the cows to sit in, tumble weeds to reside in, and on hot days the home of rattlesnakes and scorpions.

Anyhow, I remember being in the kitchen, telling someone that I needed a glass of milk without telling them what it was for, and when I came back with a regular adult drinking cup full of milk my grandpa harshly scolded me for not realizing that my newborn brother clearly could not drink out of a full sized cup.

When our family was living in an apartment after we moved out of our old house, there was a night when I went to bed early. I remember my dad coming in and telling me to come see the sky. I went out on the balcony and saw an incredible sunset. The whole sky was sharp and vivid and bright and dark and all around stunning. I remember instantly thinking of heaven. That heaven looks like that sky.

It was Christmas and my sister and I were living with our mom and former stepfather in a condo in a developing area downtown. It was a hip place for adults to live, but there weren't any other kids our age. It was Christmastime and my sister and I had been instructed to go look in the guest room in the basement for one of our presents. We rushed downstairs and began to look for our surprise. I looked under the futon and saw a kitten looking frightened next to a rolled up carpet. I was generally afraid of animals at that age, but this kitten looked more afraid of me than I was of it, so I approached it with my hand. We hadn't asked for a pet, but now we had one, and I was content to play with it at the time. My mom looked so pleased with herself. We named it Tigger.

At our summer vacation home, a lady was set-up on the beach giving people cornrow braids as a business. I saw her one day and decided I really wanted to get cornrows. I asked my mom and she said yes, I could get them tomorrow. We saw the lady's number on the wall of the poolside and my mom called her that evening, asking if she would take me tomorrow morning first, because we had to leave after that. She said that was fine. My mom dropped me off outside the pool/beach area the next morning. I walked to the lady's stand, but she wasn't there. There was, however, a girl already waiting there. I was unsure what to do: did this girl have priority, or did I? I walked back to the entrance of the pool/beach compound. I saw the lady coming in, and she realized that I was the girl whose mother had called her last night. I walked with her for a bit, towards her stand, but then fell behind and wandered off in another direction. She was confused... I simply did not want to confront the other girl already waiting there, for I felt that perhaps she had the ""right of way."" I did not want to kick her out, just because my mom had made a phone call last night. I didn't want special treatment. The confused braider simply began with the other girl, since I had almost entirely disappeared. I wandered around that way for a while, hoping that I could be second in line, but not wanting the lady to see me waiting, since she might think me wierd for not having gone with her initially and got braided first. While wandering, another girl got in line. I wandered back to the spot and realized my mistake. There were now two people in front of me and my mom was coming to pick me up really soon. I was not going to get my hair braided in time. My mom arrived, found me, asked me why I didn't have any cornrows, and began to get extremely upset. My mom explained that she had called yesterday especially for me and had dropped me off that morning, so I could get them done without waiting. My mom didn't understand that I was too shy to confront the girl waiting in line with the fact that I actually had an arranged appointment. My mom also didn't understand that I hated admitting that I had gotten what I considered to be special treatment, through her phone call to the braider. My mom dragged me back to the car, angry that I had wasted so much time wandering. All my time wandering, I was so embarrassed. Even though the cornrow lady was there the next year, I never went back to her. The fact that I didn't simply go with her when she first arrived was my biggest mistake, as she could have simply explained to the girl waiting that I was first. Instead, I wandered, embarrassed that I would have to kick someone out of their self-deserved position.

I am a terrible test-taker, so when I took the SATs, I wasn't expecting it to be great. I had taken a prep course, which I'm sure saved me from getting a horrific score, but the experience of taking a four-hour test that could make or break your academic career and, therefore, your life was beyond stressful. After leaving the test, I was sure it didn't go well because I ran out of time on every section and my hear had been racing the whole time. I just wanted to go home, sleep, and forget it had ever happened. I had the opportunity to take the test again, but it was such an unpleasant experience the fist time that I decided not to try again. This decision speaks to the fact that I tend not to try something if I know I will hate it, even if it might benefit me in the long run. This might not be the best personality trait, but I just try to do what makes me happy.

So, this happened within the past year, but it hearkens to how I could describe many aspects of my life to you. I was editor-in-chief of the school yearbook and one of my friends/member on yearbook was correcting profiles and changed a name because we thought it was a misspelling when were were seriously mistaken. The change was from ""Azzie"" to ""Abbie."" We later found out that this was wrong and the page had already been submitted. The girl affected asked me if there was anything I could do and I told her it would be corrected. Later that night, she called me and I missed her call, upon which I returned her call. She asked me to hold on and proceeded to pass the phone off to her mother. Her mother criticized me and angrily yelled at me. She referred to me as ""you people"" and said that because she had lived in North Haven all her life that ""this"" should not happen. Clearly, she was implying that because I am Asian I was incompetent and not at the status that this full-blooded Italian family in a largely Italian majority town was. I've lived in North Haven my whole life too. She was talking about my race. I remained calm and kept reassuring her I'd do all necessary to make the change. She didn't believe me. I apologized profusely. I recorded a portion of the conversation for record and even started to cry on the phone. She told me she'd be at the school tomorrow morning and get the principal involved. She criticized my work, my abilities, and the yearbook for 15 minutes and I took it all. I politely handled the situation. After the call, I sobbed and couldn't speak about it for a while. The following morning I was so afraid to go to school. I started sobbing every class and needed to be excused to the school counselor. The following day, I apologized to the classmate affected. She never spoke about her mother's actions to me. Apparently her mother does this often, I've heard.

My mom has always reminded me that I have become more introverted as I've gotten older. Apparently, I had no sense of shame or embarrassment when I was younger. However, I know I can prove her at least partially wrong, because I do recall a moment in which I was quite embarrassed. In fact, it is the first memory I can think of in which I experienced any sort of embarrassment at all. When I was about three or four, my mom, dad, and I went out for our weekly groceries. I (being a girl) stuck mostly to my mom while my dad went off to pick up a few things. However, we eventually got to the deli section of the store. Mom was waiting in line for her turn and she wanted to know if dad wanted something other then our usual (I can't remember what). So she said ""Katie, you know where daddy picks up his bread? Go get him for me."" I did indeed know the little stand where dad always picked up his rye bread, so off I ran to find him. When I got to the right section of the store, I found my daddy right where he was supposed to be, facing the bread with his back to me. There was his long brown coat, his grey slacks, and the worn out brown loafers he always wore. I (like any wonderful daughter) decided to surprise him. Dodging other shoppers I quickly ran up behind him, grabbed him around the legs, and yelled as loud as I could ""DADDY!"" Well, the guy turned around and I quickly realized that wasn't my daddy. I don't remember what happened right after that. I think I was in some sort of shock. Eventually the man got me back to my mom, my real daddy showed up with his bread, and the adults all laughed both at my antics and the coincidence of both my dad and this other man wearing nearly identical clothes. What I do remember is mom commenting (quite loudly I might add) on how red my face was. Apparently even young toddlers can experience extreme embarrassment.

Im not a huge talker and I have a really hard time speaking up in calls. But one day I remember making a point about something in the book My Antonia and we talked about what I had brought up for the rest of call.

When I was young; 4 or 5, my dad took me skiing at Wachusett Mountain, although I'm sure we had a great day skiing, all I can remember was the last run. The sun had set and the mountain was in night-ski mode, I was young and reckless on my skis, my dad had gone down in front of me and was at the bottom of the run. I ended up crashing and and having one of my skis go into the woods. I panicked, without my ski and my Dad I felt alone and scared. Luckily a woman who saw me, helped me locate my other ski and went down the slope with me to find my Dad. I remember harboring animosity towards my dad, even though it was clearly not his fault and not a serious deal. I felt alone and scared and that memory stuck with me.

When I was a kid, my mom had major surgery. She was in the hospital for a while, and being a kid who needed comfort from my mom, I remember being devastated when she couldn't pick me up. She was in pain for a while and wasn't in the condition to hold me on her lap or anything for about a week or so, and it drove me crazy. I specifically remember crying and feeling like I did something wrong or like my mom was mad at me, even though I knew she was in the hospital- I didn't understand. Eventually when I did understand, it was probably the first time I ever saw my mom as ""weak""- unable to do something for me.

In middle school I created a charity called Kids4Kids which donated money and used clothing, books and bicylces to an underpriviledged school in my area. I went to the school to donate the goods and the experience of collecting things, cleaning them with my own hands and seeing the gratification of donating them to children in need was the most gratifying thing I have done in my life. I felt good about what I had done and I think that inspired me to do more charity work throughout the rest of my life.

One summer during high school I went on a two week academic program abroad to learn about international diplomacy. Though I had gone to sleep away camps, I had often gone with friends and the farthest one from my house had only been about 5 hours. My mom and I pulled into the hotel parking lot by the airport where we were meeting everyone else from the program and I had a sinking feeling in my stomach. I was so nervous about leaving my mom for two weeks to go to Europe without knowing a single person on the program. I was on the verge of tears and refused to get out of the car. Eventually my mom persuaded me to get out of the car and go inside, but my shyness mixed with my nevousness was a terrible combination. A huge conference room of unfamiliar faces completely freaked me out and I ran into the bathroom and began to cry. After about ten minutes my mom came in with another girl and her mom who had seen how upset I was. The girl introduced herself and asked if I wanted to sit with her in the conference room. By chance, it turned out that she was going to be my roommate for the trip, and when I think back on this memory I am thankful that I was able to overcome my nervousness because the program ended up being amazing. I also always try to keep in mind how a complete stranger (at the time) had such an impact on me and was able to calm me down and make me feel comfortable, and how this is such a simple act that is too often overlooked.

I remember a day when my good friend and I had gone to the beach with my grandparents. We were sitting out in the sand making sand sculptures (where you carve into the packed, slightly moist sand with stick and stuff). My friend and I loved to play this game we made up where we decided what kind of animals all of our friends would be (like their spirit animals) or we'd talk about what we could see them doing in twenty years. I remember one of us would name a person, then we'd discuss our answers. I was really focused on carving, and she did most of the talking, but I'd throw in my opinion some. I mostly liked to listen, she was more quick at coming up with the perfect answer, but I would question her answers if I thought they weren't quite right. After conference party sophomore year of college, I got drunk for the first time. I had resisted up until that point, but finally decided that it was time to experience that part of college. I had come to college convinced that I would never drink, and if I did that I would never get drunk. I discovered that night that I really enjoy being drunk, and that everyone else seems to like having me around when I am inebriated, which has become a little of a bad combination. I also confirmed my fears that I would lose control over myself when under the influence. I feel that it is very important for a person to know their relationship with alcohol and other substances. This is why alcoholism is such a problem. I didn't fully appreciate what mine would be until this point. I now know my triggers and danger signs that need to be avoided, and I am a safer drinker because of this experience.

When I was fifteen I friend of mine had a party. Lots of people were invited and I was a little bit nervous to go. In the garage there was music and dancing. I remember the first full violin recital I ever gave. I was incredibly nervous and scared, even though I knew that I was well-prepared and fully capable of performing very well. I had played single pieces on group recitals many times before, and I was never as nervous for those concerts, but this time, the spotlight was entirely on me, so messing up was out of the question. My nerves did not go away until probably the last piece on the program, and they got worse every time I made a small mistake or almost messed up badly. By the end of it, though, I was finally comfortable and playing as well as I could. Although I still get nervous at recitals, this experience was a big hurdle to get over and it helped me to be somewhat more relaxed in the future.

We came to the decision that it was best to end our relationship, but I felt more like I was getting dumped. I just tried to hide my emotions. This creepy guy kept on walking by and it was terrible. On my way back to Prentiss a boy stopped me and said would you like to lay under the stars. We snuggle and chatted for hours. I started off venting, ad he listened. Afterwards he told me of his past year. His mother had died of cancer. His girlfriend then broke up with him. On his rowing trip he had realized his attraction to men, and He seemed completely happy. I realized that happiness can be found anywhere and found so much beauty in this conversation that I have never forgotten it.

Last spring, one afternoon, my boyfriend at the time, Paul, and I decided to just go for a drive out in to the Wheatfields. We took some dirt road out as far as it could take us. We parked our car and stared out over the absolutely beautiful valley. We then walked up into the fields through to a grove of trees and we realized that there was a hawks nest in the trees. We sat there and watched the hawks circle over our heads for an hour at least. There was a soft wind that kept blowing by. And I felt at that moment that I was doing what life was all about: experiencing something with someone I cared about. It was a very special moment to me.

Marta Tietge was my best friend growing up. Our two horses lived at her house, and they were best friends. She had 80 acres that abutted public land. We could ride. . .forever. and we did just that. On one of our MANY rides we contemplated what it means to be smart. How brains were and what "smart" actually was. School smart? Big brain smart? This was my first foray into thinking philosophically and very rationally. It was, and is, very important to me to always think very rationally and this was developed on those trail rides.

When I wrote my first full-fledged musical composition. It was very late at night, and I had to get out of bed to tinker around on the keyboard and a new computer program to work it out. I was very proud of it, and took it to my harp teacher, who said it should be longer.

At the end of junior year in high school, I was in this play, and I remember after the last time I did this one scene, the whole audience applauded and cheered (usually people only applaud after an Act or Finale).

My junior year of high school, I became very interested in one of my ex-boyfriend's best friends (who were both seniors). That in itself is another story. We were almost dating but not officially because we didn't want to hurt his feelings. It was towards the end of the year and there were a lot of graduation type events they had to attend. My mom and I went to their scholarship night to keep them company and to see who got what kinds of scholarships. After the presentations I was talking to my ""boyfriend"" and he asked, in these words, if I would like to take our relationship to the next level. Aka actually date. Of course I was thrilled and left the high school in a state of elation. It didn't last long though. Not a half mile from school we stopped at the sight of a small injured animal in the road. There was no stopping me as I jumped out of the car and ran to the little animal. It turned out to be a little kitten who had clearly been hit. It was trying to lick its legs and couldn't seem to get up at all. Kittens are probably my favorite animal so this little one was making my heart hurt a lot. I was hoping against hope that we could save it and was yelling at my mom to call the vet or do something, but I think I knew in the back of my mind that the kitten wasn't going to make it. After a few minutes the kitten's efforts slowed and I watched the life leave its eyes. My brain was starting to get overloaded with strong opposing feelings. Someone else took care of the kitten and we continued home. Another 10 minutes down the road, we were passing a field and I noticed a young calf running around with men yelling at it trying to get a rope on it. It'd probably escaped through an open gate or something. I thought it was hilarious how much fun the calf seemed to be having at the farmers expense. I was a little worried though that the calf could be in danger if it ran out into the road. By that time I just didn't know what to think. I was happy about finally dating Michael, very sad and mad about the kitten and just entertained by the calf. Too many emotions were going through my head.

Finishing a half marathon. I was injured and had been struggling through a lot that year. To finish something that I had raised 2000 dollars for (an organized called TRAID, who I ran the race for) was a huge accomplishment. To push through the pain of the injury and to cross the finish line was a very powerful moment in my life. I felt like I was on top of the world. It also made me realize how important running and being outdoors really is to me.

Sophomore year of high school I came to school running a little late, and I sneak in to my first period class to find everyone balling their eyes out, even my teacher. Confused, my teacher came up to me and told me that one of the senior's in our school had been in a severe car accident and had died instantly. I didn't know him very well, but he had a brother that was my age. That day, I have never seen an entire community so affected by one person before. It was liberating but at the same time one of the most depressing things I have ever witnessed. After attending all the various ceremonies and memorials for his death, and hearing everyone speak about what a wonderful person he had been, I realized how little of a difference I had made in the world thus far, and promised myself that I would leave this earth with everyone being able to say such incredible things about me.

For most of my middle school time, my mother was an alcoholic. At the start of my 8th grade year, she didn't show up to pick me up one day. So I wound up walking home for an hour, and when I got home I went to go use my bathroom, and I found my mom passed out on the floor. It's very vivid.

One time when I was up in Vermont, my uncle taught me how to water ski. This was extremely enjoyable because I had always wanted to try and also, that was one of the few times I got to see my uncle. I can remember that water skiing was truly enjoyable and I have always wanted to do it again since that day.

My family and I were in Puerto Rico and we met a waiter at a restaurant who told us he would take us scuba diving. I was really worried getting in a car with someone I had just met, but my parents were fine with it. The snorkeling was closed, so we went to the beach. I remember he sat next to me and started whispering to me in spanish about how beautiful I was etc. I was really uncomfortable and just wanted to get away. He wanted to go for a walk with me, and I was trying to get my dad to come, but he wasn't getting the message. The guy (Franki) kept trying to pull me out of vision and kiss me. I really didn't know what to do (I was only about 12). I started to get really panicked, and went back to my parent. I wanted to get out of there so badly, but I had to endure lunch and an entire ride back to the hotel with him staring at me the entire time. He told me he loved my red hair and glasses. After we got home I promptly cut my hair and got contacts.

There's another dream I always think of. It's night, and I am with my mom in the lawn in front of the college. She suddenly says she has to leave. She walks away from me and climbs up a ladder that reaches into the sky. At the top of the ladder is a small space ship. She goes into the space ship. I yell after her. She does not respond. The door to the space ship had closed. Then, I hear a group approaching. I turn and see cowboys in dark clothing riding toward me on horses with ropes swinging. I hastily climb up the ladder and knock loudly, screaming for my mother. She does not answer. I woke before the men got to me.

So, my best friend had the biggest crush on one of my good guy friends. So did I. Right then, you know it's going to be bad. Granted, she had liked him for about 5 years, we were both so enamored. We knew he what girls he had liked and we never fit in this trend. This was in junior year. He kept hinting that he wanted to tell me who he liked. I thought he was just flirting. Finally, one day, he called me and we got into talking about crushes and he asked me to guess. What a wonderful position to be in, right? (sarcasm) I guessed my best friend eventually and he said yes. They liked each other. What a teenage dream. I was heartbroken. Then, he asked me who I liked. I told him I was lost. He understood, or rather, he pretended he did. He wanted me to help him and asked if she liked him, which I couldn't lie about. I was their matchmaker. I made their fleeting, first relationship happen. Yet, I couldn't stand it. I cried constantly everywhere. I ducked into bathrooms at school to sob in silence. It was a terrible time for me. I could never tell him I liked him. I could never tell her how hurt I was. I just wanted them to be happy.
I am not one to speak up much in class but i remember one day in english I decided to make a point. What I said sparked so much conversation we talked about it for the rest of the class

When I was in middle school we had tryouts for the basketball team. I loved basketball at that time and all I wanted to do was to make the ""A"" travel team. When I got the call that I had made the B team i was devastated. Most of my friends were on the A team and I was angry and embarassed that I wasnt selected for the A team. That feeling motivated me to work hard that season and in the off season. The following year I made the A team.

My sister was doing some homework and was struggling so she asked me for some help. I agreed to help and went into explaining how to attack the problem. As I was explaining how to solve the problem I had an out of body experience and saw myself in the act, as if I was watching some type of sitcom.

My brother has suffered from terrible anxiety in the past, and I remember one day in high school I heard a commotion in his bedroom hallway and found my mom cleaning up his throw-up because he tended to throw up from anxiety before going to school. I have always been more sensitive to him since then.

I sat down in the long row of metal chairs. We were done! We were graduating! I was called to the front time and time again, clean sweeping the awards. I remember being disappointed when I didn't receive the AP Physics Student of the Year Award. Mr. Campbell loved me, but I knew that Evan was his favorite. I was happy anyways. I just had never been challenged and that class really stretched me. I was so excited for college but truly had no way of knowing what was to come. It all coalesced at once: I was done. Stupid awards wouldn't matter any longer. The real world was coming.

My best cross country race ever was Regionals, our last race, of my sophomore year of college. I remember the finish at that race. It was overwhelming because I had just run my heart out and could almost not stand after I crossed the finish line. I was super dizzy and had finished right behind my two best friends and training buddies on the team.

Taking the MCAT. Sitting in that waiting room to walk in to take this test was so intense. I was trying to be calm and chatted with this woman taking her med school board exam for OHSU, my dream school. I remember thinking that this was a sign and then thinking that I do not believe in signs.

If was Fall 2008 and I was abroad. Our program had a couple day trip where we went wine tasting in southern Austria. On the bus ride I was sitting between a couple girls, both who were really attractive. I remember at that point I was still trying to figure out why I had come abroad in the first place, but wine tasting was fun thing to do so I went. Anyway, one of the girls drank a lot and was drunk. At one of the rest stops, I took her into into the bathroom because she got sick. Back on the bus, she was super embarrassed and was saying all sorts of things. At one point she was praising me really loudly and I remember regretting that I helped her out. She was also super concerned of what people thought of her, something that I understood. I attempted to explain to her why she shouldn't be embarrassed but pretty much failed. The other attractive girl was playing with my hair and was flirting with me. I didn't know what to do and was glad when the bus got back to the city.

Celebrating my friends 21st birthday in Portland OR. I planned it and all of us high school friends who have not gotten together together (as in one setting) finally came all together to celebrate Rinas' 21st birthday. This day was awesome because we spent it in the city and I even booked a room so we have a place to say that night that was in a hotel and within walking distances of all kinds of entertainment. That night we danced a lot and we dranked and we just essentially catched up on each others doings and memories so far. We played cards until liek 2 am. The room that we checked out we filled out with so many balloons and decorations. That it was difficult to even move around. This was to really surprise her because we just blinded folded her from her house and brought her there. Everything that day was a surprised. Started with a dinner at a Greek restaurant where we throw plates as a tradition there and break them, moved on to having her getting lap dance in order to really make her uncomfortable since this is isn't her at all. It was all great and fun for us all to be together again.

I had a really good group of friends in highschool. They really cared for me. There was this one boy Spencer who I dated for a while. It wasn't a serious relationship romantically but he was a great friend. He told me that he loved me unconditionally. "I'm not in love with you, he said, but I do love you unconditionally." That was so nice. I would come to his house after a crazy day and he would feed me and he told me I could always sleep in his sister's room (she was at college) if I wanted. He always gave me a glass of water. That was really important to me. I never felt like I had to pay for anything. He was just kind. He is still my friend. I remember that as being so important. It gives me a template for how to treat people with love and dignity even in casual interactions like giving them a glass of water.
I watched my kitten get run over by a car as she followed me across the road.

I recall learning that my best friend was going to move to Texas during the summer after seventh grade. His family took (what I thought) a family vacation to Texas the preceding week. His sister came to our house to tell my sister about the move. At first I did not believe his sister because of her certainty that they were going to move. I recall that it was later in the afternoon and feeling surprised and betrayed. I think that it was particularly difficult on me because my friend had gone through a lot of things during the spring. He had been in the hospital for an extended period of time for reasons that I am still not sure why.

I remember once approaching my honor's english teacher after class about my grade. I was worried that I might be getting a B+ and that it might prevent me from enrolling in honors english the following year. I was so nervous and I felt the usual way I feel when I am confronted with authority figures. I cried. She assured me that I was getting an A and that I would be able to take honors english, but the very fact that I cried made me so mad. I was confused as to how I would ever manage to get anything I want out of life and I felt useless.

It was new years, I had just decided I wasn't going to drink anymore, and just started to recognize that maybe I didn't want a boyfriend so I decided I was not going to do anything with boys for a while to try and sort out my feelings, and I was at my friends house party. It was a huge party, and I wasn't really friends with most of the people there. Several of my friends has said they were going to come, but didn't end up showing up. I didn't know what to do, I was lonely and bored, and I felt like an outcast, so I decided to drink to take off the edge. I started having more fun, I dominated some guy at guitar hero, and wandered around to a couple of different conversations. It was nearing midnight and I went to the bathroom, where I dropped and broke my brand new iPhone. I was really upset, and way drunker than I had intended.. I wanted to leave but I couldn't, so I just kept milling around. When the clock struck one, two things happened. I realized I was not spending new years the way I wanted to spend 2008, and I made out with two boys. I wanted to feel wanted, but all that I felt was disgust. I was utterly disgusted by myself at that moment. I had broken two promises to myself and I felt like shit. I set my alarm for 5 am and slipped out the next morning with a new lease on life, and a broken iPhone.

when my brother and i were very young we stole a candy bar from the grocery store. it was a heath bar. we didn't really know HOW bad it was, but we knew it wasn't really allowed. during nap time that day we split the candy bar in half and ate it quietly in our beds that were across from each other. my dad came in while we were eating them and we got in a lot of trouble.

I remember trying on dresses in Betsey Johnson with my best friend in ninth grade. We were best friends for six years. We were the only two girls in the store on a summer day, and the lady working there was happy to engage in our fun. Angie (my best friend at the time) wore a pink "cupcake" dress and I wore a matching blue one. We literally waltzed around the store and I remember thinking that that moment should have been in a movie. I took a photograph in my memory, and I thought about us dancing around that pink Betsey Johnson store in those expensive fluffy dresses if I was ever down in the dumps. It was my go-to memory that I cherished during some of the dreary and dramatic days of being an underclassman in high school.

The feeling of profound relief as I watched my black balloon fly away and tossed my cap at the end of high school graduation was one of the deepest I have ever felt, next to passing my senior project. No one could take my diploma away from me; no one could make me go back. Not only was I (finally) leaving a town I never liked, I was about to start enjoying school again.

Playing at my grandparents house, there was an old phone that had been disconnected in the room we were playing in. My sisters and I decided to "call 911". At one point I wanted to see what would happen if I plugged the phone in and called. A real operator answered; terrified, we hung up and hid. The operator called the house back, and when one of the adults answered, they were told what had happened. I told them I didn't know it was plugged in, but the truth was I didn't think of what would happen if it was plugged in.

I loved writing when I was younger. My teachers had always told me I was good at it, and I enjoyed spinning stories, composing poems, and constructing essays. In the 8th grade, I participated in the Corps of Discovery program at my middle school. The program was for 7th and 8th graders, and the object was to write a 2,000 word report on a topic of your choice, completely outside of regular academic work. The reward was (besides the feeling of accomplishment), the chance to go on the Corps of Discovery trip. Four days in either Oregon or Canada (it switched every year), all expenses (except food) paid for, visiting historical sites, museums, and having all kinds of parents-free fun. (Usually about 40 students participated every year). Pretty much all of my friends did it. Writing the paper was always stressful, but the trip was totally worth it. That year, I wrote my paper about the life of Jesus, from the perspective of various people who knew him (Mary, Peter, Pontius Pilate, etc). It was a ton of work, and much longer than 2,000 words. I remember typing the rough draft over Christmas break (I'd actually handwritten my whole first draft in a notebook, but it had to be typed for the checkpoint deadline). The laptop was way too warm on my lap as I laid in my bed and worked. I listened to the Lord of the Rings soundtrack over and over. On the Corps trip in the spring (in Oregon that year), I won an award. The best papers were recognized on the last night of the trip, after having been evaluated by a panel of teachers. I was happy that I'd won the award, but also skeptical that I deserved it. I wasn't super proud of the paper; I thought it was too simplistic and not well-researched. But, on the other hand, I was a well-known straight A student in my school. I figured that I'd won just because the teachers assumed my paper would be good. I think that started my insecurity about writing that followed me into high school.

When I got my first A- in high school, I learned that not everything was always in my power. I've always been a control freak, but this put me over the edge. I had studied my brain out for the tests, done all of the homework, come in for extra help when I needed it, even gone to the academic counselor's office for tips on getting over test anxiety. Nonetheless, I had BAD test anxiety, and couldn't manage to get higher than a C (if I was lucky) on any of the math tests. For this reason, I received an A- in the class. I remember walking to the back of the classroom to see the grades posted on the back wall, organized in black ink by student ID numbers. Using my index finger, I searched for mine: 0801847. There it was, and next to it was two little characters that meant the end to my perfect 4.0: A-. It was barely an A-, too. I had a 92.8%, only 0.2% below the benchmark for an A. I remember running over to my teacher's desk and asking if she rounded grades. She said she didn't. So this was out of my control. There was nothing I could do about it anymore except accept it and try to do better the next semester.
