It was one of the first weeks of my freshman year at Whitman. I was getting lunch to go at Reid. It was crowded and some people I recognized from Anderson were standing in the pizza line to the far right of the cafe. I reached around one of the boys I recognized from the dorm for a blueberry bagel from one of the glass jars with a metal lid. He turned around and said, "Hey, you're Hayley, right?" I was sure I hadn't met him yet, so I was surprised he knew my name. I'd noticed he'd already made a lot of friends and therefore must be outgoing and social. I didn't consider myself outgoing and social, so I was surprised he'd noticed me. He said we'd met before, but I am sure we had not before that day. He introduced himself as Stephen, and I promised not to forget his name. For the next week, whenever we ran into each other, I made a special point to say his name when we greeted each other. He's been one of my best friends at Whitman ever since.

I was at a cabin in Oregon with my family and we were having a great time dancing to music and singing. I remember my older cousin got out a camera to take pictures. It was all fun until she was about to take a picture of my mom and sister and I jokingly stuck my hand in front of the camera right as she pushed the take button. I remember getting the ""that was extremely rude, and I am disappointed in you"" face and I was very embarrassed and ashamed.

I was alone at home while my family was away on vacation in Maine. It was a morning, breakfast time. I decided I wanted to make raspberry pancakes. I walked outside into the raspberry bushes and picked raspberries, storing them away in my wooden basket. I sang to myself my favorite songs. I watched the bees and other insects crowd around the raspberry blossoms, wondering why people were so fearful of them. I sang louder.

One morning, my mother and I had been arguing. She was excited though, because my cousin had just called and wanted to talk to me. She kept saying that Mary Kate (my cousin) had something to tell me, and that it would make me really happy. I thought I knew what Mary Kate was going to say to me. I had seen on facebook that her relationship status had changed, so I was pretty sure she was going to tell me that she had gotten a boyfriend. In my mind, I was angry. Why did my mom care that Mary Kate had a boyfriend? What was my mom so excited for Mary Kate about? In fact, why did my mom even know that Mary Kate had a boyfriend? I was angry that my mom thought Mary Kate having a boyfriend was special...maybe I was a little bit jealous, since I had never had a boyfriend and so my mom was giving all the attention to my cousin for having something I had never had...also, Mary-Kate is younger than me, so maybe I was jealous of her too, and that everyone was making a big deal. My mom told me to go pick up the phone and said that she (my mom) was going to listen in while Mary Kate relayed the news. Because I was so angry and my mom and I had been fighting, I threw a fit. I told my mom that she absolutely could not listen in while Mary Kate told me the news. I refused to let my mom take part in conversation, and had her hang up the minute Mary Kate and I started talking. It turns out, Mary Kate's news had nothing to do with a boyfriend. Instead, Mary Kate was going to come visit me for my graduation, and my mom had helped her convince her parents and paid part of her way. I was ECSTATIC. I could not believe it. We live a ridiculous distance from my cousins, so this seemed entirely implausible. The story literally made my day. Yet, I had refused to let my mom take any part in it. As I walked back into the kitchen, she was still a bit happy for me, since I was happy, but she had not forgiven me. She was so disappointed, but even moreso, she was just hurt. Hurt badly. I had closed her out of the good news by not letting her hear Mary Kate tell me and not letting her hear my immediate reaction. This is all because I was stupid enough to assume that I knew what Mary Kate's news was and because I thought my mom should not be a part of that news...

A year ago I went to a shooting range and shot several rifles, a semi-automatic handgun, and a revolver. It was a wonderful experience. It made me realize that while I might feel invincible against outside attackers, I could just as easily wound myself or someone I loved. It was great to feel that kind of power in your hands but it was also terrifying. The experience also taught me a lot about follow through, precision, and how long it should take you to make a decision. A normal person can only hold still for seven seconds, and if you wait too long, your shot gets messed up. In life, if you spend too long trying to make a particular decision, you will probably over think it and mess things up. Now, I just try to do what feels good and have respect for the impact that my decisions might have on other people.

I used to have a big fear of public speaking. I didn't feel confident in front of crowds, even of people I knew. I was embarrassed, and awkward, and extremely nervous. I almost threw up when I had to lead a torah service for my bar mitzvah. But I think that when I gave my valedictorian speech for high school that changed. My senior year of high school was a very intense time in my life. I had a lot of bad things happen, but I also had a lot of good experiences too. I think I became who I am now as a result of that more than any other time in my life. So I was very happy to see that at the conclusion of that time, my fear of public speaking was gone. I was scared the day before my speech, but in the hours before I gave it I became calm. I felt like there was no point in being afraid. I was confident. When I actually gave it, I felt assertive, and in control of myself, and I wasn't afraid or uncomfortable at all. It was almost like a dream, I felt like I was almost on autopilot. I ended up doing a very good job, and I think that because of how that turned out, I am not afraid to speak in public anymore. I am a much more confident person now.

When I was seven I was spending a week during the summer in Martha's Vineyard with my parents. My mom was out for some reason, and I was playing a game of Parcheesi with my dad. I got frustrated with the game (presumably because my dad was winning) and exclaimed, ""This game is stupid!"" and stomped out. From the other room I could hear my dad begin to cry. I felt so horrible and ran back in to try to apologize.

Another meaningful event that happened with my brother was about a week before I first entered college. My brother has a lot of anger problems, and I should always know better about fighting with him. One day he was at our house with his daughter and we ended up getting in some random argument about something that wasn't important. When he left, I was mad at him so I started sending him nasty texts, kind of egging him on. I clearly wasn't thinking straight. Later, when my mom wasn't home, my brother (who was incredibly angry) came back, slammed open my locked door (breaking the door), took my cell phone out of my hand and threw it at the wall (shattering it), hit me in the face and started yelling at me, telling me to respect him, etc. Obviously knowing his issues, I was terrified. But somehow (and this is probably the one thing that makes me the most proud of myself) I was in the right state of mind enough to calm him down, saying that we are brothers and we fight, that doesn't mean I need to respect him as an adult, I respect him as a brother and a fight shouldn't make him act like that, and it shouldn't make him expect me to be perfect or treat him like anything more or less than a brother. I also apologized for the things I said. He started crying, and stood me up and hugged me, sobbing (definitely the first time I saw this) and I started crying as well. He was incredibly embarrassed and ashamed for hitting me, and I was for egging him on. He called me the next day and he felt horrible for a long time. This event, as stupid as it was on both of our parts, brought us a lot closer, and we have had many many more close conversations where we can relate to each other since this happened.

I became a big fan of ultimate frisbee over the course of high school. There was a pretty clear hierarchy in my school, with each grade teaching the one below it how to play. The summer after my sophmore year I wasn't much good yet, but I was decently athletic and one of the better players within my grade. That summer some of the kids who were home from college starting having big pickup games for the better players in town, and me and a couple of my friends in my grade were invited. They were a lot of fun, but one stands out in particular. We played one evening on the school football field, and there was a massive thunderstorm. Rather than get under cover, which would have been far too smart, we kept playing, and it was a fantastic game. The lightning and thunder just lent the whole event an epic feel, like something out of a movie, and it was the first time I ever played ultimate on anything resembling a high level. I still love and play ultimate, so that game feels like the start of something that I really stuck with throughout the next few years.

My Mother was a bad woman she left me and my brother and My dad for a guy who worked in a hardware store.My dad was a disabled Veteran. when he go sick off she went with the new man leaving me and my brother dad raised me and my brother the man struggled to make ends meet. he was a great man he cared about us never let us down You know she was a bad woman she thought of herself no one else

I got very sick with the flu and it turned into pneumonia I remember my mom took off from her job and took care of me. She brought me soup, read to me, put a wash cloth over my head and took me to the Doctor to get medication. I recall this memory because it was the most love my mom showed to me. She knew I was very sick and was by my side the entire time. I never had a close relationship with my Mom, She was not the type to say I love you but after this happen we became much closer. When I went to the doctor and got medicine it was expensive because I did not have insurance. My mom borrowed the money and made sure I got my much needed medicine.

My Parents were mean to me. My older Brother was the apple of my dad s eye. my dad never was nice to me. I would feel so sad. My brother would tease me.I felt like I never wanted I began to feel distant and so unwanted by My family. To this day I do not like my Brother. When dad passed he said Good we got rid of the problem mean dad.. he was is control of dad s money to the tune of $700.000.00 which He took off somewhere We had no clue where he went,, years later He told us by that time Mother died I was left with taking care of Mother for 5 years It was very bad because she was a complete mean cruel person for 6 years dad took off with a woman Mom made me work in a bakery i was 13 working at night Friday Sat Sunday.. Frying donuts getting burned late at night i was so abused get the 50 pound bags of flower I was about 70 lbs I had to carry a 50 pound bag of flower to bake the food then the police would show up and I had to hide in the basement so I was not exposed as under age.. I would not get Salary but Joe the baker gave me food donuts butter orange Juice..as salary in school i would fall asleep because I was tired.. life was hell that is my memory about my parent 2 mean people only My brother the perfect one..he would not work

My dad was always on leave for the military, so i remember the thrill of seeing him when he came home. I remember kissing him goodbye when he left, but more importantly, i remember how excited he was to step off of his ship. My brother and I would always argue over who missed him the most. We would go out to eat, go to the movies, and go play at the park for a week straight until he had to go back to work again.

My dad is a pastor, and throughout my childhood, there was no doubt that his job was important, the most important thing for our family. And we couldn't argue with that, because his work was God's work, wasn't it? So if God called him to become a pastor, he had to do it. If God called him to become a pastor of some small church, that meant he would uproot our family--me, my two older brothers, and our mother--and we would move away from our home, our friends, whatever life we had so that he could follow this calling. Anyway, one memory I have that encapsulates this is a family vacation that never happened. It never happened, because even though we'd planned it in advance and were ready and excited (I think it was a combination camping trip and amusement park visit), at the last minute, something happened in the church. An older member of the congregation died, I believe. And of course, my dad had to do the funeral. So our family vacation was abruptly, unexpectedly cancelled, with no attempt at rescheduling, because of this church emergency. And I know that it was an emergency, and it was tragic, and there were all these other factors involved, but at the time, as a little kid, I remember just feeling angry at my father and angry at this realization that his work would always come first in our family.

It was my parents anniversary (valentine’s day) my brother and I found old sheet music for “The Anniversary Song” and proceeded to try to play it on the piano, or sing it. My mom yelled at us to stop. I didn’t understand why she shouted at us and why she didn’t want to hear it. Ended up this was a few months before my mom served my dad divorce papers.

My parents have had a very rocky relationship the past couple of years. It started around my senior year of high school. There was a lot of domestic violence and it took a toll on my mental and emotional health. My relationship with both my mother and my stepfather has been up and down for the past couple of years. My mom ended up in rehab for alcoholism last year and my parents have since split up. My mom and I both moved out of the family house and have been living on our own. My stepdad and my mother still have not finalized a divorce because both of them are really spiteful and neither wants to pay for it so they are separated but still legally married. This has made going through college and now transitioning to law school very difficult because I do not have much support from either of my parents as they are both struggling. I do not speak to my biological father as he has never really been there for me and even when he attempted, it was short lived and I went back to not speaking to him because he cannot keep promises.

My father often took me out to a local church at night and we watched bats flying around and hunting the bugs. We stopped there every night at the same time and sat on the same tombstones. It was always the midpoint in the day and it was bright enough to spot them, but not dark enough to be pitch black. This was before he passed, and the area is always going to be in my heart and memory.

My father committed suicide when I was 19.
 The last time I spoke with him I was angry that he was supposed to spend time with my younger brothers and he didn't show up - I told him to "call me when you grow up" 
 He shot himself in the chest a week later- called 911 acting as someone else to report a shooting. EMS went to the apartment and knocked, but they left after waiting a few minutes because the police never showed up. 
 He bled to death while paramedics were sitting in the parking lot.

During one of our many arguments during my childhood, my mother stormed off into her room. I followed closely behind her and watched as she threw her hands into the air, stared up toward the ceiling, and snarled, "God, WHY did you give me children?" I don't think she knew I was directly behind her and could not only hear but see as she lamented the fact that I existed. My younger sister was nearby too; we both heard it. We were young, elementary school aged, and although I'm sure we were disobedient and obnoxious, we had done nothing to warrant being literally wished out of existence. I remember feeling hurt but also perversely glad she had articulated that, since it always seemed she was thinking that anyway - now I had proof. When I'd bring it up later she'd get angry at me for suggesting such a terrible thing and insist I had heard her wrong.

I was around 11 or 12 at this time. My family was going on vacation to Florida, though it was just me, my brother, and my mother. My father was unable to get off of work at the time. While driving to Florida, I was attempting to recalibrate our GPS, which continued to give us wrong directions as it could not figure out where we were. In trying to fix it, my mother--who commonly had a short temper--asked me why it wasn't work in a harsh, yelling tone. I responded back with a yell, and she slapped my thigh hard enough to leave an imprint on her hand. She never apologized, and it solidified her as someone I could not really trust or be fully open with as she felt physical violence on her own children was okay.

My parents bringing me to their friend's party when I was 4yrs old. It was late and rowdy and they set me on a table, gave me a toy, and left me there for the night while they partied. Likely they were using drugs. I was already a fearful and anxious child. I felt confused, scared, and abandoned. This is the first memory I have where I felt like me parents were not protecting me.

I came out to them when I was 18, and they were very accepting. Before that, my dad would always complain about Miley Cyrus, but after I came out, and my dad realizing she was queer and a big supporter of queer rights, he started what felt like intentionally mentioning his like of Miley Cyrus--like my coming out shifting his thinking of her import. That felt special that I had an affect on him

When I was a young child, my father was in the Navy. He would go on deployments pretty often. I remember being about 7, and he carried me from my bedroom out to the car in the early morning. I was wrapped in a blanket, pretending to be asleep. He, my mother, and I drove to the Navy base to drop him off at his ship. When we got there, I continued to pretend to be asleep, because I was sad and didn't want to say goodbye. My father kissed me on the forehead and didn't wake me up. After he shut the car door, I cried into my blanket. I didn't see him for a few months after that. I think about it all the time, because only a few years later my father left our family and I didn't see or hear from him again for many years. I was used to the feeling of not saying goodbye to him.

When I was about 13 years old, we took a vacation to stay at the beach in a small camper in a campground about a short walk from the ocean. During that vacation stay, I had an orthodontist appointment/check up on my braces. My mom dropped me off to run some errands and said she'd be waiting for me to pick me up after. This was before cell phones. My appointment didn't take that long. I sat in the waiting area for my mom thinking it would still be a while before she was back. I waited for what seemed like an appropriate amount of time and looked out the window. I thought she wasn't there because I didn't see her. Apparently, she was there, but I just didn't see. I kept checking every few minutes, but still didn't see her. Finally, she came inside to find me, and when we got out in the car she was extremely upset. She asked about the appointment and I explained that it wasn't that long but I didn't see her. All I remember from that point was her being so angry with me that she grabbed my arm and she wrapped her hands around. Then she dug her fingernails into my skin so hard that I bled. I do not remember the words she said but I am sure they were derogatory. I just remember feeling so ashamed and like a failure, and it was all I could think about for the remainder of the trip.

I remember how proud my parents were of me at my high school graduation. I guess I forgot how much of a milestone that was because I tend to be more "practical" and saw it as a means to an end, a step towards a larger goal. It may seem like a little moment, but I really valued the way they looked at me and felt validated by it when I wasn't aware that I was looking for the validation. It made me feel closer to them even though it wasn't a real heart-to-heart moment.

When I think about my parents I think about sitting in the car and talking on the phone to my dad. I was young, in the back seat. My mother talked to him first, and passed the phone to me. I remember that at that time, I knew they were separated or at least that my dad was only going to be available over the phone. I remember thinking about being happy to hear his voice, and this memory always leads down a hole of other memories surrounding my father during that age, since there were very few and I cherished them all so much.

My parents divorced when I was about 4 years old. There were a lot of child support battles because my father was a heavy drug user. I remember being taken to my mother's law office, Micheal Friedman was the lawyer's name. I was about 5 or 6 years old. My mother wanted me to show him what I had learned in one of my visits with my father. She handed me a small square of paper and placed Mr. Friedman's ashtray in front of me. I then used the ashes and paper to roll a joint with one hand.

I remember when I was younger, my brother had joined the gay-straight alliance club at the high school he went to. My dad was very mad at him and he kept accusing my brother of being gay. I just really remember how ignorant he was. My father went off about how transgender people are mentally ill and gay people should just shut up and keep secret. I didn't understand why gay people were so bad but I was sure he was wrong. I was so sure that they weren't that bad.

One self defining memory I have of my Mom is when she was comforting me after a breakup. I walked upstairs crying, telling her I was an idiot, and all she did was grab me and hold me tightly against her chest. She didn't say a word, she just let me get it all out. This was a huge milestone because I never really show emotions with my parents. I am pretty independent and closed off, and honestly uncomfortable showing emotions to almost anyone (besides the ex I was crying over). This continues to replay in my head almost everyday, because it was just so comforting to me.

The summer before I entered tenth grade, my parents had constant fights and were clearly going through a rough patch in their marriage. Some of the fights left me hoping they would soon get a divorce so I wouldn't have to hear them anymore. Since then, things have gotten a lot better in the sense that the fights are no longer long, loud, or embarassing. Their marriage still seems strained, but they really aren't a rough domestic low-income type of constant fighting. This summer was very sudden and shocking for me and my two younger siblings.
 
 The particular memory was during this summer. My parents were screaming downstairs, mostly my dad yelling at my mom. My sister (4 years younger than me), brother (6 years younger), and myself were upstairs in the bedroom my sister and I shared, playing a game of Sorry and all of us pretended we weren't scared. We live in a rural area, so our neighbors are spaced out and I had always assumed the sound didn't travel to the nearest family. After some time (maybe 30 minutes, maybe several hours, I can't be sure) a police car pulled up our driveway. It was dark outside, and during the summer it must mean it was 10pm or later by the time the cop came.
 
 I opened my bedroom door to go down the stairs because I heard dad yelling for us, asking us which one of us called the police. My mom was coming up the stairs and I remember him pulling on her ankles from behind her. My dad has bursts of violence, but always in the way I assumed all dads had. But maybe for the second or third time in my life, I was really scared he might hurt someone. But I didn't pity my mom either. I was mad at both of them. "We didn't call the police," I had told them from the top of the stairs. 
 
 I turned around and went back to my bedroom. I think my brother was crying. None of the three of us talked to the police or to my parents for the rest of the night. My parents have never spoken about this night even though it's been 8 years since.

My parents divorced when I was two years old, and my dad lived twenty minutes north of town. When I was in elementary school and I was staying with him on weekend, he would always tear me down with words. One night, the words turned into violent action. I was brushing my teeth, and he came in the upstairs bathroom where I was brushing my teeth at. He stated that he did not like the way that I was brushing my teeth, so he grabbed the toothbrush from me. He placed his hand on the nape of my neck and used the other hand to aggressively brush my teeth. I tried to run away from him to go get his wife because I was scared. When I tried to do that, he grabbed my hair and pulled extremely hard. He then dropped the toothbrush and choked me. I felt like this memory lasted forever, and I refused to brush my teeth for awhile.

The first time I came out to my mother I was in 11th grade. It was around 11pm and she had come in my room say goodnight. After she told me she loved me I hesitated before saying, "Mom...I think I like this girl in my cooking class." She sighed, kneeled by my bedside, and told me, "Honey, when you've got three kids, and the youngest is dead and the oldest is retarded, you learn what really matters. All I want is for you to be happy."

I remember I was about 9 or 10. My parents were in the middle of getting divorced and I was confused about the whole thing, seeing as I was pretty young. My mom had cheated on my dad and was moving out of the house. She packed up all her bags, moved everything out, and got in her car to leave. I remember being in her closet upstairs looking out the window and watching outside as she drove away. I was crying uncontrollably and thought I would never see her again. That wasn't the case, but in that moment, I truly thought she was gone forever.

Up until I was ten years old, I never knew that Mickey Mouse, or any other Disney character, existed. My parents vehemently boycotted Disney for the majority of my life due to the company allegedly supporting "the homosexual agenda." I was forbidden from watching Disney channel, and had little to no exposure of the Disney universe, which is almost unheard of for an American child in the early 2000's.
 
 I remember the day that my mom announced Disney fired an LGBTQ executive, which meant that the company was no longer supporting the "homos" and we were now able to watch Disney. I was extremely excited, and we stopped by the DVD store on the way home from church to rent a Disney movie. At the time, I wasn't exactly sure what a homosexual was, but I knew it had to be something horrible and nasty if it caused my parents to boycott the company for a decade.

I came out as gay to my mom during spring break of my sophomore year of college. I was back home for spring break. I remember being nervous, and I came up to her in the kitchen while she was cooking. I told her I needed to tell her something and starting crying a little. Then I told her I was gay. She started hugging me and told me it's okay. I don't remember much else after that. I think she asked if it was okay for her to tell my dad, and I said it was fine.

I remember once that my mom was very angry at my father for something, but we didn't know what it was. She had us pack up things for the weekend and she took us camping alone. We normally would have gone camping t with both parents and a larger group of people. We went to the same campsite we always went to in Wildwood, NJ. He didn't come. I remember us driving down, but don't exactly how much my mother told us about going without him. I remember we went later than we ever did because we arrived at night. We stayed there a few days and I remember it being a good trip although it was clear that they were fighting and he was not welcome.

One memory that I return to from time to time occurred during an ice show while I was in high school. I am a figure skater, and in high school, I skated twice a day most days and coached at my rink. I had put a lot of time and energy into landing a particular jump, and was at the point where I could consistently and solidly land it. Ice shows were a big deal at my rink; they went for five days and each night was always sold out. Having a solo routine (as opposed to just being in group ones) was also a big deal; this was only my third time having one. That night, my mother and her mother were in the audience. This, again, was a big deal-- my grandmother is a little old (90+) Chinese woman who lives in California and doesn't visit us (living in Chicago) often. The first half of the show went well. My solo was in the second half. I was warming up for it on the smaller ice rink when I attempted that one jump and fell awkwardly. Instant pain. Shock, then tears. At first, I couldn't walk. Eventually, I made it backstage to a medic, who confirmed the sprained knee, tendonitis, and bursitis. Any time I tried to move or put weight on my leg, there was screaming pain. The attendants needed to know if I was going to skip my solo. I couldn't skip it. My mother and grandmother were in the audience, I worked all year for this weekend of shows, I was lucky to even have a solo; it was a big deal. So I pulled myself together. I tried to smile instead of cry. I went out and skated the solo--I just didn't attempt that one jump. And afterwards, I went into the stands, and told my mother what happened. I don't think my grandmother understood. And I know that neither of them were that disappointed in me and they both just wanted to see me skate, but I also know that my mother was just as excited as I was when I started landing that jump. And before I got my license, she was the one driving me to the rink every morning at 5 AM and every day after school. So given all that, in that moment, it was hard to feel like I did anything other than let them down by not landing that jump in that program. As a self-defining moment, I think it speaks to my tenacity and resolve in everything I do, along with a sometimes malignant desire to hold my parents together and be a light for them.

I moved from a small town to a larger city to attend college. My parents helped me move into my dorm my freshman year of college. After unpacking my things and getting settled into my new space, it was time for my parents to leave. My father cried. He continued to cry and made me feel bad about moving away to fulfill my goals and dreams. He wasn't able to hold himself together enough to drive home- my older brother had to. My mother isn't a very sensitive person, so she didn't do much to resolve the situation. Throughout my life my father has made me feel bad about doing what I feel is right for myself. He thinks many of the things that I do are to intentionally hurt him. This is a memory that I often come back to when I think about talking to my parents or giving them an update about my life- they showed that day that they can't handle my independence, so I've chose to keep them held at a distance.

I was getting ready to go away to college. I had recently come out to my sister but had not yet had the courage to speak to my parents about it.
 
 I started with my mom - my dad was deployed so I didn't have to "worry" about having the discussion with him yet. I don't remember what I said to her, but I remember her breaking down crying, saying "I don't want you to get AIDS and die." It wasn't said to be spiteful, hateful, or discriminatory - she had seen the AIDS epidemic wipe out so many people.

I remember that my grandparents took care of me as a child when my parents would be at work. They had a farm and my grandmother and I would walk in the garden and talk. I remember her loving an arbor my grandfather made for her. I remember how the light came through the leaves. This is still one of my happiest memories. I feel perfectly safe and use this as a happy memory.

I asked my parents if we could meet up. So we sat down on the couch in their living room and I told them that I am gay. My mom immediately burst into tears and my dad just sat on the couch in disbelief. They then started to try to prove to me that I am not gay by recounting old memories. After I finally convinced them, the grief set in. They started to talk about what this would mean for them, for our family, for their friends, and finally for me. They told me that I have destroyed our family and that my dad could lose his job if this came out. They asked me to not tell anyone else. I will never forget that moment.

I had a self injury problem when I was a young teenager (I was later diagnosed with PTSD). Despite the support of my parents, partner, and a number of mental and physical health professionals, I struggled with it for a while before I was able to stop (fortunately this hasn't been a problem for me for almost a decade now). After a particularly bad episode, my dad, who is usually a lighthearted goofy guy, came into my room to have a serious conversation about my problem and how he could help me stop. I was sitting on my bedroom floor working on my homework (I had a desk but found it impossible to keep clean). He came in and sat on the floor with me and started asking me about my self injury problem, in a gentle and sensitive way. It was clear that he was just trying to understand and help, and I wanted to give him solid answers, but I struggled to express myself in a clear way. 
 As we were talking, and he was trying very hard to understand my poorly worded answers, he started tearing up. I has never seen my dad cry before, not even when his sister died several years prior to this. I have only seen him cry twice since (once when his mother was near death and once on my wedding day). In retrospect, this was one of the first times I realized how much my life impacted other people, even when they weren't showing it externally. I desperately wanted to give my dad the answers he was looking for, but I just didn't have the words, and I felt horribly guilty, although I could tell he wasn't trying to make me feel this way. Eventually he realized I had told him all that I could at the time and left the room so I could finish my homework

As a child, I was something of an anxious overachiever. I was constantly asking my parents to help me study for tests or review my homework to make sure I'd done a good job. They never did. They usually said something like, "I'm sure it's fine" or "you know you're going to get a 100." However, when I was about 10, there was one time when my mom was out of town that my dad took me to a Chinese restaurant. It was quiet, and it was very rarely just the two of us, as I have six older brothers and sisters. I tentatively asked if he would help me study for my spelling test, and he actually agreed. The next 30 minutes, in which my father helped me study spelling, was the happiest time I've ever had with my father.

The first memory I think of that fits the memory criteria is in regards to my dad. I don't remember exactly when this took place, but I know it was at the end of elementary. My dad had anger issues, and we all knew it and never talked about it. He had exploded in anger before, hurling things out of windows and shouting so loud you could hear him on the other side of the house. It wasn't as bad as you see on tv or in movies, but it wasn't a pretty sight. Anyway, this one time he was incredibly mad and he was fighting with my mom. I've always been closer with her than with him - she and I were more alike. He was raging and it looked like he was going to get physical so I stepped between them and tried to calm him down. Next thing I knew he picked me up and threw me to the side. I landed on a laundry basket, breaking it. He then stormed out of the house in a rage, slamming the door. I would say there was silence after that, but I'm pretty sure we were all crying.

when I turned 18 they found a tumor in my brain and I dropped out of my first semester of college to have surgery. I wasn't scared or nervous about brain surgery but both my parents were. My mom had to go onto anxiety medication for a couple months because of it. But the worst part about the whole experience was when I came out of surgery and woke up. Initially I was on heavy medications but every once in a while my medication would wear off and I was left in pain for a couple minutes while I waited for the nurse to come and administer it. One particular night it happened it was just me and my dad in the hospital room. I woke up around midnight and could see, hear, or talk because the pain was so bad I just remember kicking my legs to get someones attention. My dad had immediately called the nurse but it was just me and him there for a couple minutes. I remember crying and begging for help and looking over at my dad who was crying next to me because he couldn't do anything to relieve the pressure in my head. The only other time in my life I have seen my dad cry was when his mother died a year or two before this.

I remember when I came out to my parents. It was on the scariest moments of my life. Well actually, my mom was the one who walked in on me and I had begged and pleaded with her that she does not tell my dad. She ended up telling my dad and I ended up getting kicked out of the house when it happened. My relationship with them suffered due to this, but I still have a very deep love for them both.

When I was 8 years old, my dad was arrested. I remember him dropping me off at the bus stop in the morning before school, hugging and kissing my sister and me good bye, telling us to have a good day at school, and that he would pick us up after school. When my sister and I got off the bus after school, no one was there to pick us up. My sister said we could just walk home. I wasn't sure about this idea because a couple of years earlier we had gotten in trouble for a similar situation but I usually did whatever my sister told me to do. 
 That night at dinner, we were having tacos, my mom told us that our dad had been taken to jail and she wasn't sure when we would see him again. I remember having just taken a bite of food and beginning to cry with the food in my mouth.

I am seven years old. My mother has recently been released from jail after being arrested for driving under the influence and petty theft. I have been staying st my father and grandmother’s house when my mother picks me up and takes me to the arcade to spend time with me. We have our photos made in a picture booth and trade in our tickets from the games for a frisbee. She promises that she is not going to drink anymore, and although it is a promise I have often heard before, I believe her.

I was 17 and it was a really warm and sunny day sometime in the summer / late fall. I had moved out of my parents house for a brief amount of time to live with my aunt but had come back home after she kicked me out as well. 
 I had been dating a girl for several weeks and was desperate to move back out of my parents home. She invited me to move in and so I decided to tell my parents I was a lesbian. 
 
 My mom came home and I went downstairs to our basement where she was and told her I was moving out. She asked where I was going and I said I was going to live with Rachel. She said OK. I asked her "you know that we are dating, right?" and she said she did know, and didn't understand it but as long as I didn't tell my siblings then she couldnt stop me. My siblings were about 9, 10 and 15 at the time. 
 I began arguing with her and said I should be able to be out and open and bring home my dating partners for holidays / etc just like I would be able to if I were straight, and we began to argue about the issue heatedly. My dad came in to see what was going on and essentially said my siblings didn't need to know about my "sexual preferences" and that was the end of it. 
 I packed up my stuff, left and barely spoke to them for years.

Growing up, I was never close to my dad. We fought a lot in my childhood, and grew even further apart as I grew into a teenager. Surprisingly, when I moved away to college at 18 years old, that changed. I remember my dad helping me move into my tiny dorm room. He didn't talk much. After helping me carry everything into my room, he hovered awkwardly. For the first time I can remember, he cried. 
 
 That night, I got an email from my dad that I have saved for 8 years now. The subject was "ramblings from dad". It must have been 20 paragraphs long. My dad expressed his love and admiration for me. He said that he'll miss my laugh. He said that he knew I would be successful ever since I was on student council in middle school. He said that he wished my mom and brother were silly and goofy and like me. He ended the email with "olive you". Since that email, our relationship has changed. We text each other daily. I have dinner with him weekly. We're closer than we ever were before.

When I was in elementary school, my parents signed me up for an IQ test to be admitted to the "gifted" program and didn't tell me about it. One day in third grade, an adult I didn't know came to the classroom, asked for me, and my teacher told me to go with them. We went to a tiny room and, to my knowledge as a third grader, played games for about two hours before I returned to class. I didn't think it was anything special, but when I got home and told my mom what had happened that day, and that I wish I hadn't had to miss class, she started crying and apologized. I couldn't understand why she was upset. She kept apologizing for not telling me, for not talking about the decision with me, and I couldn't understand for the life of me why she was having such a strong reaction to what I though wasn't that big a deal. 
 We haven't talked about that event since, but there have been a lot of other times where, as I've grown up with anxious, perfectionistic, self-disciplining tendencies, that my parents have talked about feeling like they set me up to fail, that they put me in too many situations where I was rewarded for academic achievement. I still don't completely understand what was going on during that memory, but it makes me wonder how much stress my parents put on themselves trying to raise me, how specifically they imagined my future, and the extent to which they've navigated the balance between letting me choose who to be and making decisions based on what will set me up to achieve to their standards.

One of my memories is hanging out with my mom while she quilted in the front room. I would often dump out a bucket of Legos on the carpet underneath the quilt that she was working on at the time. It would be a time to talk and just to be together in the afternoons after school. Oftentimes it was just me and my mom but sometimes my brothers would be there or the dog.

When I was in first grade, my middle sister was in high school and our oldest sister was away at college. My middle sister was struggling with an eating disorder and in full on teenage rebellion. I remember being in our living room and staring at the corner next to our upright piano trying to disappear because my mom was screaming at my sister and I couldn't make it stop. I couldn't escape. I think my dad was downstairs in my sister's room with my mom and sister. It was fall or winter because it wasn't very late but it was dark outside. The TV was on in behind me either PBS, "The Nanny", or "Jeopardy" because we didn't have cable.

The last time I saw my mother, she was laying in a hospital bed. Her mouth was open, she was wearing the peach turban that covered her head when she had gone bald from chemotherapy, and I'm not sure if she was alive or dead in that moment. It was all a blur and yet I've never gotten that image of her laying in that bed out of my head in the nearly 23 years that have passed since she passed away that October morning.Someone, I believe it was one of her doctors, said that I had arrived "just in time". My father was already with her - she had been rushed to the hospital the night before, where he remained overnight while I stayed with family friends up the road, as I'd done almost every time she had to stay for chemo treatments, surgeries, or whatnot. Somehow, this last time all felt different, like I knew on a very visceral level that something was wrong. I can still feel just how overwhelming it was. Sadness, confusion, anger, being shuffled into that hospital room to "say goodbye", which I couldn't because too many people were around and I was scared. A scared teenager who had no idea how to cope and was so overwhelmed emotionally it was almost as if I had to "perform" the act mourning my mother's loss. To this day, it bothers me that those last moments in the hospital are often what comes to mind when I think of her. I hate that it overshadows her warm smile, the laughs and good times we shared, and how loving and beautiful and vibrant of a person she was. That hospital room is the lens of grief that I can't seem to remove when I see my relationship with my mother and the years I've lived without her.

My mother was going back to college in the evenings (while working full-time) when I was in grade school. My father was a family attorney who did a ton of divorces. He'd often take me out bowling or for pizza on the nights my mom had class. He was terrified of divorce and losing custody of me. I remember sitting in the side booth of Pizza Hut when he went on and on about how other dads at Pizza Hut probably thought he was divorced too, and that if my parents ever got divorced, he would never, ever agree to only see me every other weekend. I distinctly remember eating pineapple pizza and nodding. I was 6 or 7 and had no real idea of what he was talking about. To this day, my parents are still together. I think about this a lot because my dad and I are incredibly close and confluent in our emotional lives.

My memory is of complaining that my tooth was broken and I told my father I was in a lot of pain. I was crying and asking for help, but he got angry with me. He didn't comfort me and then opened his mouth. He then said "Look at my teeth!" and acted as if I shouldn't be crying out in pain or asking for medical care for my tooth issues because he had worse teeth. I remember feeling guilty for needing help. I stopped telling my parents when I had aches and pains out of fear of their reactions. I also remember complaining to my mother and she sighed. She ignored the problem as well.

I remember when I was in grade 2 or 3 when I came home and found a green metal lunch box with a few gadgets in it that my mom had purchased for me from Ebay. I remember this as a positive memory because I don't think I remember her getting anything for me that wasn't necessary during that period of my life. We weren't well off at all, and my dad was a little emotionally abusive when It came to spending money, so I remember It as a really self less act on her part that she did solely to make me happy, and not as any sort of necessity.

An important memory was when my parents visited. Since I moved to Texas 5 years ago from California, I hardly get to see them. I remember setting up a tv mount with them. It was frustrating and difficult because the instructions weren’t well illustrated, but despite the frustration and the tension, we were able to mock the instructions and find ways to laugh about it. Flailing the papers around and using silly voices to read made it feel comical rather than stressful by the end. It meant a lot, that my family was there. It meant even more that we still found ways to make do with a smile even in frustration so that we could enjoy our limited time together.

When we lived in our first house,a three bedroom, 2.5 bath house on the corner, there were times that we didn't have a lot of money so vacations and other things that were normal for my classmates as a child, road trips, gaming systems, non-hand-me-down clothes, were few and far between. One way my parents tried to still expand my siblings and I's growth and understanding of the world was through music. We didn't have much but we did have a media player that could play CD's, cassettes, the radio, and it was hooked up to my dad's record machine. My siblings and I would have dance parties to my parents old records and songs that were on the radio, one time my younger sister and I had a flashlight dance performance for our parents and my mom had to reassure the neighbors who called that yes we were home and that no no one was breaking into our house. Another time during a family dance party, "Tubthumping" by Chumbawumba was played and I can remember dancing around the living room with my mother and every time it would get to the chorus and they would sing "I get knocked down but I get up again," my mom and I would hold hands and shimmy down until we were both crouching on the ground or in some cases accidentally letting go and both of us falling backwards onto the floor.

When I look back one of my earliest memories that brings on a smile is when mother tried to teach me how to whistle. I was terrible at such things. But she wouldn’t give up. This stuck with me because when I got older I always remember how I practiced and practiced and finally became good at whistling. It was a life lesson never give up and practice does make perfect. We used to watch Sesame Street together. I would sit on her lap, leaning on her chest and learn numbers and alphabets with her helping me out. We used to make audio tapes of my non-stop banter which my mother still has to this day.

When I was about 4 years old, my mother picked up my brother and I from my grandmother's house after she got off work. When we arrived home, my dad was there. We were all in the computer room when my mother found a purple pager laying on the desk, presumably belonging to another woman. My mother screamed and cried and my father denied the allegations.

One defining memory that comes to mind is regarding my father. When I was young, I spent school breaks and half of my summer vacation at his home in a different state. I vividly remember being very emotional and upset leading up to each and every visit I made to his home. One memory in particular, I begged and cried to my mother to not make me go to his home because he was mean and unpredictable. Unfortunately, there was nothing she could do to prevent the visit, as they were legally mandated. In an attempt to avoid going with him when he arrived to my mother's house to pick me up, I hid between the mattress and box spring of my bed to try to "hide". This was the exact moment I remember beginning to "hate" my father, which eventually spiraled into a series of fights, and abuse by my father.

When I was born my biological father left my mother at the alter, so I never knew too much about him. I remember, when I was five years old and he decided that he didn't want to have visits with me anymore. I carried the weight of feeling like I was not good enough for years, constantly trying to figure out who my father was. My mom went on to marry my step-dad, but we were never close and often times argued. I just remember feeling upset and alone. I always had it in my mind that I wasn't good enough and that was why my biological father left. I mean I understand now, that he left because he wasn't happy, but at a young age it still hurt.

In regards to a self-defining memory about a parent, my mind jumps to my mother. This memory is from childhood, from when I was about 10 or 11 years old, it was the Summer of 5th grade. As a family, we had a difficult year that year, my sister left for a semester abroad, and my mom's panic disorder had a flare up of intensity. I remember helping my mom through a particularly bad episode. There had been a few bad panic episodes leading up to this situation, where my mom had called 911 because the physical symptoms she was experiencing were severe. During this panic attack, we were both in her room, sitting on her bed. We had our dogs surrounding us, as they had a grounding affect on her at times. I remember sitting in front of her, with the landline phone next to us. She was talking about needing to be checked into an in patient facility and we were trying to go through our breathing exercises. I remember just looking into her eyes, and keeping my breath steady. I was just trying to stay solid, grounded. And after a long time, it passed, and we just rested afterwards.

When I was in kindergarten, my dad was a police office and was arrested for illegal drug use. I remember seeing it on TV. He was in prison for a few years and I remember taking trips to visit him as a family. It was a weird experience and one that I didn't fully comprehend being so young. After he got out, it was difficult for him to gain a job at some points. We moved so that I could go to a private school and that is one of the things that I try to focus on when thinking about it. He put a lot of effort into making sure his kids didn't go down the same path and did as much as he could to support us while I was growing up. I barely ever talk about it with anyone but it is still something I think about a lot, especially what others would think about him if they knew.

When I was 16 or 17, my mom found out I had been self harming. She had gone through my computer and saw something I said to one of my online friends about it. I had been in my bed, but not asleep, when she opened the door and turned on the overhead light and asked me, with anger in her voice, "Where have you cut yourself?". I felt like my heart actually stopped beating. The light was so bright but the words she was saying and the look on her face were so dark. I couldn't speak. It felt like there were hands around my throat. When I didn't answer she told me to get out of bed and show her my legs. I did, but not where most of the cuts and scars were... just a few.She told me to come with her downstairs. I did, and my older brother was waiting for us. She yelled at me. She wanted to know why I did it. When I told her I hated myself, she said "We all do. But that doesn't mean we go around cutting ourselves." She never asked me why I felt that way, or how she could help. She never told me it would be okay. She didn't tell me she loved me. She continued to yell, told me she regretted becoming a mom. That it was unfair of me to put her through "this shit". I cried so hard that night and I felt so very very alone. My brother was quiet, and I spent the night in his room. I cut for three more years before working through it on my own.

My mom had me when she was young with a man I don't know. My dad adopted me when I was 2 but I did not know this until I was about 12. When I was around 5 or 6 they were fighting and my dad said he was leaving and told me I was going to end up with another (third) dad. I did not understand what he meant at the time but knew he said it to hurt my mom.

The self-defining memory I have for my parents is of my mother and father. My father was very abusive towards my mother as I was growing up, and the night, in particular, has to do with the night that he was arrested for domestic violence. My mom had taken me to softball practice out of town while he took my sister and brother to my sister's softball game in town. My mom and I arrived back home before they did, and I raced to get ready for bed before he got home so that I would not have to talk to him. I raced to bed just as he was coming in the door. I put in my headphones and pretended to be asleep when he came to tell me goodnight. I fell asleep not long after, and the next thing I remember was getting a phone call from my mom a few hours later. I thought that it was weird that she was calling me because she was right down the hall from me, but I answered and immediately knew something was wrong. She asked me if I was awake and listening and told me that she was driving to the hospital with my father chasing her. She had called the police and they were on the way to the house. She had barely been able to escape as my father tried to strangle her. I checked on my siblings and told my sister to go back to bed that everything was okay and my brother was still asleep. I got the dogs in my room and a baseball bat for protection. My father arrived back home before the police got there, and he came upstairs and woke me up from my fake sleep in order to tell me that he was about to be accused of something that he didn't do. He then ran back downstairs, and I watched him in his room until the police came a few minutes later. They handcuffed him and took him out to the police car. They then came and got me and my siblings and told us all to pack bags that we were going to stay with our grandparents for the night. We went to their house and were put to bed but I didn't sleep. My mom and grandma showed up later to take us to my grandma's house.

While I was in high school I was expelled for some stupid and silly action I did. My mother came to school to pick me up after the principal called her. As we were driving home I told her I was sorry. She also did not seem upset so I asked her why? She said that sometimes even if you did something wrong and everybody seems to be against you, it is important to have someone on your side. she said, “We are family and I am your mother. I will always be on your side, come what may.” I never forgot that and I have to agree that it made our relationship better and stronger.

When I was around 16 years old my father was unemployed while my mother was the only one bringing in any money for the family. Even though my father would say he was working hard on things when I would walk back home from school he would be in the community pool just laying around. The stress put on my mother was great. So my brother an I got together, spoke to our mother. We said we didnt care where we had to go and what we had to do but she had to leave him.

As long as I can remember my parents have never gotten along. There is no love or affection only arguing and frustration. A memories that always strike me was when I was in elementary school. From the ages of 4-5 I rarely was home. My parents had me living with several different people, usually people from our church. I would only be home on the weekends, which is when I'd see my parents fight. To this day I've always questioned why I was sent to other peoples homes. My parents worked, but even when I was home they rarely acknowledged me and became angry if I tried to. At the same time they were always angry that I didn't enjoy sports and hated when I played video games. I've known since I was little I wanted to be better than my parents and I'm still striving towards that goal.

I feel bad that this is the first memory to come to my mind but I do feel like it fits a lot of this criteria. About 4 years ago, I had a normal dental checkup that my mom drove me to. I was maybe 16 or 17, something like that. We drove to our dentist office for my appointment. My mom is a single mom who often sticks around for appointments and extracurriculars that I have. Sometimes I think about what she could be doing with that time to have her own fulfillment. I dont know, I know she likes sticking around for me because she cares but it seems like she could be doing something cool instead. 
 
 Anyways, I had my checkup and they found 11 cavities. 11. I never even had one before that. They were inbetween my teeth so they were affecting two at a time. I was numb and sad. We're not exactly rich and I am always very conscious about how my life costs money for us. I felt like absolute trash, like even worse than a child who couldn't take care of their own teeth. Children get cavities. Older teens don't and not 11 at a time. I look back on it now, espeically after their fillings didn't hold up and ruptured in my mouth causing me severe pain for days on end, and wonder if I actually needed all of those and if there was something they could have told me before that check in. Whatever. 
 
 Anyways, I was devestated and left the dentist office and walked into my mom's car. I immediately started crying, I felt so bad. From the finances to the shame, it was just a lot. My mom immediately started demanding information on what happened and asked me if they had done anything to hurt me. I choked out a No and kept crying. Then she demanded to know if they had touched me inappropriately. What? I answered No again and then told her that I needed some time to just calm down. So she starts driving and I'm still crying, trying to pull myself together. Then she says "I suppose if you can't answer then you can't hang out with your friends later today." What? How is taking away time with my friends supposed to get me to stop crying? Ridiculous honestly! I was annoyed by that which ironically helped me stop crying faster. I eventually told her I was embarrassed and worried about money and she lightened up and started comforting me. But the whole incident really stuck with me, just how much she cared that it really just ended up with her handling it poorly. She cared so much that she was just trying to do or say anything to make me talk and then it just shat on itself. A mess truly haha

When I was eight my family drove cross country from North Carolina all the way to California. It took us four days to get to our hotel in California. I remember playing different car games and sing a longs during our trip. We would drive all day and stay at a nice hotel each night. I remember my parents planned the trips very well and we had an awesome time. I had been looking forward to our trip/vacation for months because we were going to visit Disneyland while in California. Our hotel was very fancy and had an indoor pool which every night we would swim in. Every night we would eat at a different restaurant and I always got to pick which places we would eat at. I was young and innocent I did not have a care in the world. One specific memory is of riding the roller coaster and the spectacular view I had of the setting sun at the apex of the ride.

Divorce of parents at a young age. I think about how growing up with separated parents and their partners afterward has impacted me. It resulted in a divide over different issues growing up, what time and holidays are spent with each parent, created financial issues that probably wouldn’t have been an issue if they stayed together, and more. I also think about how this has changed relationships with me and my siblings, a lot of the time relating to how when arguments or disputes came up and some of my siblings see it more through the eyes of one parent or another.

My father came to the door to pick us up for his weekly visitation when I was in fourth or fifth grade, and when i answered the door I asked him why he left my mother for some other lady. He responded, I didn't love her anymore. I made the decision to not fall in love and make a commitment with someone unless I planned on loving them forever and keeping my commitments in life.

I don't know where to start, I was raised in a broken home, My mother always worked, My father was in and out and when he was around it was very abusive, When my parents got divorced, My mother started dating a woman, Whom I fell in love with as a mother figure, She was there more than both of my own parents combined, It was easy to talk to her, Because when I was in the 4th grade, I confided in her and told her I liked boys, and she welcomed it with open arms, and said it will all be okay, My mother was welcoming, My father not so much, He hated it so much, That one day in the 6th grade he nearly killed me by putting me through a wall in our home, and started bashing my head into the floor, he got away with it.

My parents are very supportive of me. They always ensured that I had all the emotional support I needed. I am very lucky to have kind parents. They were strick but fair when it came to discipline and following the rules. They tried to keep me out of trouble...mostly with success. Every person gets into trouble sometimes, but have a good support system is key to not letting it have a big impact on your life.

I remember waiting in the hospital as my father, in his capacity as a pastor and friend, visited a family friend who had just been in a serious accident. I remember reading books in the lobby as my father visited with the family. I briefly remember the husband of the woman who had been in the accident coming to speak with me. I remember feeling nervous, but not as nervous as one would expect in spending time in a hospital. There was large artwork in the lobby where I was sitting. I think the book I was reading was ''Hitty: Her First Hundred Years," a book about a doll who had a variety of owners over time.

When I was in third grade, I really did not want to go to school. I went to a small school from prekindergarten through 12th grade. My mother taught art for 6-12th grade at the school. The same day my mother had a hair appointment at a fancy salon. 
 I remember refusing to go to class. Crying and making a scene. I don’t remember why I didn’t want to go, but inevitably my mom drove us both home. I remember she refused to talk to me on the car ride home and when we got in the house. 
 Naturally, I felt awful because I made her miss an appointment and her refusal to talk to me only made me feel worse. She went to her room. I went to the kitchen and got a knife. I think this was the first time I seriously considered killing myself.

I remember when I was about 5 or 6 my parents had had a fight and my dad took me and my brothers into his truck to take us to our grandma's house. My parents fighting wasn't an uncommon occurrence. What made this night stand out was the fight my dad started with two guys at a gas station on our way to grandma's. While he was inside paying for gas, two guys came up and started to admire his truck. I remember hearing them say things like, "That's a cool truck" and "Looks good." When my dad came out of the store, he didn't take kindly to these two and started yelling things. Everyone started swinging fists and yelling. Eventually my dad jumped into the truck and peeled out of the station without even getting the gas. As we drove away, one of the guys pulled out a gun and shot at the truck. I can still picture the bullet hole in the back.

When I was 15 I had come to the realization that I was gay. I had explored this with guys and found that I wanted to tell my parents who I was. I was raised as a christian and had my mom tell me at one point that if she found out that I was gay she would kill herself. I pushed off coming out for months. Each month had a new event that would come up that I did not want to negatively impact with my news. September, it was back to school season and I wanted to make sure I would have new clothes for school. October, my little brothers birthday. November, my dad's birthday and my older sister's birthday and not to mention Thanksgiving. December, well Christmas of course. January, my older brother's birthday. February, I couldn't ruin valentines days now could I? March, my mothers birthday. Then April came around and I feel in love with my first boy. After a month of dating and sneaking around I could not contain it any longer. The 1st Saturday of may rolled around and I had to sit my parents down and tell them I was gay. I had packed my bags and suitcase with my clothes including the set of dishes I asked for that Christmas thinking Id be kicked out when I came out. When I told my mom and dad that I needed to talk to them both privately my mom yelled at my siblings to leave the room. As if that was not setting the stage for what was to come. I said, "Im gay." My mom broke into tears and my dad grew a stoic stern look on his face as he turned and looked away from me in silence. After a few minutes he asked if I had any attraction towards women what so ever. I said no. My mom continued to sob. He asked what he should do given the new information and I said to do nothing. That I only wanted them to know who I truly was. He told me that he loved me and would always love me no matter what. It took them time to adjust to the knowledge but eventually years later and many many arrangements too they grew to accept me openly.

The property on which my family lives has a pond in the back field with a crick running to it, which has become wide and deep with mud over the past few decades. When I was about ten years old, one of our horses fell into the crick and became trapped in the mud. My father discovered him late in the morning on a Sunday. It was summer. The horse, Harley, was still alive but had struggled enough to get sucked up to his chest in mud, so that the only part of him above water was his head. He'd stopped panicking and was laying still by the time my father found him. 
 My dad, being the way that he is, sprang into action. He ran back to the house and returned minutes later in waders, rubber boot/pants that extend to his chest and fit like suspenders. He climbed into the muck and attempted to get Harley out by hand, while telling me to run and get others for help. I returned with my grandfather (father's side) who in his early seventies was still very much able to help, my grandmother (father's side) who owned the property we live on and at this point in her life was going about everywhere on a motorized scooter, my mother, and my other grandmother (mother's side). 
 While my father, mother, and grandfather worked to get Harley out of the crick, I stood to the side with the grandmothers. My mother's grandmother, overwhelmed by the drama and not wanting to be involved, left to return to the house. My other grandmother stayed by me. After some struggling, my parents realized this was not going to work, and went to get the tractor and straps to try and mechanically pull Harley free from the mud. 
 This worked, but there are two things that stick with me about this memory. Firstly, my parent's immediate leap into action, so sure that something could be done to save the day and that they would be the ones to do it. I want this to be a defining feature for myself as well. I've thought about that a lot. I want that ineffable bravery, that act without thinking kind of attitude. The other thing that strikes me about this memory is the way my grandmother was crying and screaming next to me, going absolute hysterical, and how my mother climbed out of the crick covered in mud to yell at her and make her leave as the other grandmother had. When I asked why my mom was yelling, she told me that crying and panicking did absolutely nothing to help, and that "if you're that damn scared, you haven't prayed hard enough about it." I think about that advice very often.

One of my best memories of my parents was watching my Dad labor for weeks over this styrofoam board that had index cards all over it. Every week, my Dad would give my mom a clue that she would have to decipher. If the clue was deciphered correctly, she was able to remove one index card of her choosing. By the end of 12 weeks, all the index cards had been removed and underneath each index card was an image. Each image spelled out the sentence "First Class Flight to Paris For Our 30th Anniversary. I Love You!" It was so cute to see them play a game to show their love.

I vividly remember arguing with my dad about whether my mom took me to the zoo. We were discussing whether my mom spent time with me. He claimed that I was remembering wrong or had been brainwashed. I told him that I had been a tiger, which fueled his argument as it's one of those things kids say that isn't meant to be taken literally. Now I no longer have the memory of going to the zoo at all.

I remember that when I was 13 years old, my dad was given tickets to a Barry Manilow concert from his job, and he decided to take me to the concert with him. It was the only time I had ever been to the ampitheater in Pittsburgh, and my first time ever attending an outdoor concert. We didn't have much disposable income as a family, so getting to do anything outside the house was a special treat. I remember my dad smiling and laughing, and enjoying the music with him. This stuck out to me so much because I don't have very many good memories of my dad...he was either working or golfing most of the time growing up, and we rarely spent any quality time together. I also had other siblings who he could have taken to the concert, but he picked me to go to the concert with him, so I felt special because of that. To this day, when I hear a Barry Manilow song, I think of my dad and attending that concert with him as a young teenager.

When I was about 10 years old I was playing in the pool with my dad. We were using a pool noodle to blow water in each other's face. I thought it would be a good idea to blow the water while he was breathing. As soon as I did that, my dad who is a very strong swimmer, went under. My mom stood there yelling at him to stop messing around. After about 30 seconds to a minute my mom pulls him out of the water and he starts coughing up water.

I remember it being a warm summer night in August. I haven't been eating well and I've started to self-harm since I was so scared to tell my parents that I was gay. Mom noticed that I wasn't eating well and would occasionally check in and ask if I wanted to talk about anything. I usually said "No", but that night I said "Yeah". I was under my bed covers and my mom was sitting next to me. She asked what was up and I prefaced with "I don't want you to get angry with me, and I'm scared that you'll think of me differently." She asked me what was wrong again. I put the covers over my head, took a deep breath, removed the covers, and said "I'm gay." Mom looked at me for a long time without saying anything, and then said "Are you sure?" I said yes, and she was in disbelief. She turned away from me and a tear ran down from one of her eyes. I've never seen my mom cry. She then started saying things like "Did I give birth to a woman? Now I won't have grandchildren." I remained calm during all of this. I told her that being gay is not a mental illness, and she agreed. She then hugged me tightly and said "Don't worry, we'll find a way to change you." I remember feeling uncomfortable and unsafe at that moment. I told my mom that I was going to check on my sister, and left the room. I told my younger sister what happened, and i bursted into tears. My sister said that nothing's going to happen to me and that my parents will have to go through her if they wanted to get to me. I slept in her room that night. My mom knocked on my sister's door an hour later and asked if I was sleeping. My sister said yes, and my mother left.

A rather intense memory that I re-visit often has to deal with my mother. It was around the holiday time and I knew that my church was doing its "giving tree." This meant that a number of gift ideas for children in low-income homes had been hung on the tree. Our family would usually grab a few names to buy for from this tree. Knowing this, when my mom asked "would you like a Wiffle ball bat?" I thought she meant it was what she had bought for the name off the giving tree - I remember I was maybe 10 at the time and the one name we had picked up was "an 8-year old boy." I answered honestly: "that would be a good gift for an 8-year old, we already have enough though." I didn't realize my mom had bought the wiffle ball bat as a gift for me. When I realized I was extremely (more-so than what was warranted) overcome with guilt. I felt that my mom had just done this spontaneous and kind thing, and rather than give her the satisfaction of gratefulness and happiness at a gift, in my confusion, I had been honest and admitted I didn't really need or want that.

This memory may have been a while, but I often remember it. One time I went with my father in a market. We ran into old beggars and looked very weak. He asked for money to eat. My father did not give money and we passed away from that place. Not long after, we passed a middle-aged father who sat pensively in front of a shop. My father was momentarily stunned, then my father gave him $ 100. The man fell silent and with tears in his eyes said thank you then left quickly. I was confused by my father's behavior. 
 Then we stopped for a moment at a cafe to drink. Father told me about Dad's strange behavior. The old beggar who looked weak was actually a lazy young man. Father had seen him erase his old face makeup and he was actually still young. He should work hard instead of begging. When I was a seven years old my mother was deathly ill and needed emergency surgery. She was sick and home from work with what assumed to be a minor sickness. One crucial self-defining memory surrounding my parents is when I came out as being gay.  Well, at one point, I had gone on a school trip to Seattle, and during the trip, I got a necklace with my then-boyfriend's face imprinted on it.  He said I was confused, and it was just a phase, etc. He would make jokes about me at the breakfast table. Then, when I went to Denver for my first year of college, he refused to help pay. That was years ago. Now, in the present, my Dad and I are fine. We get along well, and he has come to accept me and my sexuality.

I came out to my parents while home for Thanksgiving. At Christmas, I was the only child home (I have three siblings, but they are all partnered and were spending Christmas with the in-laws). My parents initiated two or three lengthy conversations about my being gay, and about my decision to pursue same-sex romantic relationships. (They are conservative evangelical Christians, though moderate in some significant ways, such as politically or reading the Bible literally.)
 
 I could write at length about that time, but i'll highlight one moment. I remember waking up earlier than usual one morning and hearing my parents talking in the living room. I pressed my ear to the door to make out what they were saying. It was difficult, but I remember hearing my mom repeat some of the things I had said from the day before. It was clear she was taking my beliefs very seriously, and wanting to make them her own. But it was also not something they wanted to work out in front of me. In part I respect that -- it is stressful to have to walk through every twist and turn with your folks -- but in part it was isolating.
 
 My mom did read the books I recommended to her. I don't recall precisely if she had begun reading before that Christmas or if it was only later. But it was good to hear my mom being sincere behind closed doors.

It was Christmas eve of 2010. My brother and I were home from college at my mother's apartment in Davie, Florida. I remember coming out as bisexual to my mom and dad. They were not very understanding of what i had told them at first and told me that it was just a phase and that everyone goes through it. My mom got breast cancer when i was about 12 years old. Finding out a loved one has cancer is hard especially for a 12 year old. This was super hard on my entire family. When I was young, I stayed with a baby sitter who also had a son. He was twice my age, I was 6 and he was 12. He molested me on a few occasions and eventually, I told my mother.
