 I know she was certainly upset, devastated, at what I was telling her as we've discussed it well into my adulthood. We were in elementary school and McDonald's was doing a Happy Meal promotion with Nintendo, giving away Super Mario toys. I was desperate for the Koopa Troopa toy that bounced when you squeezed a little pump. Our McDonald's didn't have any, and it was a couple weeks into the promotion and I'd been hoping for this prize every time (as children of a single mom going to school and working full time, we got a lot of Happy Meals). We went to several McDonald's locations until we finally found one that had the bouncing Koopa toys. One time, I spoke to my dad outside of our house when I was around 16. My mother had just had another meltdown, and so he and I were outside, trying to cool down from the intensity. Now, even though that I really do have a dad but in most times I feel that I don't have one because his vices of smoking and being an alcoholic. When I was a teenager, I was tasked with recording a racing show for my dad in the evenings while he was outside doing yard work. This show came on every other day. When I was going into kindergarten I remember my mom sitting down with me with my cello. My preschool had offered group cello lessons that I had participated in for at least one school year. It felt like a very big decision for a 5 year old, and the rest of my cello playing career began after that. Practicing cello was always my "chore" because I had decided to continue with the lessons at kindergarten age. This was a big defining moment because I played cello from 4-16 years old. Another memory i have about my parents they where in the room fighting on day and i walked in to grab the remote and my dad was smacking around my mom. My mother called me, inconsolable, on a Friday because she was fairly certain that my grandfather was dying. I got on a plane out to Wisconsin to be there for her and to help my family as he slipped away in hospice care. As the oldest of my generation, my family relied on me to help with little things. I confronted the decline of a man Ioved and respected every day for a week. But what surprised me the most was how much my parents relied on me emotionally in this time. I was a rock for them as they held the rest of the family together, and my presence calmed and soothed them in ways that none of us had expected. Even though it was a pretty traumatic experience for everyone, I was able to be there for them when they needed it, and that became incredible affirming and character-forming for me moving forward.

My mom taught me how to read when I was three. 
 
 Before then, I would take out newspapers once my parents were done with them. I would look at the pictures and make up a story to the picture. I'd tell my parents I was "reading." My mom took it upon herself to teach me how to read.
 
 At this point in her life my mom was 22-23, and she stayed home or worked odd jobs, and sometimes jobs that required a night shift. We were broke as can be. We didn't have a lot at all, But my mom bought workbooks and books from the dollar store. We sat, and she would teach me letters and how to put those letters together. I remember sitting with her and writing the word "the" on thick-lined paper, the kind with green lines and those hyphens all the way down the middle.
 
 From then on, books were my everything. If I had a week when I was "good," my mom would take me to the dollar store where she would buy me a Sesame Street book. I had a whole set of them when I was little. I do not remember a world in which I did not read because it was always so encouraged, even if my parents didn't read more than the newspaper.

The first time I saw my father cry was the day my brother died. He came into my room at 7am and turned on my light, so I rolled around to face the wall and mumbled, "Five more minutes." He hesitated before saying quietly, "William died in his sleep last night." I shot out of bed and said, "What?" As we stood facing each other and I saw he was serious, he was crying, I started to cry too. I kept repeating, "I made plans for him, he was gonna be the one to live," while he silently hugged me back.

I remember another time I was at my dads and it was around the same age as the last one and there was a boy next door that I had a crush on. In my household, my Dad worked and my Mom took care of the children and the house.My first memory of my parents is in my grandmas family farm house. We were living there along with an uncle or two. I always felt that feeling attracted to men was right for me, but something you never talk about. I am however lucky that she didn't push the issue after that.

During high school, I begin to come to grips and acceptance that I was a gay male, while simultaneously realizing that there was nothing wrong with identifying as LGBT. I had steadily increased my self isolation during the past year, and was becoming more and more bitter towards my parents blatant homophobia. Finally, one July evening, my mom came in and sat down with me and asked why I had been separating myself from them. With a secure housing plan in the dorms, and a car in my possession, I decided that the time was right for me to come out. I remember telling her "Mom, I'm gay, and I'm so tired of hearing you and Dad be bigoted and hateful towards the LGBT community. I cannot stand it any longer." 
 
 We both held each other and cried. She was not exactly accepting, but she did not kick me out of the house either. Later that week, she gave me a book titled "You Don't Have To Be Gay."

I remember on Halloween as a kid. We went to pizza hut before trick or treating just my mom and I. She told me while eating that my cousin was a lesbian. I believe she came out not long before this. I was shocked but accepting. I already had a gay uncle. I remember vividly her mentioning feeling bad for my aunt and it must be hard. I didnt understand and later when I realized I was gay had a very hard time telling her. This memory running through my mind. Scared she might not accept me.

When I was 14 years old, I became addicted to gay pornography, and would often look at it on my flip phone (back then, it was amazing that a flip phone could access the internet). Knowing I'd been caught using my phone after bedtime, I handed it to her. She opened the phone and it had stayed on the current Google image search I had pulled up. She hit the "Back" button, each time showing me the image and asking, "Do you like that?"
 A few minutes later, I was called into the living room. My parents were sitting on the couch. I perched on the piano bench, not really looking at them. They told me that they still loved me no matter what, and obviously had my phone confiscated at night (though, thinking back on it, I think they gave it back after just a few days.)

My dad would take me to mcdonalds to get a kid's meal and I remember the toy being a CD of various kids-oriented musicians, like S Club 7 or others you would hear on radio disney. About 2 years after my mom died, my dad started dating secretly. He would go out and although me and my younger brother knew (he was 15-16 at the time), my dad refused to address it. While our sense of family was severely disrupted after the death of my mom, this threw our relationship completely out of balance. He refused to accept that not discussing bringing someone else into our house might be painful for me and my brother, and said that it meant that something was wrong with us. He said many toxic things during this time, including that he wouldn't love me or support me if I didn't support this relationship. While eventually I accepted it, my relationship with him never fully recovered.

This is about how I'm gay, right? Let's get to some of that! Alright, so I was a member of Delta Lambda Phi at Iowa State, which was started as a fraternity for gay guys. My dad wasn't in it, but it'll make it seem less out of the ordinary when I mention about how every single one of my fraternity brothers was gay. In the early aughts in Iowa, it was still pretty interesting to people in the media. A couple of our members were photographed for one article and a prison inmate wrote to them afterwards, having developed a crush. I don't believe they put any effort into finding out what he was in for, but they were just not into it, and felt very uneasy about the exposure afterwards and a little fearful for their safety. I did read one of the letters, and it didn't seem threatening. It would not have gotten a good grade in one of my English classes and my guess is he wasn't super intellectual.
 
 Young me, though, was not anti-gun like current me and was interested in helping my friends feel safer. My dad was just as super duper fond of guns then as he is now, so I asked him if he knew what went into getting a concealed carry permit. He DID wonder why I was asking, and I explained the situation, and he told me what he knew (I didn't fact check it, but I passed it along to my fraternity brothers, just to sorta show I was paying attention, they sorta got over it without actually arming themselves or changing anything about their lives). Since then I've gotten a lot more pro-inmate and, for a year or two, had a prison pen pal in Texas who was a murderer. Well, I also cursed out a recently released scary dude who kept pocket dialing me after a mutual friend gave him my number, so there's that. I never heard from him again, and we never actually spoke at length about anything ever, so it's not like I miss him, but I wish I'd handled it differently now that I'm older and wiser, not because I fear retribution or anything immature.
 
 My dad hadn't really thought my friends were at risk either, but it was the first time since I'd come out to him via mom in high school that we'd ever really discussed men being attracted to other men. It went pretty well! Besides all the half-assed attempts by my parents to butch me up as a kid, I also flipped out when my dad used the term "faggy" to describe something (I think someone's gloves?) shortly after I'd officially come out as gay. He never officially declared he was cool with it, so I assumed he was still really uncomfortable with me being gay as of that moment. He's been far right ever since I started barely paying attention to politics around the time of the 1996 presidential election, I'm talkin' John Birch Society, all of that, and I have gone the complete other way with my own views. I had girded my loins in anticipation of a possible confrontation and angry storm off upstairs, but I realized he still wanted what's best for me as his son. It was the lamest reason to feel better about him as a parent, but I did.

The day I came out. We all had dinner and were about to wrap up the night. My mom and dad called me and my sister to the kitchen. They had told us they wanted to talk to us. They said that we all needed to talk like adults and they announced their divorce. They asked if I had anything to say. I said yes and I came out to them right there. My mom was crying and my dad was speech less.

My dad had pretty serious mental illness and he and I had a really strained relationship. Once my brother and I were in the garage with him. I was only about 13 when this happened and I remember how mad it made me and how I felt like my dad hated me and only cared about my brother.

The summer between my sophomore and junior year of college my grandfather became very sick. We soon discovered that my grandfather had a rare and serious brain tumor. He was receiving most of his care in the city that I was living in at the time (about 2 hours away from my hometown where all my family lived). That summer I had a large role in care giving for my grandfather. He eventually was sent to a care facility back in his hometown. I knew he didn't have much time left, so made efforts to visit my hometown more often. By this time my junior year of college began. I didn't have class on Thursdays, so I was planning to leave Wednesday afternoon to go visit my grandfather. While driving on Wednesday, I received a text message from a close friend expressing his condolences about my grandfather. My parents hadn't told me he had died earlier that day. I felt betrayed.

When I was in college I went to the city near my home for spring break. I did not have a good relationship with my mom but somehow she found out me and my friends were near and insisted that I meet with her. I was not out to her about having a girlfriend but I knew I should tell her soon. Instead of a pleasant dinner with my mother, it was an ordeal. She "confronted" me about dating a woman and somehow knew who it was and knew that my partner was older than me. She told me that I did not actually know that I was queer. She told me that I was naive and wrong about who I was. She told me that I was being influenced by the people around me, including my partner, who was manipulating me. I was crying. She left me in the restaurant, crying.

I was very active on the internet when I was a young teenager. I had a few friends from school, but I rarely spent time with them during the evening or on the weekends. The majority of my social life was dominated by friendships I had formed with other young people online. My internet friends came from all over the world. Part of maintaining my social life was frequently posting on Tumblr. It became a great space for me to discuss my interests in books and television shows but also a space for me to explore my burgeoning identity. I first became aware of the fact that I wasn't straight in seventh grade, when I was about 13 years old. By the time of this memory, I was 14 years old and in 8th grade. I had come out to a few close friends in real life, none of my internet friends, and certainly not my family. I had posts on my Tumblr that indicated support for LGBT people and rights, but nothing that suggested I was anything more than an ally. 
 
 One day, my parents sat me down. They had looked at my blog and were concerned about me. I instantly felt betrayed - I never told them about my Tumblr. I didn't use my full name or share any identifiable personal details online either, just my incredibly common first name and what state I lived in. My parents had to dig through all of my online presence to find connections to this Tumblr, and decided to confront me about it. I imagine both she and my dad were like this, but I specifically remember my stepmom demanding me to tell her that I was straight. I lied and said that I was. All three of my parents - my mom, my dad, and my stepmom - told me that it was not okay to be outwardly supportive of LGBT rights because I was a few months shy of going to high school. According to them, my high school classmates would bully me for this position. This was 2011, when same-sex marriage was a prominent political issue. We lived in a somewhat moderate region of Pennsylvania; close to a diverse and strongly Democratic city, surrounded by moderately red suburbs. 
 
 I knew that they were wrong. I had already found some supporters among my peers, and was developing a thick enough skin to deal with any bullies. What hurt me the most was what their argument meant. If this was how they reacted to me being an ally, how in the world could I come out to them? I knew they would never physically abuse me or kick me out of the house, but I couldn't feel confident that they would support me in the future. Any plans I had to tell them about my identity were delayed for another one to two years, a lifetime at that age.

When I was growing up, my mother was very vocal about supporting gay rights. She also had a friend who was gay while I was growing up that I remember visiting with her sometimes. When she found out that I was interested in girls and not just in boys, that seemed to abruptly change. She used to go through my things and had found a note that a girl I was dating had written me. She yelled a lot. She insisted that it was just a phase or that if it wasn't a phase that I had to be a lesbian. If I wasn't a lesbian and I wasn't straight I must just be confused. She grounded me and attempted to ban me from being allowed to see the girl that I was dating, who I had also been friends with for a long time. She also tried to claim that another girl I had dated must have made me gay or at least been the one who caused me to be confused. After that my mom ungrounded me and removed her ban of me spending time with my girlfriend. She acted like she had just needed time to adjust but it had really been because she didn't want to have to tell anyone. Now she continues to just act like it was a phase.

My dad used to take us camping back in the woods close to the 2nd German house. We would pack up the car with the tent, 3 sleeping bags, the 2 jungle-themed sleeping mats, assorted tools and small machetes, 2 or 4 lbs of frozen ground beef blocks, and bottled water. We'd also get Heidi's food, a water bowl, and her leash. We would drive the 3 hours back listening to AFN's days-old NPR broadcasts and singing, while Grace or I read in the backseat. We would get to the woods in the late afternoon, find a good flat-ish spot for the tent and begin to unload. I was usually the 'fire-master' and Grace helped to clear the ground of stones for the tent.

My dad was a farmer, and my mom a teacher. Neither of them made a lot of money. One year, in the summer, my parents sat me down on the edge of their bed. They needed to pay to have a field sprayed to kill weeds or something like that, and they couldn't afford it - I believe it was roughly $1,000. However, I had been saving any amount of money I got my hands on from Christmas, birthdays, helping with the family business, since as early as I can remember. So there I was, sitting between my parents when they asked if they could borrow money from me to pay for this. My mom did the talking, trying to explain to me why they needed money and how they would pay me back. I think my dad was too ashamed to say much really. I said yes, and for the next several years they slowly paid me back, often in the form of buying me things. We would be in the store, and my brother would ask for something he'd want and they'd say sure, then I'd ask for something similar, and would be told that they would but it would count against what they owed me. 
 
 This set the tone for all of my childhood really - my parents were terrible with money and by the time they finally started getting their act together, it was in the form of trying to save every cent they could, from not running the AC in the summer to never eating out because it was "wasteful." I was acutely aware of my parent's financial state as a child, and the strain it put on them (and by extension my brother and me).

I was in late high school, and I was talking with my dad about A Lot of Things. We were discussing my religious education, and how I felt it was lacking, but now that I was close to adulthood, the onus was on me to define what I wanted to learn and to make it happen, which felt like a big responsibility, and I felt behind. At some point, the conversation shifted to what I wanted to study in school and "do with my life." (Perhaps we were discussing whether I wanted to become a religious professional.) I remember asking my dad his thoughts about whether to pursue work that felt important, felt like it was affecting human lives directly and positively, or whether that did not need to be a focus, as those jobs can be less stable and lower paying. He told me that he really didn't know what advice he wanted to give. He explained that part of him so wanted to tell me to pursue whatever was in my heart, take risks, be an artist, whatever it was, and that the money would follow if I was being fulfilled. But part of him wanted to say, go for stability. When you are financially stable, you can have so many more options. In giving me both of those sides, and not knowing which way he would send me, he opened that huge, important world of decision making up to me. This is a question that I come back to often, as I experience more of the world and different personal financial situations. It hasn't yet become uncomplicated for me.

I remember going camping with my parents and they would always drive up with all of my siblings in the car. We would drive through all of these country back roads and we would also talk to one another about everything going on in our lives. I never felt like I could be as open with them about things going on so I would more less just stay quiet the whole time. I realized at this moment that I was hiding so much that was going on in my life and I would never let those things come to the surface, especially during these trips.

I remember having to come out and how terrified I was. Especially telling my mother. I knew my father would be fine with it. Oddly that is the opposite of most of my peers. My dad is very open minded, liberal, and dropped hints to me that he knew I was gay and supported me. When I told them, my mom was shocked. But she eventually accepted it and my dad helped her through it. Then I noticed that my dad is the dominating personality. My mom would probably be like the rest of her family: conservative and closed minded, but my dad must seem to set her on a path of being accepting and liberal.

I've never physically met my dad and probably never will. I have however found him on facebook. I have found out that he was married before I was born so he cheated on his wife. I messaged him and he has never responded. I applaud my mom because she was a single mom my whole life. It let's me know that I can do good for my kids even if I do end up alone.

When I was maybe 13 or 14, I remember my mom made chili for dinner. It was nothing out of the ordinary. She usually made dinner, and my family ate together nearly every night at 6pm on the dot. But one time my dad didn't like the chili. He said it wasn't seasoned correctly. He yelled at my mom, and she cried. He threw the food away. Dumped the whole pot in the trash, which was devastating since we didn't have much food. I always grew up worried that one day I would marry a man who screamed at me for not making food to his liking.

When I was a sophomore in high school, my anxiety was at its peak, and I was obsessed with doing well on school assignments, and especially what my teachers though of me personally. I felt like their opinions of my "goodness" as a person were direct results of my academic success and that if I did less than my best possible work they would be disappointed in me.
 I was bringing in a draft of an essay for a teacher to review, and I was so anxious about what he would think of the essay that I started panicking on the way to school, like, hysterical sobbing and hyperventilating. My mom was driving me (we didn't have school buses and in the winter when it was too cold to walk, she'd often give me a ride), and kept telling me to calm down with increasing intensity and volume. When I didn't, she threatened to turn the car around and take me back home, which made me panic more, as I was terrified of missing school. Instead of taking me to school or home, she drove me to our GP's office, (by which time I was already late for school, knew I wouldn't make it, and had gone quiet) and took me inside. She told me to sit in the waiting room, and I heard her asking the secretary if there was "anything we can give her, just to knock her out or something. I don't know what to do with her. I can't take her home."
 They said the weren't going to give me any drugs, but that they could schedule an appt. with a psychologist at a branch of the children's hospital later that day. We went back home, not speaking, I went up to my room and waited to leave for the doctor's appt. (sorry this is getting so dark and dramatic, I didn't expect this memory to come back in so much detail) I cut up my shoulder and put on a sweater, we left for the psych appt., it was an unremarkable appt. where the doctor told me to try deep breathing when I was stressed, and then we went to get ramen. The thing that sticks out is how many different relationship dynamics happened between us that day. When we left the psych office to go get ramen, I was calm again, if a bit frustrated, my mom was calm again and, I think, felt like she'd done her part to fix the situation, and we went out to my favorite restaurant and had a really good, calm time. I went back to school the next day and after that week we never talked about it again.

My parents fought a lot. It was always scary and we never got used to the damage. I remember one time getting up with my siblings, how im not sure, but we got up and my mother got us up and i had to help my siblings get dressed. She then lead us to a room where a police officer( female) was there and she gave us teddy bears. My mom left and then another officer came in and told us that my grandma was going to pick us up. We were excited but confused. I remember hearing the officers say that they weren't putting handcuffs on my mom until we left. The officers kept telling me that i was a big girl and that i had to watch over my siblonsg. Eventually, my grandma came into the house and she carried my brother and me and Victoria walked behind her.
 
 I remember seeing broken glass all over the house. My mom looked decent with her hair a little messed up and she didnt say anything. As we walked outside i saw my father handcuffed and bleeding. He was talking with a translator and i remember him seeing me and he was about to say something until one of the officers blocked his view. I remember getting into my grandmas van and on the way back she just kept talking about how my parents weren't okay and that they shouldnt have fought like that. I remember looking around and seeing my brother and sister fast asleep. I tried to go to sleep but i just couldn't. It took about an hour to get to my grandmas house and the whole time she was talking. i know i didnt understand most of what she said because i was around 5. i just kept thinking about all the broken glass i saw.

My dad would take me to work with him a lot. He often had me help him installing cabinets at his second job. We'd go to his shop and make the cabinets, sometimes with my brother helping. It was a great time to spend with my dad and learn what he did every day. I learned how to saw wood, plane and sand wood and the importance of hard work. We installed cabinets and countertops in people's home and sometimes businesses and would often spend a couple days to a week installing them.

In our house, our kitchen used to be small. My parents used to say it was a "two-butt" kitchen because with the dishwasher open, no one could get to the sink and only two people could fit in the remaining space. It became a running joke in the family about people's kitchens. There's a family beach cottage on Cape Cod that's pretty much a one-butt kitchen. When there are nine or ten people there, it gets very crowded very quickly. It's such a small thing, but every time I walk into a kitchen, it makes me think of my parents. And it makes me think of how many butts we could fit in it. Wherever I am, it reminds me of them and how many times I've seen them in the kitchen together. It reminds me of the goofy kind of love they have for each other. That's the kind of love I want to have in my life.They tore out the dining room and doubled the size of the kitchen, but in places, if the dishwasher is out, it's hard to get to the sink, and it's still a two-butt kitchen.

This memory is fuzzy but important. My father was arguing with me about something and he became enraged enough to leap over the couch at me. He pushed me on to the floor and started choking me which caused a lot of noise. My mother was on the phone with her boss at the time and all she did was mute the phone, and scream for us to shut up. I remember feeling dizzy and clawing at him to let me go, and eventually my mother came into the room when she was done on the phone and made him get off of me. Everyone was screaming and I just left. I walked out of the front door while they were fighting and walked miles and miles to my friends house. I was 15 at the time and I lived with my best friend for the next three years until I was 18 after that night.

Another memory of my parents is saying goodbye during one of their visits. I had work later that day so my family said goodbye at my 3rd floor apartment. My father came back up, seemingly out of breath- but not from the stairs but because he was crying. He gave me one last hug. I remember how his quivering body felt as he cried silently. I think about it a lot and it can bring me back to tears even now. I miss my family.

My family has always been very close. I think this is mostly because of our time overseas and that for that period of time we only really had each other, no extended family, no close friends and so we became a unit. I always knew I was going to go to college and I always knew I was going to become a scientist but I didn't really think much about not living with my family until it was about to happen. I am very much a homebody and prefer to be around people who I know care about me. I remember vividly arriving in the city with my parents and being shown the dorm that I would spend the next year in. My mom came in with me while my dad went to park the car. We got to my room and it was tiny, smaller than the bathroom at home. I was shocked, my mom tried to make me feel better but at this point I just wanted to go home. We left my dorm (on the way out my mom tried to say hello to other new students but I just wanted to get out) and found my dad and everything felt normal again. Like the three of us were just going out to lunch or something, which is exactly what we ended up doing. We went to a little Italian restaurant and for awhile I forgot that I wasn't going home but was going back to that little room instead. I remember laughing a lot and trying to keep my nervous feelings at bay. Eventually lunch had to end even though my dad tried to prolong it. They walked me back to my dorm and asked if I wanted to do anything else before they left. I decided that if they stayed any longer I was going to get over emotional and we quickly said goodbye to each other. No one cried, apart from me but that was back in my dorm. I stayed there until someone knocked on my door and asked if I wanted to come hang out. I made my first college friends that night and I really didn't need to worry that much in the end. I still saw my dad about once a week for lunch since he worked in the city and I was only ever an hour away from home if I needed anything.

When I came out to my parents in 2010 I remember sitting in the front room of their house one weekend that I was home from college during my first semester. The lights were not on and I was sitting in the rocking chair while my mom was sitting in these high back chairs that look like they could end up in some period piece film while my dad stood in the door way. The previous week had been national coming out week up at school and a picture of me in a pride shirt had ended up on Facebook. I had come out to friends in high school and college but hadn't yet come out to anyone in my family. I told my mom that I had something I wanted to talk to her about but I was afraid and she said "You can be gayer than Logan, and we would still love you." Even after hearing her say that I was still terrified of rejection. After I was able to utter the words, I got into the car with my dad and he drove me the 2 hours back up to school, it was one of the most quiet car rides I have ever experienced in my life. I wasn't able to look at him or anything, I could tell he was still processing everything I had told him and my mom. When we got up to where I was going to school he got out of the car, gave me a hug, and told me that he loved me no matter what.

When I was a teenager, our lives began to improve. Daddy gets a permanent job with enough salary. We build a more decent and comfortable home. From that moment on, my father began to come home often late. Father also began to often forget about my activities at school. Even my birthday, he often forgets. Our economic life did improve, but our family harmony began to falter.

When I was young--about 11-12--all I wanted in the world was to get to spend time with my dad. I begged him to spend time with me. He would always offer to let me come to work with him (he owned his own business) or hold the flashlight while he worked on our vehicle. I didn't want to do those things with him. I wanted to have meaningful conversation with him. I wanted him to be interested in the things I was interested in. He never was, though. And no amount of begging and pleading would get him to begin to be interested.
 
 As I mentioned in my previous self-defining memory, my dad is a diagnosable narcissist. He has always been that way, and it has shaped the way that I view and relate to authority figures all my life. I am slowly recovering from my upbringing--something that didn't help at all was that my parents decided to homeschool, and I very rarely got to spend any time with friends growing up--and I believe I am rather well-adjusted today. However, my life living at home growing up was truly hell.
 
 When I was 12 or so, I was very obsessed with board games. I LOVED Monopoly. I thought it was so fun. I had played the game numerous times with my siblings--I had five youngers--and my mom, but my dad had never joined us in a game. He didn't enjoy playing board games, he said. 
 
 I was determined, though. I saw other kids' dads playing with them and doing things with them that they enjoyed, and I believed that my dad could do the same, and that he was just being selfish. It would be years and years before I would connect the dots and realize that my dad avoids, at all costs, doing ANYTHING that he doesn't want to do. And many times, when someone asks him to do something, he will be sure to NOT do it just because he is so insecure about having control over his life and his domain. Such was the case with the game Monopoly.
 
 I begged and begged him, for at least six months, to please play a game with us. It would be so fun, I thought. This was before I became embittered toward my father. This event actually was what started me on the path toward bitterness and resentment, because it was the first time I realized that my dad was different from other dads. 
 
 I had been asking for him to play Monopoly with me for maybe six months or more, and he really didn't want to, he would say. I would ask him to play with me anyway, even though he didn't want to. I wanted him to do it because I wanted to do it with him. I wanted him to enjoy it just because I enjoyed it. That's not how my father operates. He said that he would, "someday." I would continue to ask, maybe once per week, if we would be able to "schedule" a time to play the game, thinking that if we set it out far enough, it would be more likely to happen. He continued to say he didn't want to, but that he would play with me "someday."
 
 My dad was in leadership at a church's men's retreat many years in a row. At the time, we were planning to go together to the men's retreat in a few months. I begged him to please let me bring Monopoly and play it with me at the retreat. He had said at one point that he was going to be taking fewer responsibilities at the men's retreat because he wanted to "spend more time with his son." That was a joke. 
 
 He did let me bring the game, and surprisingly, he promised to play it with me at some point during the weekend. I was SO EXCITED. I had planned what pieces I was going to play with, and I planned what music we would listen to while playing... I had everything planned. I had picked the day and time during the retreat that we would play together, just the two of us, and I told him. He said it was going to work.
 
 The day came, and I confirmed with him that we would be playing the game at such-and-such time in the evening. He said he would. The time came. A camp-wide meeting had just finished, and my dad was sitting around talking with some guys. I went into the adjoining dining area and set up a table and the game. I gave each of us the proper amount of fake bills, and I had the playing pieces all set up. I had my bluetooth speaker set up and was ready to play the music I had chosen for the time.
 
 My dad kept talking to the men.
 
 I sat and waited patiently. Even at this age, I was not allowed to speak to my parents when they were in conversation with others. I had to wait my turn. 
 
 I waited. 
 
 Thirty minutes went by, then forty-five, then an hour, then an hour and a half... my dad continued his conversation. He could clearly see me from where he was sitting. He could see that I was just waiting for him to join me. I continued to wait, feeling more discouraged all the time.
 
 Two hours went by. I was playing on my iPod Touch. I was beginning to get angry. As I realized that my dad was not going to come play, and that he was just going to continue his conversation indefinitely, I felt defeated. I wanted to cry. For so long I had wanted this, and I was realizing it wasn't going to happen.
 
 Three hours went by. I had given up. He was still chatting with his friends in the next room. 
 
 Two family friends of mine walked through the dining area and saw that I had the game set up and was wanting to play. They asked if I would like them to sit and play with me. I said yes. I figured, if I wasn't going to get to play with my dad, I might as well play with someone. These two guys played with me for awhile until it was time for bed. We finished the game and packed it up. My dad was still talking to the men. I walked-ran to our cabin with tears streaming down my face. I couldn't even talk to my dad I was so angry. I sat and read a book--Jonathan Swift's "Gulliver's Travels"--until my dad finally came to the cabin. We didn't say a word, even though I think he could see that I had been crying. I continued to cry silently until I fell asleep.
 
 In the coming weeks I would confront my dad about the situation. I was so angry. He told me that he had *not* promised to play with me that evening at the retreat. He said that he had only promised he would play "someday." And he said that that promise was still good. That he would play with me someday. 
 
 I would continue to press him to play with me and my siblings on multiple occasions. Another date was set. We gathered with my mom to play. He was in his room on his computer. We were calling for him to join us. He came out and announced, "I was just checking the scheduled movies at the theater and [such-and-such movie] is playing, and I want to take you all!"
 
 My young siblings were overjoyed. They didn't care about the game, or the promise. They were happy with the announcement because it was a movie that they had wanted to see. As the reader can imagine, I was not enthused. I ran to my room and cried immediately after his announcement. My mom took my side. I could hear her telling my dad from my room that I had been really looking forward to the game, and that it was very hurtful that he would change plans so short notice. I can't remember what his response was exactly, but it was something to the effect of "he'll just have to deal with it."
 
 I never asked my dad to play with me again. The hope that he would remember his promise to me and ask to play continued to diminish over time. I have never played Monopoly with my dad.

One time when I was in high school, I was self-conscious about my body hair, so I bought a bottle of Nair and used it on my chest. I accidentally left the bottle in the bathroom. Later my dad confronted me about it. He told me, "you don't need to do that" in a way that gave me the impression that he was telling me that I shouldn't be removing my chest hair. I found the confrontation really embarrassing and didn't try to remove body hair like that again until well into college.

I remember formally coming out to my mom, but I never really came out in a formal sense to my dad. With my mom, I remember she was working on her computer and I was telling some story about field hockey practice from that day. I was 15 at the time. And I remember she said something along the lines of "you've been hanging out a lot with Ashley", and Ashley was the openly gay girl on the team. I said something to the effect of "no mom, that's just me" and then we just kind of sat in silence. I think I cried. I know she cried. My folks are really supportive, but due to their academic nature we never really talked about personal things. I came out to my mom and then we didn't really ever talk about it until more than a year later.

I was very small when my parents split, they were divorced when I was four. My dad had us every weekend. He was the oldest of my grandparents' six sons, so my brother and I were the first grandkids.
 
 I have this rather distinct memory of being sick one weekend. I was throwing up, and I remember being in a little twin bed in my dad's apartment, and he seemed a little worried and a little overwhelmed. He kept giving me Sprite just so I'd have some fluids in me. He called my grandmother over, and then had her advising him on what to do. The Sprite part stopped, but they kept pushing fluids, and I remember him being so worried, and her being so reassuring, more to him than to me, and it's just something that sticks in my mind as so sweet. They're the kind of parents I want to be.

They gave me a good birthdays gift. They gave me a fishing set. I don't know what they mean of this. They knew that i like fishing. There is river near our home. I try to catch some fish with it. I go for fishing every morning and evening. After several month, i knew what they want by giving that fishing set. They want me to be independent and responsible with my life.

Our father used to give us lectures all the time about all the things we would do wrong. On one of these occasions my brother decided to talk back to my father. At that moment in front of me my father slapped my brother right across the mouth. My brother continued to talk back and walk away. At that moment I knew it was a bad idea to talk back to my father.

We used to go on vacation every year as a family, my mom, dad, sister, and myself. One year we went to Hershey Pennsylvania, the Hershey factory. It was great, we had an amazing time. This was before I came out as gay. I was messaging a guy at the time and my mom asked why I kept looking at my phone. I just said I was on Facebook or something along those lines.

The older I get, the more time I find I spend with my mother. One day, my mother and I went to visit an IKEA that's about an hour away. We knew exactly what we were going to buy, but upon reaching the showroom floor, we see a similar item at a much better price. We decided we wanted to purchase the cheaper one, but because we were waiting for my sister to arrive, we remained at the entrance to the showroom floor. While we waited, we conversed about the house in which we currently live, and she confided in me that she hoped I would inherit the house instead of my sister because it was clear that I wanted to fix it up and convert it into something good.

I remember going to the mall pretty frequently with my mom during middle school. I didn't really have any friends so we would spend the Saturday together. We would go to the stores she wanted to and mine and she would usually buy me something or for my brother. I would get jealous of him even though he wasn't with us. I would sometimes be mad at her even though she hadn't done anything.

I remember my mom going back to school after raising four kids (me and my my three siblings). I think about how she wanted a more fulfilling life and things to do after raising four kids and I often feel inspired that she followed her dreams. This is partially related to the previous memory and how it started a lot of issues that resulted in my parents getting divorced, but that it helped her realize what her goals and priorities are and it inspired me to do the same, especially with regard to my education as well.

This is one of the earliest memories I have. I was probably about 3 or 4 because my parents were still together. I loved the ice cream man and his truck and whenever I would heart my parents would give me money to get my favorite, the Red Italian Ice. When I was 3 or 4, one of my parents ran after the ice cream truck and got it to stop a couple of houses down. I was in the baby seat of a bicycle, and my other parent rode us down to where my first parent stopped the truck. I can't remember which parent did which, though I feel like my dad probably had me on the bike. This is one of two memories I have of my parents TOGETHER in my life that is of importance. It makes me feel upset that I can't think of any more than this one and the previous memory

I remember one time when my dad was in the back yard using an electric saw to cut lumber for something and I was about 4, I wasn't in school yet. Anyways, I remember my nanny was in the kitchen with my sister and I but I kept running out to see my dad and get a piece of wood from him to play with and run back inside. I always love this memory because he was so giving and obviously he was trying to build something but he kept stopping to just to make sure I was having a good time. I just remember the way he smiled at me filled me with joy. He was present for the fun times sometimes.

When I was a little kid, up until I was about ten years old, my parents grew most of their own vegetables. They had two big gardens in the backyard on either side of a big hickory tree. I loved their garden. In the spring my dad would dust off the rototiller kept in our basement and mutter and curse over it as he tried to get it started -- something that was, in retrospect, more of a production than it would have been had proper maintenance been a higher priority to my parents. I loved watching him tilling the garden plots, turning up the soft, dark soil with its worms, shredded bits of tree roots, and occasional treasures (plant tags from the previous season, the rare rusty nail). When he got to the second plot I would stand at the edge of the first and practice my long-jump, measuring my distance by my footprints in the soil. Or, if they were in seed already, I'd pick dandelions and blow their seeds over the beds so that I could watch where they'd land. My dad never stopped me doing either of these things. He was working hard, getting hot and sweaty, doing something that was more of a financial obligation than a hobby, and there I was, compressing the soil he'd just loosened or spreading weed seeds where he intended to produce food. He saw, and sometimes he teasingly chided me a bit, but he never got angry or told me outright to stop. My dad has always been a bit of a brusque man, impatient and a little quick to get irritated by people not doing things the way he thinks they should be done. When I was a kid I didn't always notice the size of his soft spot for children but when I think about things like letting me mess up his garden with hardly a word, I see it. I see how much more patience he had for kids than anyone or anything else in his whole life.

When I was in junior high, probably 8th grade, my family went to the lake near our house. We weren't at our usual spot on the lake but a place further down the road with a little cliff overlooking the lake and a path down to the small beach. My brothers and I were swimming and playing around while my parents hung out up on the little cliff. When I got tired of swimming I went back up to sit in the shade for a while. I'll never forget my mom calling me buffalo butt when I got back up and making fun of my weight. For years afterward, I wouldn't be seen without a shirt on and wouldn't get in the water and the lake or a pool. She adopted buffalo as a nickname for me. It wasn't done in a mean spirited way. It just never occurred to her how it felt to me.

Coming out as a lesbian to my mother was a decision I debated tirelessly about. She herself had never expressed opinions on it one way or the other, but she'd struggled with me starting to express more masculinely as a teenager before I'd come out as anything, even to myself, and she could be unpredictable. I wasn't sure what to expect. 
 I was seventeen and in my junior year of high school, my first year at a new school after getting expelled from my last one, and I was fairly sure that my coming out was the "yearly tragedy." I was having a lot of self-esteem issues, had pretty much decided that I was an absolute burden, and hated that I was going about and making another ruckus, even though keeping the secret felt terrible. My mother and I had always been very close. It was strange to know something about myself that she didn't, at that age. 
 I planned the whole day painstakingly. I took her to a local art museum, since art museums are one of her favorite places and we'd had many nice trips to them before. I told her ahead of time that I had something big I needed to tell her. She would later tell me she'd been wondering about pregnancy, drugs, or another potential expulsion. When I told her, it was without any confidence at all, just "I think that I maybe might like girls." To which she said, "Oh, yeah, I know." 
 We spent the rest of the day talking about it, and though there were several tense moments where she asked if I was sure I wasn't just asexual, if I'd ever had sex with a man to know, etc. Where I tried explaining what I thought were "warning signs" from my childhood, which I thought at the time justified my current way of being, she disagreed with me about my own memories and feelings from childhood and said I was just thinking of those things that way because of this news. That was all fine though. We spent the entire day out, and everything was fine. 
 High school being as busy as it was, with class and clubs and an after school job, I didn't realize that we hadn't spoken for about three days until I found my mom crying in the kitchen one afternoon. I stopped short, in the mouth of the room, and asked what was wrong. My mom isn't prone to crying. 
 The tone of her voice stabs into my chest as I type this. She snapped back, "What do you think!?" and I honestly wasn't sure yet. Then she said, "My daughter told me she thinks she's gay!" 
 She went on a tirade after that, screaming and carrying on. This wasn't normally how we talked to each other. In fact, expulsion besides, I was a pretty easy kid, very timid and passive, if a little strange now and then. We never fought. We didn't scream at each other. 
 Two more lines are prominent from this memory. Her asking, "Don't you have anything to say for yourself?" to which all I could do was apologize, and "You're tearing my religion apart!" 
 I don't know if I'll ever forget that last one. I don't know why it sits so heavily with me, but it's the first thing I think of every time I think of coming out to my parents. I always think of how my mother looked, half-dressed in her "going to town clothes," sweating through her shirt, with a towel tied around her head and no makeup yet. Barefoot. Making a sandwich or a salad, I can't remember. I remember feeling frozen and rooted to the spot, at a loss for words because I'd thought things were fine, I hadn't expected to have to defend myself. 
 As i think of this again, I also remember her saying how she understood now how parents could disown their children, and that her life must have been so hard and horrible because God was preparing her for this. I left, went to the front porch, and hid outside for the rest of the day. 
 Things are better now. My mother is one of my biggest supporters, but I cannot remember for the life of me when or how she started to come around to the idea.

My family is originally from southern Louisiana. When I was 18, I went away to NYU for uni, which was a very unpopular decision with most of my family. My mom came with me to get me set up. We went to the Cake Boss restaurant, a Red Lobster, and more. We also had this awesome caricature done of us together. Recently, I had started to look more like my mom and less like my dad. This really showed in the caricature and was very amusing to me.

My dad was a hard working man he worked as a carpenter and electrician. One of my first toys was a wood jeep he made for me. I played with it all the time and always brought it with me. He worked so hard even on the holidays. On the holidays he would cook a big dinner for all our family members. He would usually make ham or turkey regardless of what he made it was always a great meal. When I was older I learned he had a woman on the side and when my mom found out she cried whenever she was alone and did not think anyone would see. Our family was perfect from the outside but on the inside it was a different story.

A lot of my memories with my parents are from family vacations. In particular for my dad, I have a lot of memories of what I did as a kid up at our family cottage, like shooting off and looking for model rockets, fishing, and starting campfires. One of my favorite memories was the first time we snorkeled and looked for crayfish under the rocks. I remember the taste of the old yellowed rubber mouthpiece that used to be clear, the too-big orange flippers with a crack, and looking through goggles that kept filling with water. I remember moving around at the base of the large tree that grew partially into the water moving in and out of shade and through patches of cold and warm water. Whenever my dad would flip over a good-candidate rock a little cloud of silt and dirt would unfurl and settle down and out in slow-motion. It seemed very mysterious to me how the rocks were being selected, and how my dad was able to spot any crayfish through the cloud of silt. I remember seeing them sometimes and how they would propel themselves backwards in very quick little bursts. The combination of their claws and quick movements had me on edge even though they were only an inch or so in length. I remember my dad would catch them and try to get me to hold one, or at least transfer it into a bucket, but I was too scared to hold them.

Another self-defining memory that I have about my parents involves my mother and how I found out that she had stolen from my checkbook. I received notification from my bank at the time that there had been forgeries on two checks of mine, and I immediately noticed the handwriting as belonging to my mother. Unfortunately, on top of my checking account getting overdrawn, I ended up having to file police reports in two different counties because of what had occurred - one because of where the checks had been stolen and another because of where the checks had been cashed. It pained me to do it, but on the other hand, I knew that I was doing the right thing.

Father always attaches importance to family affairs rather than his own interests. When I'm going to university, I need a lot of money. Father at that time also needed a lot of money for the development of his business. But he was more concerned with my educational needs than his business. He relented giving the money to my college. 
 He tried to streamline his business expenses to survive. He was willing to work on a bus instead of buying a car. The distance between the house and the office is quite far.

One day I had a severe accident. I ran out of blood and had to get a blood donor immediately. The mother's blood type doesn't suit me, while daddy fits me. But now father is having an important meeting with clients in another city. Mother contacted my father and said that I had a serious accident and needed blood donation as soon as possible. Father said goodbye at the meeting and went to the hospital. Luckily it's not too late. With my father's blood donation, I was finally helped. Father prioritizes family over others.

When I was young my parents would get along pretty well but every once in a while they would have a large fight. One of these fights, I don't remember how old I was, maybe 10 to 12, but I found out the reason they were fighting. My dad has a gambling addiction and he had lost a very large amount of money at a casino. I remember her saying that we might lose our house, and she didn't know what we were going to do. I think having knowledge about these kinds of financial issues and hearing them fight like that contributed to issues dealing with anxiety that I still struggle with today.

I remember swimming in the lake at my grandfather's lake house. My dad had need to get gas for the pontoon boat, but the nearest marina was closed and my mother need to buy bread for sandwiches, but it was a thirty minute drive to town. I thought it would be a great idea to have a marina/grocery store that would come to you so that you didn't have to travel for fuel and food. I made up a jingle for this "floating marina" and sang it all day.

In terms of public services, we also get different services. I will have my mother checked because of a hospital illness. I felt something was wrong in this situation, then I asked the receptionist. They did not answer and left immediately.
 My mother said that we must be patient with all this. We do not make noise that can cause us harm. Everything will be fine in time, according to my mother.

When I was in high school, I had a friend that was a girl. She turned out wanting more out of the relationship than I was interested in providing...  We finally got to my friend's house and seeing the look on my mom's face turn from interest to disgust as she found out that my friend was not the same race as me is something that will always stick in my memory. I learned on this day that people can't be trusted with their public emotion because it is so hard to tell what fucked up prejudicial nonsense exists in their mind when they don't think people are listening or watching.

I was a couple of months into my first relationship when I came out to my dad by accident. It wasn't planned by any means and I was afraid of what he would say. I asked him why and he said "it's because they think you're a couple" I replied "What if I told you we are?" His response? "We'll you were kind of my last hope for grand kids." 
 
 Forget the fact that my older brother and his wife have 2 kids already. Granted they are not my brother's biological children, but they are family. He made it seem as if my uterus stops working because I'm not into men. As if that's my only purpose in life, to reproduce. Never once stooping to consider if I even wanted kids in the first place.
 
 Now, knowing how he feels about a child needing to be biological to be considered 'his' I'm nervous that when my partner and I decided to have children, that if we adopt that he may not accept those kids. And that would only serve to harm our relationship that much more.

Similar theme to my last memory, on my first day of high school, my dad drove me to school. I was nervous about starting school but happy that he had taken me and I did not have to ride the bus that morning. He dropped me off at the front of the school, and I leaned over to hug him goodbye and say thank you for the ride. I caught him off guard, so I was sort of able to wrap my arms around him before he stiffened and rebuffed me. "Not cool son. That's not cool," he said, as I pulled away. He did not hug me back. I got out of the car, and he drove off to work. To my knowledge, no one saw me hug him, and no one said anything to me about it, but his reaction was so shocking to me that I wasn't sure how to process it. He explained later that he was worried that someone would see and tease me for it and that he wasn't declining the hug, but it did make it uncomfortable to be vulnerable around him for a while.

I had a rough time in junior high and high school. Looking back, I very obviously had mental health issues and should have gotten therapy, but at the time, nobody really understood what was going on, least of all my parents. Around 7th grade I started hating myself. I started questioning my faith, which seemed like the worst thing a pastor's daughter could do. I didn't understand certain oxymoron's of our Christian denomination, and it made me feel like a terrible person, that I couldn't just "be a good person" and believe what I was supposed to believe. Anyway, so I spiraled into a deep depression and began self-harming and really struggled with suicidal thoughts. In 9th grade, when my parents found out, they sat me down in the living room and proceeded to have one of the most awkward conversations of my life. They asked me why I was hurting myself, and I wouldn't respond. My mom asked the worst questions. One of her first ones was, "Are you GAY?" And I was horrified. This wasn't the first time someone had asked--I was really close friends with this girl at school, who also struggled with self-harm and thoughts of suicide--and I had heard the whispers before about our friendship, and had been made fun of. "NO!" I responded (And I honestly believed it, at the time. Being gay just wasn't an option for Christians, I believed, and I was so deeply closeted I wouldn't realize the truth until my junior year of college). My mom's follow-up questions weren't any less uncomfortable. Had I been molested? Did one of my brothers sneak into my room at night and hurt me? Had anyone else? (No, to all those questions). Apart from the mortifying embarrassment of having this sort of conversation with one's parents, I also remember feeling frustrated that they couldn't understand my depression, that (they believed) there must have been something else wrong with me, or something else done to me, that made me this way.

This one is a little fuzzy. It was my 22th birthday and I had made plans to spend all day with Zee. We had a great morning in SF. My biological father attempted to always claim that my stepdad was the reason he did not come around much when in actuality, it was his own fault because he is selfish and a deadbeat. Today, I laugh about the situation that happened that night but in reality, it is me laughing at the trauma that occurred, not because it is actually funny.

Another bad memory about my father was the second and last alcohol drama he made before he had to leave home. When I was a freshman in high school, I qualified to go to state for golf. I was the youngest person to get to go, and the only person from my school. I was gifted a condo to stay in while there, and I was allowed to bring one adult and a friend. My best friend was definitely coming with me, but I had to decide whether to bring my mom or grandpa. My mom has always been my biggest cheerleader, but my grandpa was the person who taught me to golf. We had been going to the course since I was five years old. My mom and I didn't even have to contemplate; my grandpa had to go with me. 
 
 That trip was one of the best trips of my life. My coach and my grandpa were so proud of me. I was so happy to see my grandpa so excited for me. With my dad out of the picture, my grandpa was my father figure.

My mom always told me that money doesn't buy you happiness. I always disagreed. Money may not be able to buy you happiness but you need money to be financially secure. You need money to be able to live life without worrying about things being shut off or cancelled. I had always believed my mother had to tell us that money doesn't matter because she didn't have much of it. Now, I realize that wasn't the case. She was teaching us to be less materialistic. To remember that life is about happiness, not money or material.

Growing up, I would go to my dad's apartment every weekend. I loved going because we would also go rent movies, play games, or just do really fun things. I remember one Friday we went over to my aunt's house to see their new baby chickens. I was about six or seven at the time so I was in LOVE with these things. They were honestly probably the cutest things I'd ever seen at this point. I stayed for over an hour playing with those guys; and when I got home they were all I could think about. The next morning, it was obvious what I wanted to do that day. You guessed it, go visit the chickens. I begged and begged and BEGGED my dad to go back over to my aunt's house. I probably begged from 8 am to 2 pm. I knew I was annoying the hell out of him but I really wanted to go see those chickens. After six hours of begging my dad finally had enough; that's when he hit me. This had never happened before and I was in shock. I was still super young so I had no idea what to do, so obviously I started crying, but he didn't stop til he made sure I would be quiet.

My wife and I got engaged in Paris, and it was every bit as lovely as you would think. I called them from the customs line at JFK, and all my mother said was "well, I guess it's legal now so we can't stop you. But I hope you think about it a lot because divorce is really expensive and it will ruin your life"
 
 Not a word of congratulations.

I was the first of my mother's children to attend college, and at the time the rest of the family was living overseas from where I would be attending school. My mom flew with me to meet my grandmother and aunt to move me in to school a little early. At a certain point she had moved me in, but was having trouble leaving me behind. I had some trouble with it too - I desperately wanted to start my new life, but the separation was incredibly painful for her. I can distinctly remember her pulling away after my aunt almost forced her into the car for the night. The slightly painful thing about his memory is that it was the start of a long and unnecessary amount of distance between us; I made myself more busy than necessary with school and friends and started a pattern of accepting, but not necessarily returning or freely giving attention back to her. We're very alike, and it sometimes means we chafe against each other, and this was a moment where that crystallized our relationship to each other as adults.

This one is more recent, but officially a year old last month. I had a boyfriend and I broke up with him. My mother still continued to talk to him. I remember getting fed up and telling her that this man that she thought was so great, had drugged me, and he wasn't great, and she needed to stop talking to him. I broke up with him because he was cheating on me, and he had drugged me (not as dramatic as it sounds, but he gave me alcohol to drink with weed-infused into it. He didn't tell me it was in it, and he gave it to the whole party and thought it was hilarious). I thought this would be enough to get my mom to stop talking to him. I thought my mom, who saw how much this man had broken my heart, would understand. Instead, she told me "That didn't happen. You're lying." Then, she told me that if I really loved him, I wouldn't be going on dates .. Even though my dates were after we broke up, and he was going on dates WHILE WE WERE TOGETHER. It upset me so much and it perfectly describes my relationship with my mother and how hard it is for me to trust people. It's like every time our relationship gets better and we start to bond over something (In this case, heartache), she shows me how truly crazy and manipulative she truly is. People don't understand how terrible my mother was to me as a child and continues to be because she is so great to other people. Everything she does is behind closed doors and denied if brought up later. It has been such a frustrating battle for me to trust others when I grew up with a mother who would so frequently switch just like that on you.

My childhood dog passing away. It was so weird, because I had seen her two days prior and she was completely fine. My dad called me the next day and told me to come right over, because he had taken her to the emergency vet because she was having trouble breathing. I stayed over at his house until 12:30am that night, petting her and laying with her. My dad finally had me go home to get some sleep and took over looking after her. He says he woke up at 5am and she had calmed down, and was breathing normally. When my stepmom woke him up at 6am, she was gone. I had never been to a crematorium before, but I helped my dad, my stepmom and my little sister take her to be cremated. I will always be grateful for my dad taking care of her in her last moments, and also for making sure we had the money to take her to the vet and to cremate her for me.

When I would stay with my dad, he liked to watch a lot of movies and fall asleep loudly on the couch. He would wake up randomly from the nap to comment on the movie. One movie that he watched included explicit nudity of a woman. I was young, so I covered my eyes. My dad uncovered my eyes and said to look at the movie. I did what he said, and then he said "you better not become a lesbian." This sounded like a violent threat, especially after the previous choking incident, but I was extremely confused. I did not know what a lesbian was, and he did not explain much after he said that.

When I was 19, my eldest brother killed himself. He jumped out of the balcony of my mom's apartment. He had had a psychotic episode two weeks before, and the doctor suggested he stayed at my mom's. It looked like he was getting better, and that day, he asked my mom to go for a walk. When she went to take a shower before the walk, he went outside and jumped. 
 I always think about what my parents did wrong for that to happen. Could they have prevented it in some way? Not only if my mom hadn't gone to take that shower. But also more generally, thinking in our upbringing, in how improvised they were, in why they decided to have three kids when they didn't have the money to support them well (we weren't poor or anything, just middle class, but sometimes it was hard making ends meet). And then, divorcing when things went wrong, and my sister was just 5. I think about this, and I think that's why none of my siblings (or I) has had kids, and we're all in our thirties.

I remember once, when my dad and I were downstairs watching T.V. I had popped off a snarky comment or something similar. He grabbed the spoon and I ran from the room and hid upstairs under our tall sofa table. He came stomping up the stairs, ready to spank me. I remember how angry he looked, first at me, and then I watched the anger turn inward. Looking back, I realized he hated seeing his children so afraid of him.
 In his anger, he bent the spoon in half, but it didn't break. I was terrified, because I believed the spoon was wooden (I learned later it was plastic) and that my dad was so angry he could BEND WOOD.

I'm getting really bored of my parents, not gonna lie. My mom just sort of brushed off some woman we didn't know at Kmart or wherever we got it. Dad would've preferred I picked something else, certainly. We also changed into costumes for part of the day at school and various classmates I didn't value the opinion of remarked about it as though they were speaking quietly enough I wouldn't hear but loudly enough that I did. In the dark for actual trick-or-treating I guess I passed, I don't remember anyone refusing to give me candy or hate criming me or whatever the night of.
 
 There are lots more memories out there of me getting in touch with my feminine side, but just to add more context to the classmates thing, there was also a costume trunk you could sign up to play with at a certain time of the day and I definitely threw on an oversized dress and chilled more than once. I thought nothing of it, but the same bitches I didn't like seemed to. I started thinking back to the Halloween costume because of all the weird social media parents getting way too much praise every year now for letting their kids dress as this or that gender nonconforming thing for Halloween now and I always post something about how they're not exactly trailblazers. I do wish my appreciation for "girl toys" and stuff hadn't been discouraged so harshly at some point after that, but it had been a high point for my opinion of my mom at the time. She's definitely supportive now, so all's well that ends well.

While my parents have shown support for me in the past, we did recently get into an argument. My parents argued with me about why transgender people should be allowed to transition. While I am cisgender, this was a self-defining moment because I had never talked to my parents about my transgender friends. I have also never told them that I support trans rights because they are so adamantly set in their ways. However, it was the first time they had actually listened to my side of the story. I told them about recent studies that had come out about transgender individuals having brain activity similar to that of the sex they transition into. I told them about struggles my friends have been through. It was the first moment that they 1) listened to me and 2) admitted the humanity of transgender individuals. They normally disregard what I have to say, but this was the first moment I realized they were trying to be more educated about the community I inhabit.

When I was in high school my parents and I had discussed how they were spoiling my sister. We would often argue about this as she had cancer and they felt that spoiling her was okay at the time. They admitted to me that I was right about not listening to them and that they apologized.

On Christmas, my mom gave my brother and I a leash or a dog collar. She told us we could get a dog. We were so excited. We had wanted a dog our whole lives. My mom is also very attached to the dog hut treats him like a human child.

I remember going to see the United States Women's Softball team play before they headed off to Athens for the Olympics. I was worried that we wouldn't make the trip but it didn't phase my parents, they both said "We have another car" and took all of our stuff out of that car and packed the other car.I remember arriving to Connecticut and my Mom finding a ticket and happily sending me in alone to watch the game.

Thinking about family dynamics after a marriage is a big deal for many people, and it certainly was for me. Having been married and divorced from my ex-husband and having had a very "traditional" feeling wedding and in-law relationship between my ex and my family, I wasn't quite sure how things would go with my second marriage - to a woman. After my wife and I got married and we walked down the aisle, we turned and waited to greet people. The very first person to come up to us was my dad. He hugged my wife and said, "welcome to the family, daughter!" I've never felt more proud of him and grateful for who he is.

When I was 16 I told my parents I was molested. I told them that it was a family member and that it happened when I was 8. I'm not sure why this memory made such a dramatic impact on me, but somehow it did. When I was about 7 years old, my mom was cooking in the kitchen and so I decided to join her. In that moment I was embarrassed, devastated, and very disappointed in myself. I expected my mom to be angry or upset with me, but instead she responded with grace and love. She encouraged me, helped me clean up, and got out a new box of brownie mix.

I kept it to myself for so long, but one day I decided that I needed to tell someone else, since I thought that professional help might be a good idea. I remember crying, and saying that I believed that I had anxiety and depression and that I didn't know what to do. I still remember how much it hurt to hear by mom brush aside what I was saying, explaining that everyone in high school feels that way.

My parents always prided themselves on being very open-minded. They're the kind of liberals who imagined themselves to be completely LGBT friendly but wouldn't use they/them pronouns for my sibling when they first came out in 2015. My dating life in high school was abysmal, a string of unrequited crushes and rejections punctuated by a 2-year long crush on a guy who later came out as gay. I remember one time, before I ever came out or even realized I was queer, my mom was asking me about my dating life. "Do you have a boyfriend?" she asked. "No," I said. "Do you have a girlfriend?" "No, mom. I'm not gay." "Hm," she said. "You'd be much cooler if you were a lesbian."
 
 At the time, I thought it was funny. It's still funny. It's a story I tell often, with the added layer of humor now that I actually ID as queer. It's also emblematic of my family's relationship with queerness. Being LGBT is something "cool," something "interesting". How could homophobia still exist if my mother, in the mid- 2000s in Wisconsin, could joke about something like that? It's also a good example of the attitude my parents had towards me at the time- that I would never be good enough, cool enough, smart enough. Even something like my sexuality, that I couldn't change, could have been "better".

This memory revolves around my mother. A more recent click of just how much my mother loved me. I was in elementary school and the hype for Harry Potter was all too real. When my dad went to jail the first time, out of many times, my mother sat me down to explain why exactly he was in jail. I could tell my mother was flush and embarrassed. I remember us both thinking that he was insane to not believe the physical proof of him being a parent to another person. I was hurt because I had always wanted a sister after thinking I was an only child for years and I had made this desire known to my parents.
