I stopped speaking to my dad three weeks before he died. I don't know what I would have done if I knew he was dying, but it was the right decision for me at the time and I couldn't regret it afterward. My dad was an alcoholic and had been very ill. My sister and I had moved our dad to live in the same town with us, knowing that his health was bad. He was in the hospital for several weeks over the summer and had become increasingly unkind, or just downright mean. I was working full time and trying to help him out, at the hospital almost every day, and the stress was weighing on me. Over the years, my own mental health has been a constant struggle, and at that time I was really struggling to stay balanced. I took on a lot of extra stress whenever my dad was in the picture, in large part because I could identify with him so much that I experienced simultaneous sympathy, frustration and hurt throughout our relationship. (I am not addicted to any substances but our mental health struggles have been similar in trajectory.) On the day that he was due to be released, I went to the hospital to pick him up, and my dad was in a foul mood. He was rude to the hospital staff and hateful and demanding to me. I told him I was done with him and didn't want him in my life anymore and left him money to take a taxi home instead. It was not a spur of the moment decision, although it probably seemed like it to those around us. I had become so frustrated with my father that I could no longer appreciate the side of him that loved me, taught me important life lessons, and supported me in all my endeavors. Was I sad that my father died without a reconciliation? Of course. However, his behavior warranted my reaction, and I had no way to know what the future held. My sister was furious with me, and accused me of cutting people out of my life without reason. I needed space, and emotional safely, and I no longer got that from the man my father had become in the late stages of his disease. After his death, I found an apology note my father had drafted. His disease was pronounced in the shaky hand-writing on his letter- the first draft I found was almost illegible, and the second one not much better. But I was grateful to have that sign that he wanted reconciliation, and it went a long way toward helping me to forgive him in the years after his death. I keep that note in my jewelry box next to other precious memories.

Once, my dad told me, as if it were a bon to his great virtue, "At least I haven't molested you."
 
 And it's true, he hasn't. But my relationship with my dad regarding my body has always been very troubling for me, and I have only just now, within the last few months, been able to unpack some of the internalized shame and manifested body dysmorphia that was caused in part by what he said to me growing up. 
 
 This is a very short memory, but it sticks out in my mind very clearly.
 
 Some backstory. My dad would always make passing comments about my body. He would say that I would get "all the girls... if I would just workout." He would say that my legs looked weak. He would tell me that he noticed my "breasts forming" (I have gynecomastia caused by taking risperdal for a mental health disorder), and that he thought that if I would just do some bench presses, I would be able to "take care of that."
 
 I always knew he was ashamed of the way I looked. He never made any positive comments about my body. They were always creepy negative comments. 
 
 He would also take liberties with me since I was very young that I was not okay with and never agreed to. He would tickle the back of my neck, even when I was a teenager, with his fat, stubby fingers and I would ALWAYS look at him like he was irritating the heck out of me, but I would never say anything because in those days I was afraid to confront his narcissism. He did things like that all the time. He would lightly tickle me or poke me when I wasn't expecting it and I would glare at him, but it never stopped.
 
 Until one day.
 
 When I had had enough, and was more brave and would soon be leaving his "domain," as I call it, I confronted him. He had walked by me and lightly tickled my knee. I jerked away and glared immediately. He said something about "how hairy I was getting." I had had enough. I told him to please not touch me like that ever again. That it was no longer okay for him to tickle me, or poke me, and it was certainly not okay for him to comment on my body like that. I was so angry, yet I was also so scared. I knew I had poked him back with that demand, and that his authority in his "domain" had been tested, and that never went well. 
 
 He responded in anger. "YOU ARE MY SON. I CAN TOUCH YOU WHENEVER AND HOWEVER I LIKE."
 
 Keep in mind that I was 17 or 18 at this time. 
 
 "That is a serious violation of my boundaries. It has always bothered me that you do that, and I have never been okay with it, and it IS going to stop."
 
 "YOU ACT LIKE I'VE MOLESTED YOU" he said. "I AM NOT A CHILD MOLESTER. I TOUCHED YOUR KNEE."
 
 I told him I didn't care, and that he would not ever touch my knee or any part of me again if I did not want him to. I told him I was old enough to set my own boundaries on physical affection, and that he had crossed the line many times in the past, and that it wasn't going to happen anymore.
 
 This conversation was happening while my whole family (there are 8 of us including parents) were gathered in my parents' room for our evening prayer, so everyone was privy to this conversation.
 
 "Well I have never molested you, and you shouldn't act like I have because I have been a GOOD DAD to you and your siblings."
 
 Still, I said, it will never happen again.
 
 This was just another stone in the wall built between me and my father. To be honest, I have no wish to reconcile with the man. I only care for my mother and siblings (my siblings do not have contact with me and haven't since I came out, because my dad is concerned that I will "indoctrinate" them with my "lifestyle").

Trying to explain to my mother why I haven't spoken to my sister in almost a year was difficult. My mother and sister were planning a trip up to Boston for my graduation from graduate school. Most of my saddest memories of my mother come from times when she realized how far apart different parts of our family really were, and how little many of us had in common. 
 
 Talking to my mother on the phone, I tried to explain how I had always felt like I could rely on my sister, but when I came out, she couldn't bring herself to compromise her beliefs to support me. I was sitting on my bed, talking to my mother, watching my lizard pace around his tank. He was hunting crickets that I'd just fed him. Watching him was helping me keep calm enough to talk, but I was still crying, and my mother was crying, because she couldn't understand how I could just cut my sister off. I don't think I managed to explain my reasons, or my hurt. And I still feel like my mother thinks it's my fault for not being able to accept that my sister just believes "differently" than I do, and talk to her despite that difference.

In 2014 my mom was diagnosed with breast cancer. She had a double mastectomy and her surgical scars became infected with an antibiotic-resistant bacteria. She went septic and very nearly died. When she was finally able to return home, she still needed full-time medical care that her insurance was unwilling to pay for. They would either pay for hospice care or twice weekly home nurse visits, while she needed several times per day wound care and antibiotic administration through a PICC line. Because she did not want to enter hospice care, I moved back into my parents home for a while to provide the care she needed. It was a very intense time and also kind of awkwardly intimate -- we've never been a very physically affectionate family, we all have fairly large personal space bubbles, and yet I had the responsibility to express the fluids building up in her wounds, clean her wounds, change her wound dressing, etc. It also put her in a position of depending on me for her care and well-being, and me in a position of being responsible for her survival. I don't want to say it was a role reversal, I hadn't been a child for many years by that point, but there was a certain out-of-place feeling associated with the kind of relationship we had to one another during that time. And also fear -- it seemed so likely that she wasn't coming home at all and for too long there was a severe risk of reinfection. I was a grown woman but I had some definite "I just want my mommy" moments while she was still hospitalized. 
 
 It was also very traumatic for her -- I don't mean being cared for was traumatic, I only mean that so severe a medical event and a recovery spread out over a period of months was traumatic. She tells me now that she doesn't remember most of it. She barely remembers me administering her antibiotics, which was a four times per day event over a long period. She doesn't remember me cleaning her wounds which was, again, a twice daily event until she finally recovered enough to do it on her own. So these memories and the feelings associated with them, even though they involved close contact between my mother and myself, are mine alone.

My grandmother died of a terminal cancer. Towards the end of her life. My mother had us visit. At the time, I had no idea that she was in a hospice. My mother had gone to visit weekends prior but as my grandparents lived 5 hours away, I really didn’t want to sit in the car.
 When we visited, I was shocked that she wasn’t at the house. When we visited, my grandmother couldn’t talk and was a deteriorated version of herself. She passed the week after. I felt like I had an extremely strong connection with my grandmother. 
 This emotional distress translated to anger towards my mother for seemingly keeping me in the dark. I still don’t understand why she didn’t explain the situation better. I constantly think if I could have talked to my grandmother one last time, but sadly that isn’t how life works. My mother is spacey and leaves out details; it’s just who she is, but this made me resent her for it.

A memory of my father during my childhood before my parents divorced. It was in our first house in my hometown, my dad had an "office" in the house, a room with his papers and stuff for work. The room had his desk in the middle, with two drawers underneath it on the right side, filled to the brim with office supplies that were carefully organized, the walls had shelves with books, Tom Clancy and Ian Flemming novels, encyclopedias, books on biology and chemistry, and a few knickknacks he'd collected over the years, a tiny wind-up robot, a replica of a James Bond car, model cars, and old hearing aids . Tools and instruments he used for his job as an audiologist lined another shelf along with suitcases and backpacks with patient information and the like.
 
 I was three years old, running around the house with nothing but a diaper on, it was early evening and I noticed my dad was in his office reading a novel at his desk, illuminated by yellow light from a desk lamp. I peered from the open doorway watching him read and waited until he turned the page so I can run up to him and give him a hug. And I did, he was wearing dress pants for work and still had his penny loafers on, and with his signature sleeveless undershirt. But after a few seconds he merely snapped back "Enough, its too hot today, go back to your room" merely patting my back and not returning the hug. I felt sad and guilty for annoying him as I sulked out of his office, thinking that I must have really angered him if he was capable of denying a hug, which to me was (and still is) something of deep importance; and with a deja vu feeling I realized that this has happened before multiple times, my father saying the same excuse "its too hot today", or "get out of the office", "Don't bother me", not just in his office but when he was just sitting on his armchair watching tv, or eating in the kitchen. And although my father was crass from time to time with us, I knew he never meant us harm and I loved him along my sister just the same.

One night when I was a kid, maybe 20 years ago, I woke up in the middle of the night and I was cold. So cold I couldn't stop shaking. There was no reason for it--my room was warm, my blankets were sufficient, I just couldn't get warm. I knew I wasn't supposed to wake up my mom in the middle of the night unless it was really important, and I didn't feel like it was important, but I also couldn't function. So, hesitantly, I got out of bed and knocked softly on her bedroom door and when she answered I told her I couldn't stop shaking and I didn't know why. She left the door for a second, put on her terrycloth robe, then came with me back to my room and she crawled into bed with me. She spooned me from behind and held me tight and eventually, little by little, I stopped shaking. I remember feeling so exhausted, both emotionally and physically. I'd never before felt like that. But I also felt really loved, like I knew my mom would do anything for me. I miss cuddling with her, like I did when I was a kid. After I stopped shaking for good, she tucked me back in and went back to bed. She smelled like skin and lotion, and I slept well for the rest of the night.

A very vivid memory I used to think about often was when I became separated from my parents at a theme park, I was maybe three at the time. Me and my sister, who was older than me, were left to play in the kiddy-pool section. She was supposed to keep her eye on me and then we would meet back up with our parents (she knew where to go, but I was too young to be on top of that information). There was a pirate ship in the pool and I followed my sister up to the top of the ship. There were water guns, a bucket that filled with water and tipped it out in a huge torrent periodically, and all sorts of fun things that we were amusing ourselves with. Then my sister said we should go down the slide. I remember at that age I was scared to go down plastic slides because I always used to get static shocks when I would go down them at play places. She went right down the slide but I hesitated for a few moments. Finally I got up the nerve to go down the slide and when I got to the bottom I couldn't find my sister anywhere. The summer of a few years ago, my second-youngest sister was 14, just having finished eighth grade, and kept sneaking out of the house to meet boys--young men, really--she found on Tinder. She'd made a habit of sneaking out during the school year, but that was mostly her tagging along with my then-eighteen-year-old middle sister. Going to parties, joyriding in my mom's car, drinking, things like that. By that summer it had escalated to hooking up with dudes way too old for her. I got a tip from the 18 y/o that the 14 y/o had sneaked out to meet an 18 y/o who thought she was his age, and they were going to hook up.
 
 So I went into my mom's room to tell her. My mom knew she sneaked out, but she did not know whom she was meeting, and when I said what was going on, my mom just said "Okay." Didn't get up, didn't call the police, nothing like that, just said okay. Eventually Faith did come home, and my mom told her she was going to get STDs if she kept doing that, but there was no real discussion, no discipline or punishment or anything.
 
 Faith told her counselor later that week that Mom didn't punish her, and the counselor called CPS, and my mom was infuriated with Faith for lying to the counselor, even though neither I nor Faith thought Faith had lied at all. I tried to bring that viewpoint up later and my mom got mad at me, saying I was pinning the entire incident on her. My mom was seeing things in a completely different way from the rest of us and seemed to legitimately believe that all of this was just happening to her with no ability to stop it even though she totally could have deescalated the situation before it reached that point.

Three years ago, my dad was cutting down a tree -- he's cut down hundreds in his life -- and it fell weird and nearly killed him. He was in the hospital for a month, including a week in ICU.
 
 It was a traumatic time for everyone. My mom was incredibly strong. She stayed a dingy motel next to the city hospital nearly every night for that whole month. I drove from my city (about four hours away) every weekend to help relieve her -- my brothers helped fill in some of the other time based on their work schedules and travel availability.
 
 I remember my first night in the ICU. My mom had gone to sleep and I was in the room. This was a day or two after the initial accident. My dad was still heavily medicated and intubated. A nurse came in frequently, speaking loudly and slowly to try to penetrate my dad's medicated stupor. It was pretty clear at that point my dad would not die, but whether he'd recover was unknown. He wanted to pull the tube out but couldn't, so he was strapped down. It was overwhelming. I remember leaving the ICU at one point and just breaking down in the hallway. I wanted to help so bad, and I was completely powerless.
 
 I recall looking down at my dad's face at some point, seeing his vulnerability and confusion. I felt love for him, pity.
 
 This was my initiation into middle age. A little early (31), but there it was.

I was incredibly depressed most of my younger life, suicidal for quite a few years as well. I did cut when I was younger, always wore hoodies or long sleeve shirts to cover it up, no one really knew because I had no friends and considered myself to have no family either. I had tried talking to my parents about it but got no where with it. One day I was having a really bad day and said screw it and came downstairs with a tshirt on, my cuts all over my arm plain as day. Rather than seeing that it was a problem or seeing I was being serious, I got screamed at grounded etc, and was told to stop doing it and that I was simply doing it for attention. They said they wanted to never hear about it again or see them again. They never did, but I still cut for quite a while and I am still clinically depressed to this day.

I felt pretty vindicated until I told my mom about it and she asked why he waited so long to say sorry in the first point, which was a good point and made me feel like maybe I hadn't won after all.

For a solid few months in to our relationship, I would refuse to say that I loved him, which perturbed him, but he never stopped saying it, because I was wanting to say it, but I was just not able to. Each and every day he would say it, until eventually I relented and said it back, which allowed me to begin to talk about other emotions I had bottled up for years, all of which he supported me through.

I came out as a consequence of a big crush I developed on a gay friend, which finally helped me put it all together. While we never dated (he was in a relationship), I harbored a crush on him for a long time, and we were close friends.
 
 The crush started at friends' wedding (we were mutual friends of both the bride and groom, and were both groomsman). In particularly, he wanted to ask me questions about my faith, knowing I was a devout Christian and few of his friends are.
 
 After the wedding reception (on the bed and breakfast grounds) we ended up going to the pool with a friend of his and then he and I ended up in the hot tub together. Bear in mind I wasn't out -- to him or to myself -- though I imagine he had his guesses. I was at least tipsy from wine being passed around during the dancing. He asked me questions about my faith, which I answered, and all the while I was overcome with this desire to kiss him. I was startled by this; I had never quite had that urge with a particular person before.
 
 The next day, he left his shoes at the venue. I volunteered to take them to him the next week, even though it was well over an hour to get to him (big city). It wasn't yet clear to me this was a crush, I just wanted to be around him. Within a few weeks, I knew.

About two years ago I began the study of a Taoist martial art by the name of Ba Gua Zhang. This was my first time learning it and the teacher showed me a very simple form to get me started. This form involved walking in a circle holding a fairly static upper body posture and occasionally alternating directions. The teacher, demonstrated the form, had me do it, fixed my posture, and then left me uninterrupted to do the form for a very long period of time. After what I later learned was an hour, I began to have the intense sensation of what felt like very warm electric current flowing the my entire body. The teacher then came over and what I asked him what I was experiencing, he told me it was Qi. A form of energy that is present in everyone, but it usually unconscious. I practiced the form for two more hours and I began to feel it more intensely. I consider to be the start of my Qi Gong or subtle energy practice, and I have grown increasingly more aware of my body and my connections to the world around me as a result. This was one of the times when your perception of the world is forever changed by one event.

One of my most prominent memories, which I feel relates most to other memories that I have and to a theme that would perhaps help others to understand who I am today would be when my parents told me that they were going to get divorced. I was eleven and it was the summer I was about to enter into 6th grade. I hadn't seen my dad that much around the house because he often would stay late at work, but on this particular night we had a pretty long family dinner. I think it might have been on the weekend, maybe on a Saturday night, and because it was summer, I think it was still light out. My dad and mom told me that they were planning on getting divorced at the end of dinner, and I didn't really have that clear a conception of what this would mean for me in the long run, looking back on it. We went over to my neighbors house later that evening. They were really good family friends - their family was made up of a mom, dad, and two (fraternal) twin sisters who were two years older than me. When we were going to elementary school together our bus driver thought we were triplets because we'd always share one bus seat and act like sisters. When I told them I wasn't really upset, and I remember the more emotional of the two twins was surprised that I didn't cry when I told her. Later on these friends came over to my house and we played hide-and-go seek in my basement, and my wrist got cut on a nail sticking out of a board that was from construction work we'd done on our house earlier that year. My mom was really upset about it, but I didn't even realize it was cut until I came out of my hiding spot somewhere light where I could see that I was cut, and then it did hurt a little.

I remember a desire to come back to Whitman College, even though it was a place of great sadness for me. I withdrew from Whitman in the Spring of 2006 and vowed never to return. But the four years since, I had been through a number of troubles and I wanted to get my life in order and make something of myself. So, I wanted to go back to school. Originally I didn't think I would ever come back to Whitman; I'd hoped to go to the University of Chicago, though I was worried I wouldn't be accepted. But I had a dream, and in this dream I saw myself content and actually happy to be back at Whitman. This dream troubled me and so I talked to a few close friends about it, and they told me that maybe it was time for me to go back to school. I agreed, but still, the fact that it was at Whitman (of all places) got me to thinking. I came to the conclusion that maybe I needed to look into going back to Whitman. I looked into it and submitted my application for re-admission and luckily it was accepted. I had mixed feelings, but I had learned throughout all of this that I needed to be optimistic. And well, thankfully I interpreted that dream as such because now I can call myself a Whittie!

We were put in the car and taken to a location, where we opened an envelope to reveal a gift certificate to Red Robin. We proceeded to be driven to Coldstone, Old Navy, and another store I don't remember to redeem gift cards in small envelopes with my mom's writing.

This memory is of a day when my mother out of no-where took my brother and I to a shelter. At that age I was young and did not really understand a lot of what was going on. I was very much innocent and confused. The shelter was a great and fun place. This was a time where I just grew and really expanded my own social circle. I was in the car, racing home to be by my computer at 3pm. The admissions letter was supposed to be in then, and I had no idea what to expect. I read my application tens of times, maybe even hundreds. Was I good enough? Did they want me? Was it my destiny? I got home, checked my email: nothing. Really? I waited and paced and panicked and distracted myself and waited more. Finally, at 6pm, the letter came. Thanks for your application, but no thanks. I read it, said to my mom, "I didn't get in." Then it hit me. I sobbed, finally releasing the walls of pressure I had constructed for months. It's over. It's over it's over it's over. It was release, not sorrow. It was finally over.

I sat in the middle of the courtyard, meeting the gaze of interested young men. Who is this white person, I'm sure they all wondered. I was seated next to Leah, a 25-year-old blonde girl from Minnesota. She had a guitar and a Bible. We began singing, quietly at first, courage building. We had a message that we wanted to share. We knew love! We wanted to sing until the entire village gathered around us, singing in Spanish, wondering why we would give up the comforts of the exoticized America to show them why we live, why we have hope. I began singing and beautiful, rhyming words flowed out of my willing lips. It was the harmony of my life, my thoughts, Leah's music, God's words. It was beautiful.

My mom finally came and got me, I felt like such a bad person. I was so stupid at the time to do something like that. I don't know what I was thinking.

The first time I preformed CPR on a real person profoundly affected me, I was in a hospital doing a clinical internship for an EMT Basic class I was taking, and my partner and I received word that there was a code (person in cardiac arrest) in the intensive care unit. We rushed there and being a student I was offered the chance to preform CPR. I eagerly jumped in and began CPR and while we were successful in restoring the patient to a normal state. In the preceding weeks I experienced very intense and recurring dreams of the event. This dreams were so vivid at times that I couldn't sleep because I could still see the white rolled back eyes of the patient as I preformed CPR.

One time I had an episode of cyclical vomiting syndrome (CVS) while I was hiking in the wilderness, CVS involves intense episodes of vomiting for days at a time, and without medical intervention(IV re-hydration) it can be very dangerous. At this point I had been suffering for a day and was beginning to become very dehydrated. I was still 20 miles out and with no way of signaling for outside help. Our only choice was to hike for 20 miles straight in order to get me out. As the day (and night) wore on I began to become even more dehydrated, and by the time we reached the nearest hospital I was close to death. I now know what is meant by the expression "the drive to live" It took me everything I had to get myself through that.

For me doing research at OHSU is and will be a great memory. This is simple but important because it was so much work. I took on a large large research project that included interviewing (and transcribing), observations, and statistical analysis or the on-line survey. Just getting doctors to be on board and patients as well and coordinating the appointment schedule to when i would come in and be an observer. Also, sending several reminder e-mails to the providers in order to complete the project. The challenge for me in particular that i would not forget is the transcribing and open coding in order to identify themes that was done individually and then in a group to come to consensus. We had sticky notes everywhere and they were all over the walls and the meeting was about 4 hours long.

While studying abroad in New Zealand, there wasn't much work to do. However, the final exams at the end of the semester were worth a significant portion of our grade. I had two exams that fell one after the other, and one of them was very detailed and comprehensive. A week before the exam I started studying everyday for the entire day. I would complete one sections a day for one course, and two sections a day for the other course. I have never studied so much before with such intensity for such a prolonged period of time. It really paid off in the end and I ended up learning a lot. Although it felt like cramming at the time, there is course material that still stick with me even till this day.

I pulled on my pink leggings and ran out to the parking lot. For all of the verbal buildup I had for the weekend, I wasn't too excited. He jumped out of the car and my heart did nothing. I had emotional confirmation: it was over. He followed me up to my room, gave me some tacky pink flowers, and wanted to cuddle. Had I ever been this uninterested? Yeah, but I couldn't admit it to myself before. I knew now. I talked to him in the most objective way possible, tried to rationalize continuing, but it wouldn't work. The next day I half-heartedly went to breakfast, climbed in the car, figured that driving away would make the problem go away too. I took him with me, though, so it had to be confronted. We finally decided to break up. I sobbed for 8 hours that day - but again, it was release. It was not sorrow. Sure, I was afraid of what would happen. But I was more excited at the prospect of the future without him, without being tied to my past, without wondering what could have been. Was it mutual? Sure. But my heart had moved on, I was done with complacency. I wanted out.
